## Mushi Mushi — know why your AI-built app broke, with the fix ready

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs

---
title: Mushi Mushi — know why your AI-built app broke, with the fix ready
description: "Your AI shipped it. Mushi tells you why it broke: a plain-English diagnosis and a ready fix in your editor. Open source, Sentry optional."
---

Your AI wrote it. Mushi tells you why it broke.</>}
  lead={LANDING_HERO.lead}
/>

## What it takes

- **No monitoring stack.** No Sentry, no logging service, no AI key of your own. Mushi's AI writes the diagnosis.
- **Free to start.** One app and 100 diagnoses a month with no card. Repeat reports of one bug count once.
- **Your AI does the fix, you approve it.** Mushi hands Cursor, Claude Code or Lovable the prompt. Nothing ships until you say so. If you let an agent open the fix as a pull request, a second AI reads it next to the original report and can refuse it: [here is one it held](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/pull/864).

## What this is (and is not)

Mushi Mushi is the bug mediator for AI-built apps, an open-source tool that gives every bug your users report a plain-English diagnosis + a ready fix, in your editor.

**Who it is for.** {LANDING_WHAT_THIS_IS.who} {LANDING_WHAT_THIS_IS.boundary}

**Where it stands.** Live and free to try: hosted service, npm packages and public source. Built by Kenji Sakuramoto, a solo developer in Japan ([kensaur.us](https://kensaur.us), [X](https://x.com/sakuramotokenji), [GitHub](https://github.com/kensaurus)), who runs it on his own 8 live apps; [the numbers are public](/proof), with bugs his own checks found counted apart from bugs people reported. Native iOS, Android and Flutter libraries are previews.

Words you will see on this page

- **Diagnosis**: Mushi's written explanation of one bug, with how serious it is, the likely cause and a suggested fix.
- **Fix prompt**: the diagnosis plus the evidence, written as instructions you paste into your AI editor.
- **SDK** or **script tag**: the small piece of code you add to your app. It shows the report button and sends reports to Mushi.
- **MCP**: the standard way AI code editors such as Cursor and Claude Code connect to outside tools. It is how your editor reads Mushi's reports.

More: [Who it’s for](/who-its-for) · [What else it does](/what-it-does) · [How a bug moves, step by step](/concepts/closed-loop) ·

## Incident loop: from bug report to fix prompt

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/quickstart/incident-loop

---
title: "Incident loop: from bug report to fix prompt"
description: Run npx mushi-mushi, ship, and let Mushi Mushi turn your first user-reported bug into a plain-English diagnosis and a paste-ready fix for Cursor or Claude Code.
---

# Incident loop

- A user reports a bug in your live app. Mushi explains it in plain English.
- Your editor pulls the diagnosis and a ready fix prompt over MCP.
- Your AI applies the fix; you review and ship. No extra AI key needed.

## No MCP? Copy the fix prompt

Open the report in the console and click **Copy fix prompt** (under **Fix it
with your coding agent**). Paste it into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or Windsurf.

What the fix prompt contains

One self-contained prompt: the diagnosis, the suggested fix, repro steps, page
and browser, the key console lines, likely files, and what "done" means. No MCP
or editor setup is needed. The steps below are the MCP route, which lets the
agent fetch the details and close the report itself.

## Before you start

- A Mushi project and API key ([credentials](/concepts/credentials)).
- At least one report: from the SDK, the test report `npx mushi-mushi` offers, or a Sentry alert.
- MCP connected to your editor ([MCP quickstart](/quickstart/mcp)). The agent needs write access to mark the report fixed. Signing in through the hosted MCP (the default for Cursor and Claude Code) gives it; a key with only `mcp:read` does not.

## The loop

### Capture or pick a report

New project:

```bash
npx mushi-mushi
```

The wizard writes `.env.local` and offers a test report. At the end it offers
to run `mushi connect`: say yes to wire Cursor's MCP config and wait for the
first heartbeat from your app.

Existing report: open **Bugs** in the console and copy its ID, or ask the agent *"list recent mushi reports"*.

**You'll see:** a report ID, and the report in the console with a plain-English title.

### Pull the fix context

In Cursor, ask:

> Use Mushi MCP: call `get_fix_context` for report `` and summarize the root cause in plain English.

`get_fix_context` returns the classification, repro steps, blast radius and a
**`fixPrompt`**: a paste-ready fix brief built on the server. For most bugs you
can paste `fixPrompt` straight into Cursor and skip to the last step.

**You'll see:** the root cause in plain English, and a `fixPrompt` you can paste.

### Get a deeper fix plan (optional)

Run the MCP prompt **`summarize_report_for_fix`** with the same report ID, or ask:

> Run the Mushi prompt `summarize_report_for_fix` for report ``. Give me a paste-ready Cursor prompt to fix it.

It combines `get_fix_context`, `get_blast_radius` and `get_similar_bugs` into one plan.

### Paste and ship

Paste the agent's output into a Cursor chat (or keep going in the same thread)
and ask it to implement the fix. When GitHub is connected and **Automatic
fixes** is on (console → **Integrations**), `dispatch_fix` can open a draft PR
instead.

**You'll see:** the code change in your editor, ready to review and commit.

## MCP server for bug fixing in Cursor & Claude Code

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/quickstart/mcp

---
title: MCP server for bug fixing in Cursor & Claude Code
description: Set up the Mushi Mushi MCP server with npx mushi-mushi setup. Read bug reports, get fix context, and dispatch fixes from Cursor, Claude Code or any MCP client.
---

# MCP server

- MCP is how your AI editor (Cursor, Claude Code, VS Code) talks to Mushi.
- Add the server in one click, sign in once in your browser. No key to paste.
- Then ask your editor about bugs: it gets the report, the diagnosis and a fix brief.

## Connect in three steps

### Add the Mushi server

One click: pick your editor on the [Connect page](https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/connect).
No signup needed for the read-only demo. Or run one command:

```bash
# Claude Code
claude mcp add --transport http mushi "https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/hosted-mcp/"

# Cursor (writes .cursor/mcp.json)
npx mushi-mushi setup --ide cursor
```

### Sign in

The first time your editor calls Mushi, your browser opens. Sign in, pick which
projects it may see, and click **Approve**. In Claude Code, run `claude mcp login mushi`
(or `/mcp`) to start it.

**You'll see:** Mushi listed as connected in your editor's MCP settings.

### Ask your editor

Try *"list mushi tools"*, then *"Get the latest Mushi report and fix it."*

**You'll see:** the Mushi tools in the list, then a fix brief: the cause, the files to change and how to check it.

The rest of this page is detail: how sign-in works, manual config files,
the hosted transport for headless agents, and the tool list.

## How sign-in works (OAuth, no keys to copy)

The hosted MCP endpoint speaks the standard MCP OAuth flow (authorization
code + PKCE), so clients that support MCP login connect with **zero manual
credentials**:

```bash
# Claude Code
claude mcp add --transport http mushi "https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/hosted-mcp/"
claude mcp login mushi   # or run /mcp inside a session and pick "mushi"
```

Your browser opens the console consent page. Sign in, choose what the
connection reaches, and click **Approve**:

| Choice | What the client gets | Revoke it from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **All my projects** (default with several projects) | An account key that reaches every project you can reach, now and later | **Editor agents → Account keys** |
| **Only the projects I pick** | An account key limited to the ticked projects | **Editor agents → Account keys** |
| **One project** | A project key (label `mcp-oauth`); needs owner or admin | **Manage apps** (the app's key list) |

- An account key does in each project only what your role there allows. The
  agent calls `list_projects` and passes `projectId` to project tools.
- To keep one connection on a single project, add `?project=<project-id>` to the
  server URL, for example `https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/hosted-mcp/?project=<project-id>`.
- A pinned connection, or one limited to picked projects, leaves out the
  organization-wide tools (portfolio, connectors, spend, accounts register).
- Cursor and VS Code follow the same flow when you add the hosted URL as a
  remote MCP server. Do **not** set an `Authorization` header if you want the
  login flow: a static header tells the client that OAuth isn't needed.

Use the `kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/hosted-mcp/` URL for the login flow. Clients
look for the OAuth metadata at the root of the server's host
(`/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/…`), and only that host serves it; on
the `supabase.co` URL the lookup fails with an HTTP 404. With an API key
header (below), either URL works.

Self-hosted on your own `.supabase.co`? Point Claude Code at the
function's own metadata document with its `authServerMetadataUrl` override
(`npx mushi-mushi setup --ide claude` writes this for you):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mushi": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://<ref>.supabase.co/functions/v1/mcp",
      "oauth": {
        "authServerMetadataUrl": "https://<ref>.supabase.co/functions/v1/mcp/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## One-liner setup (recommended)

```bash
npx mushi-mushi setup --ide cursor
# or: npx mushi-mushi setup --ide claude
```

For Cursor and Claude Code this writes the **hosted MCP URL with OAuth login**
by default. No API key lands in your repo, the entry is safe to commit and
share with your team, and each teammate signs in from the IDE on first use.
Pass `--stdio` (or `--ci` in headless environments) for the previous local
subprocess entry with a key.

It reads CLI config at **`~/.config/mushi/config.json`**, or **`%APPDATA%\mushi\config.json`** on Windows ([full order](/sdks/cli#config-file); written by `mushi login`; legacy `~/.mushirc` auto-migrates on first load), detects the IDE config path, and writes the `mcpServers` block for you. Restart the IDE and ask the agent: **"list mushi tools"**.

## Claude Code plugin

One command installs the hosted MCP hookup plus a `mushi-debugger` subagent
(report triage → fix context → implement → close the loop):

```
/plugin marketplace add kensaurus/mushi-mushi
/plugin install mushi-debugger@mushi-mushi
```

Then: `/mcp` → pick `mushi` → sign in via the browser. Ask Claude to
"use mushi-debugger to fix the top report".

## Smithery (hosted MCP)

Install from the [Smithery registry](https://smithery.ai/servers/kensaurus/mushi-mushi) with
Streamable HTTP at `https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/hosted-mcp/`. The server card at
`https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/hosted-mcp/.well-known/mcp/server-card.json`
lists every tool for directory scanners.

  Run `npx mushi-mushi project create` on a brand-new machine to sign up,
  mint a project, and write `.env.local` + `.cursor/mcp.json` in one flow.

## Manual setup: Cursor

Add to `.cursor/mcp.json` in your repo root:

```json filename=".cursor/mcp.json"
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mushi": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@mushi-mushi/mcp@0.30.0"],
      "env": {
        "MUSHI_API_ENDPOINT": "https://<your-ref>.supabase.co/functions/v1/api",
        "MUSHI_PROJECT_ID": "YOUR_PROJECT_ID",
        "MUSHI_API_KEY": "mushi_..."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

  
    Mint a key on **Manage apps → Generate API key** (preset **MCP read-only** or
    **MCP read + write**), or use **Connect → Add to Cursor**. The card that shows
    a new key once also offers a ready-made `.cursor/mcp.json` snippet.
  

## Manual setup: Claude Desktop

Add to `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`
(macOS) or `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json` (Windows):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mushi": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@mushi-mushi/mcp@0.30.0"],
      "env": {
        "MUSHI_API_ENDPOINT": "https://<your-ref>.supabase.co/functions/v1/api",
        "MUSHI_PROJECT_ID": "YOUR_PROJECT_ID",
        "MUSHI_API_KEY": "mushi_..."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## Hosted Streamable HTTP transport (no subprocess)

Skip the local subprocess: use the hosted MCP endpoint when you're
running OpenAI Agents SDK, ChatGPT Agent, CrewAI, or any remote orchestrator.
Headless orchestrators can't drive the browser OAuth flow, so this is the
one place a static API key header is the right tool:

```json filename=".cursor/mcp.json"
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mushi-hosted": {
      "url": "https://dxptnwrhwsqckaftyymj.supabase.co/functions/v1/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "X-Mushi-Api-Key": "mushi_…",
        "X-Mushi-Project-Id": "YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## Available tools

| Tool                    | Purpose                                      |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| `get_recent_reports`    | Filter by status, severity, component        |
| `get_report_detail`     | Full detail incl. screenshot + classification |
| `get_fix_context`       | One-shot fix brief: root cause, blast radius, repro and a paste-ready `fixPrompt` |
| `search_reports`        | Semantic + keyword search across reports     |
| `dispatch_fix`          | Start the Mushi fix agent for a report (needs GitHub connected and Automatic fixes on) |
| `triage_next_steps`     | "What should I fix next?": a prioritised list of next actions |
| `get_similar_bugs`      | Ask "have we seen this before?" (similar reports) |
| `run_nl_query`          | Natural-language → SQL questions about your data |

  The MCP server speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 with `tools/call` semantics, and the
  agent surface is also discoverable via the
  [A2A Agent Card](/concepts/architecture#a2a-agent-card) at
  `/.well-known/agent-card.json` on the API.

## Cursor rules hook (optional)

After setup, run:

```bash
npx mushi-mushi setup --ide cursor --with-rules
```

This writes a `.cursorrules` file that tells Cursor to call `get_fix_context`
before writing a fix and `submit_fix_result` after, closing the loop from
inside the editor. Download the template:
[cursor.cursorrules](/integrations/cursor.cursorrules)

## Smithery registry

Hosted Streamable HTTP endpoint: `https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/hosted-mcp/`

Install from the [Smithery server page](https://smithery.ai/servers/kensaurus/mushi-mushi).
Tool metadata is also published at `https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/hosted-mcp/.well-known/mcp/server-card.json` for directory scanners.

## Quickstart: install, first report, first fix

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/quickstart

---
title: "Quickstart: install, first report, first fix"
description: Install Mushi Mushi with npx mushi-mushi, connect Cursor or Claude Code over MCP, and turn user bug reports into plain-English diagnoses with ready fixes.
---

# Quickstart

- One command, `npx mushi-mushi`, adds a report button to your app.
- When a user reports a bug, Mushi Mushi writes a plain-English diagnosis.
- Your AI editor reads it and writes the fix.

### Install

Run this in your app's folder. It finds your framework, signs you in through
your browser, installs the SDK and writes your settings to `.env.local`.

```bash
npx mushi-mushi
```

**You'll see:** a report button in your app, and a new project in the [console](https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/admin).

### Send your first report

Tap the report button in your app and write one sentence. Or say yes when the
wizard offers to send a test report.

**You'll see:** the report in the console with a title, severity and likely cause, in about 10 seconds.

### Get your first fix

Connect your AI editor. One click on the [Connect page](https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/connect), or:

```bash
npx mushi-mushi setup --ide cursor
```

Then ask your editor: *"Get the latest Mushi report and fix it."*

**You'll see:** a fix brief in your editor: the cause, the files to change and how to check it. You review the change before it ships.

## Pick your framework

The wizard detects your framework for you. Pick yours to see what it installs
and the one line it adds to your code.

- **No terminal (Lovable, Bolt):** [Mushi in Lovable or Bolt](/quickstart/lovable-bolt), one script tag pasted through your prompt.
- **Mobile previews:** [iOS](/quickstart/ios) · [Android](/quickstart/android) · [Flutter](/quickstart/flutter), installed from the GitHub repo.
- **Go deeper:** [Incident loop](/quickstart/incident-loop) · [MCP server](/quickstart/mcp) · [CLI console loop](/quickstart/cli-console-loop)

What you need first

- An app you are building, for the web or for phones.
- A Mushi account. The free plan is enough, and the wizard signs you in through your browser.
- Optional: an AI code editor such as Cursor or Claude Code.

`npx` runs a tool from npm (the public library of JavaScript packages) without
installing it for good. Here it runs the Mushi setup wizard.

## Where to start

## Keys and settings

Setting it up yourself? See [Project ID & API keys](/concepts/credentials) for the setting names each framework expects.

  The SDK needs only two settings: your project ID and API key, named with the
  prefix your framework expects (see
  [`examples/sdk.env.example`](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/blob/master/examples/sdk.env.example)).
  The repo's root `.env.example` is only for **running the Mushi server
  yourself**. You do not need Supabase or an AI (LLM) key to use the SDK.

## Troubleshooting

## Android (Kotlin) quickstart

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/quickstart/android

---
title: Android (Kotlin) quickstart
description: Try the Mushi Mushi Kotlin SDK on Android. Shake-to-report, a bottom-sheet widget and an offline queue; a preview built from source, not on Maven Central.
---

# Android quickstart

`dev.mushimushi:mushi-android` ships shake detection (via `SensorManager`), a
bottom-sheet capture UI, a file-backed offline queue, rage-tap and slow-screen
detection, and an optional Sentry bridge.

  **Preview, not on Maven Central yet.** A `dependencies { implementation(…) }`
  line alone will not resolve until the first release is published. Until then,
  build the library from the repository and consume it from your local Maven
  repository, as below. `npx mushi-mushi` does not set up native Android projects.

## Build from source

The library lives in [`packages/android`](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/tree/master/packages/android)
and has no Gradle wrapper checked in. CI builds it with Gradle 8.9 and JDK 17;
use the same versions, plus the Android SDK.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi.git
cd mushi-mushi/packages/android
gradle publishToMavenLocal
```

Then add `mavenLocal()` to your app's repositories and depend on the version
from `packages/android/build.gradle.kts`:

```kotlin filename="settings.gradle.kts"
dependencyResolutionManagement {
  repositories {
    google()
    mavenCentral()
    mavenLocal() // preview build of dev.mushimushi:mushi-android
  }
}
```

```kotlin filename="app/build.gradle.kts"
dependencies {
  implementation("dev.mushimushi:mushi-android:0.4.0")
}
```

CI only runs `gradle assembleRelease` on this module, so the local publish is
the less-travelled path. If it fails for you, `gradle assembleRelease` builds
`build/outputs/aar/mushi-android-release.aar`; add that file as a dependency
together with the libraries it needs (`androidx.core:core-ktx`,
`androidx.appcompat:appcompat`, `androidx.fragment:fragment-ktx`,
`com.squareup.okhttp3:okhttp`, `com.google.code.gson:gson`).

## Initialize

`endpoint` is required: use the hosted API below, or your own if you self-host.

```kotlin filename="app/src/main/java/com/example/App.kt"
import android.app.Application
import dev.mushimushi.sdk.Mushi
import dev.mushimushi.sdk.config.MushiConfig
import dev.mushimushi.sdk.config.TriggerMode

class App : Application() {
  override fun onCreate() {
    super.onCreate()
    Mushi.init(this, MushiConfig(
      projectId = "YOUR_PROJECT_ID",
      apiKey = "mushi_...",
      endpoint = "https://dxptnwrhwsqckaftyymj.supabase.co/functions/v1/api",
      triggerMode = TriggerMode.BOTH, // SHAKE | BUTTON | BOTH | NONE
    ))
  }
}
```

```xml filename="AndroidManifest.xml"
<application
  android:name=".App"
  ...>
  <!-- ... -->
</application>
```

## Open the widget or submit a report

The bottom sheet needs the current activity to be a `FragmentActivity`
(for example `AppCompatActivity`).

```kotlin
// Present the bottom-sheet widget
button.setOnClickListener { Mushi.showWidget() }

// File a report from code, no UI
Mushi.report(
  description = "Search results sometimes appear twice.",
  category = "bug",
)

// Forward a caught error
try { riskyOperation() } catch (t: Throwable) { Mushi.captureError(t) }
```

## Sentry bridge (optional)

With `io.sentry:sentry-android` on the classpath, call
`MushiSentryBridge.install()` (from `dev.mushimushi.sdk.sentry`) after
initialising Sentry. It resolves Sentry by reflection and does nothing when
Sentry is absent.

Full API: [`dev.mushimushi:mushi-android`](/sdks/android).

## Angular quickstart

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/quickstart/angular

---
title: Angular quickstart
description: "Add Mushi Mushi to an Angular 17+ app: one provideMushi() call registers the service and error handler, so uncaught errors and bug reports reach your queue."
---

# Angular quickstart

Same steps as the [React quickstart](/quickstart/react); only the install and the boot call differ.

```bash
pnpm add @mushi-mushi/angular
```

Angular CLI does not expose `import.meta.env`, so keep the project ID and the
public API key in an environment file (`ng generate environments` creates one):

```ts filename="src/environments/environment.ts"
export const environment = {
  mushiProjectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
  mushiApiKey: 'mushi_...', // public report:write key, safe to ship in the bundle
}
```

Register Mushi once in your app config. `provideMushi()` provides
`MushiService`, routes uncaught errors to Mushi through Angular's
`ErrorHandler`, and starts the SDK at startup:

```ts filename="src/app/app.config.ts"
import { type ApplicationConfig } from '@angular/core'
import { provideMushi } from '@mushi-mushi/angular'
import { environment } from '../environments/environment'

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideMushi({ projectId: environment.mushiProjectId, apiKey: environment.mushiApiKey }),
  ],
}
```

  **1.0.2 and earlier:** `provideMushi()` did not return Angular providers,
  and the package needed the JIT compiler in production builds. Upgrade to
  1.0.3 or later. If you cannot, register the providers by hand:

  ```ts snippet-skip="1.0.2 fallback; the same file as the example above"
  import { ErrorHandler, type ApplicationConfig } from '@angular/core'
  import { MUSHI_CONFIG, MushiErrorHandler, MushiService, type MushiConfig } from '@mushi-mushi/angular'
  import { environment } from '../environments/environment'

  const mushiConfig: MushiConfig = {
    projectId: environment.mushiProjectId,
    apiKey: environment.mushiApiKey,
  }

  export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
    providers: [
      { provide: MUSHI_CONFIG, useValue: mushiConfig },
      { provide: MushiService, useFactory: (config: MushiConfig) => new MushiService(config), deps: [MUSHI_CONFIG] },
      { provide: ErrorHandler, useFactory: (mushi: MushiService) => new MushiErrorHandler(mushi), deps: [MushiService] },
    ],
  }
  ```

Report from a component:

```ts filename="src/app/feedback-button.component.ts"
import { Component, inject } from '@angular/core'
import { MushiService } from '@mushi-mushi/angular'

@Component({
  selector: 'app-feedback-button',
  template: '<button type="button" (click)="reportIssue()">Report a bug</button>',
})
export class FeedbackButtonComponent {
  private readonly mushi = inject(MushiService)

  async reportIssue() {
    await this.mushi.report({ description: 'Something feels off on this page', category: 'bug' })
  }
}
```

API detail: [`@mushi-mushi/angular`](/sdks/angular). Widget behavior: [`@mushi-mushi/web`](/sdks/web).

## Capacitor quickstart

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/quickstart/capacitor

---
title: Capacitor quickstart
description: Add Mushi Mushi to an Ionic or Capacitor app. Install @mushi-mushi/capacitor, set up shake-to-report and screenshots, and file your first bug report.
---

# Capacitor quickstart

Ship the same bug-report widget on iOS, Android, and web from one Capacitor shell.

The Capacitor plugin delegates to the native iOS / Android SDKs at runtime
and falls back to `@mushi-mushi/core` on the web.

## 1. Install

```bash
pnpm add @mushi-mushi/capacitor
npx cap sync
```

## 2. Configure

```ts filename="src/mushi.ts"
import { Mushi } from '@mushi-mushi/capacitor'

await Mushi.configure({
  projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
  apiKey:    'YOUR_PUBLIC_API_KEY',
  triggerMode: 'shake',          // 'shake' | 'button' | 'both' | 'none'
  captureScreenshot: true,
})
```

## 3. Submit a report

```ts
await Mushi.report({
  description: 'Date picker is in UTC, not local',
  category:    'bug',
})
```

  **Coming from Cordova?** Migrate in place to Capacitor first. The
  [Cordova → Capacitor migration guide](/migrations/cordova-to-capacitor)
  walks through the plugin map and the Mushi widget swap.

  Considering React Native? See the
  [Capacitor → React Native migration guide](/migrations/capacitor-to-react-native)
  for the full porting plan, plugin map, and CI/CD recipe.

See [`@mushi-mushi/capacitor`](/sdks/capacitor) for the full API surface
(listeners, `setUser`, `setMetadata`, `triggerInset`, `useNativeWidget`).

---

## CLI ↔ console setup loop

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/quickstart/cli-console-loop

---
title: CLI ↔ console setup loop
description: How npx mushi-mushi creates a Mushi Mushi project, mints an SDK key and installs the SDK through browser sign-in, and how to recover when the setup loop fails.
---

# CLI ↔ console setup loop

- `npx mushi-mushi` does the whole setup: sign-in, project, API key and SDK install.
- You never paste a key. You click **Approve** in the browser and the terminal carries on.
- Something stuck? See [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) and the manual fallback below.

## Set up in five steps

### 1. Run the wizard

```bash
npx mushi-mushi
```

The wizard auto-detects your framework (Next.js, React, Vue, Expo, …).

**You'll see:** a box with a verification code, and a browser tab opening.

### 2. Approve in the browser

A browser tab opens at `/cli-auth?code=XXXX-XXXX`. Click **Approve CLI connection**.
The browser waits until your terminal claims the token, then shows connected.
Nothing to copy or paste.

**You'll see:** "CLI connected!" and "Switch back to your terminal now" in the browser.

### 3. Pick or create a project

The wizard lists your existing projects. Choose one or enter a name to create a
new project. The SDK API key is minted automatically.

### 4. SDK installed

The wizard installs the SDK package and writes the project ID and the SDK key
to `.env.local` (or `.env` if that is the file you have), named with your
framework's prefix: for example `VITE_MUSHI_PROJECT_ID` and
`VITE_MUSHI_API_KEY`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_MUSHI_…` on Next.js, `EXPO_PUBLIC_MUSHI_…`
on Expo. It adds `MUSHI_API_ENDPOINT` only when you point it at a self-hosted
server.

**You'll see:** a next-steps checklist in the terminal, and the Mushi settings in `.env.local`.

### 5. Wire Cursor MCP (optional but recommended)

At the end the wizard asks whether to run `mushi connect --write-env
--wire-ide --wait` now. Say yes. It writes `.cursor/mcp.json` and waits for the
first SDK heartbeat to confirm the connection is live.

To run it later by hand, pass the key, project ID and endpoint yourself
(`mushi connect` does not read them from the saved login):

```bash
MUSHI_API_KEY=mushi_xxx npx mushi-mushi connect \
  --project-id <uuid> \
  --endpoint https://dxptnwrhwsqckaftyymj.supabase.co/functions/v1/api \
  --wait
```

**You'll see:** the first heartbeat confirmed in the terminal once your app runs with the SDK.

The rest of this page explains each command, how sign-in works, and how to
recover when it fails.

## Which CLI command?

The bare `mushi …` form needs the CLI installed (`npm i -g @mushi-mushi/cli`).
Without it, run the same command as `npx mushi-mushi …`, for example
`npx mushi-mushi login`.

| Command | When to use | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`npx mushi-mushi`** / **`mushi init`** | First SDK install in an app repo | Detects framework, opens browser auth, installs SDK, writes `.env.local` |
| **`mushi login`** | Authenticate the CLI without installing | Browser sign-in only; persists to the [CLI config file](/sdks/cli#config-file) (`~/.config/mushi/config.json`, or `%APPDATA%\mushi\config.json` on Windows) |
| **`mushi connect`** | You already have credentials; want env + MCP + proof | Merges env vars, wires `.cursor/mcp.json`, optional `--wait` heartbeat |
| **`mushi setup`** | MCP-only wiring | Writes Cursor/Claude MCP config (signs you in first if needed); **does not** install the SDK |

  `mushi setup` is for MCP wiring only, not SDK installation. To install
  the SDK for the first time, run `npx mushi-mushi` (not `mushi setup`).

  **SDK ingest keys** (`report:write` scope) come from **Set up → Test it** or
  **Manage apps** in the console. **Settings → AI keys** is for your own
  LLM and Firecrawl keys, not Mushi project credentials.

## Browser sign-in flow (recommended)

`npx mushi-mushi` uses browser sign-in (no paste) via RFC 8628:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Dev as Developer
  participant CLI as npx_mushi_mushi
  participant Browser as Admin_console
  participant App as App_repo

  Dev->>CLI: npx mushi-mushi
  CLI->>CLI: Detect framework
  CLI->>Browser: Open /cli-auth?code=XXXX-XXXX
  CLI->>Dev: Show anti-paste banner and wait
  Dev->>Browser: Click "Approve CLI connection"
  Browser->>CLI: Token arrives automatically
  CLI->>Dev: Approved — pick or create a project
  CLI->>App: Install SDK + write .env.local
  CLI->>Dev: Next steps checklist
```

### What happens in the terminal

When the wizard starts the browser sign-in step, you will see a box like this:

```
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Browser sign-in — follow these 3 steps                  │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │                                                          │
  │  1. A browser tab will open (or visit the URL below)    │
  │  2. Sign in if prompted, then click "Approve"           │
  │  3. Come back here — setup continues automatically      │
  │                                                          │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Verification code (show in browser — NOT terminal):    │
  │                                                          │
  │    TGKX-PBXP                                            │
  │                                                          │
  │  ⚠  Do NOT paste or type this code in your terminal     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  If the browser didn't open, visit this URL and approve:
    https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/admin/cli-auth?code=TGKX-PBXP

  ⏳ Waiting for browser approval… (Ctrl+C to cancel)
```

**The terminal waits automatically.** You do not need to type or paste anything.
Switch to your browser, approve, then come back to this terminal.

### What happens in the browser

The console shows a 3-step guide and displays the same code:

1. Confirm the code matches what your terminal printed
2. Click **Approve CLI connection**
3. Switch back to your terminal; setup resumes automatically

After you click **Approve**, the browser shows a **waiting** state while the CLI
claims the token. When the terminal picks it up, the page switches to **"CLI
connected!"** with **"Switch back to your terminal now"**, and the terminal
continues to the project picker.

## How sign-in reliability works

Each machine gets a stable `client_id`, stored in the [CLI config file](/sdks/cli#config-file)
(`~/.config/mushi/config.json`, or `%APPDATA%\mushi\config.json` on Windows).
The CLI sends it when starting device auth so concurrent logins on the same
machine behave predictably.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant CLI as CLI
  participant API as API
  participant Browser as Browser

  CLI->>API: POST /device/start with client_id
  CLI->>Browser: Open /cli-auth
  Browser->>API: POST /device/approve
  loop CLI polls
    CLI->>API: POST /device/token
  end
  loop Browser polls until claimed
    Browser->>API: GET /device/status
  end
  Browser->>Browser: Show connected
  CLI->>CLI: Resume wizard
```

**Concurrent logins:** Starting a new `mushi login` or `npx mushi-mushi` on the
same machine supersedes any older pending approval for that `client_id`. If you
have two terminals waiting, only the newest poll wins. Close the stale one and
run the wizard again.

**Re-running the wizard:** If credentials are already saved, the CLI validates
them with `GET /v1/sync/whoami` before reinstalling anything.

## Console URLs

| Environment | Admin console | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Hosted (production)** | [kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/admin](https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/admin) | Default for external apps |
| **Local monorepo dev** | [http://localhost:6464](http://localhost:6464) | Run `pnpm dev` from the mushi-mushi repo |
| **Override** | Set `MUSHI_CONSOLE_URL` | CLI hints + browser opens use this base when set |

The CLI resolves the console in this order: `MUSHI_CONSOLE_URL` → `consoleUrl`
saved in the [CLI config file](/sdks/cli#config-file) (`~/.config/mushi/config.json`,
or `%APPDATA%\mushi\config.json` on Windows) → localhost `:6464` probe → hosted default.

## Manual paste (fallback / self-hosted)

If the browser auth path isn't available, select "Paste a Project ID + API key"
in the wizard, or pass flags directly:

```bash
npx mushi-mushi init --project-id <uuid> --api-key mushi_xxx
```

To get the values manually:

| Value | Where to find it |
|---|---|
| `projectId` | The app's UUID on [Manage apps](https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/admin/projects), or on the success panel shown after you create a project |
| `apiKey` | [Set up → Test it](https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/admin/onboarding?tab=verify) → **Generate API key**, or **Manage apps → Generate API key** with the **SDK ingest** preset (scope: `report:write`) |

  **Settings → AI keys** is for your own LLM and Firecrawl keys, not SDK ingest
  keys. Make `report:write` project keys on **Set up → Test it** or **Manage apps**.

## CI / non-interactive

Pass all three flags so the wizard skips all interactive prompts:

```bash
npx mushi-mushi --yes --project-id <uuid> --api-key mushi_xxx
```

Or use the non-interactive connect command after minting a key in the console:

```bash
MUSHI_API_KEY=mushi_xxx npx mushi-mushi connect \
  --project-id <uuid> \
  --endpoint https://dxptnwrhwsqckaftyymj.supabase.co/functions/v1/api \
  --write-env --wire-ide
```

`connect` writes a key to `.env.local` only when the server confirms it is
ingest-only (`report:write`). A key that can read reports still works for the
CLI and MCP; pass the ingest key separately with `MUSHI_SDK_KEY` or `--sdk-key`.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `command not found: TGKX-PBXP` | You pasted the verification code into the shell | That code belongs in the **browser**, not the terminal. The terminal waits automatically. |
| Terminal exits immediately after showing code | Browser tab didn't open; terminal was closed | Keep the terminal open. Open the URL from the banner manually if the tab didn't open. |
| "Wizard opens wrong console URL" | Hosted default while you meant local dev | Run `pnpm dev`, or set `MUSHI_CONSOLE_URL=http://localhost:6464` |
| "Invalid project ID" | Pasted name instead of UUID | Copy the app's UUID from **Manage apps** |
| 401 / whoami failure | Wrong key or revoked key | Mint a new key on [Set up → Test it](https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/admin/onboarding?tab=verify) |
| "Browser sign-in timed out" | 10-minute code expired before approval | Run `npx mushi-mushi` again; a new code is generated |
| `--write-env` unknown or ignored | An older global CLI | Upgrade: `npm i -g @mushi-mushi/cli@latest`, or use `npx mushi-mushi connect` |
| Non-interactive hang in CI | TTY prompts with partial flags | Pass `--yes --project-id  --api-key mushi_xxx` |
| Browser says connected, terminal still waiting | Stale browser tab, wrong terminal window, or superseded poll from a second login | Close old `/cli-auth` tabs. Use the terminal that started the most recent `npx mushi-mushi`. Run the wizard again if needed. |
| Browser stuck on "waiting" after Approve | CLI has not claimed the token yet (slow network) or terminal was closed | Keep the terminal open. After ~45s the browser shows stale-tab help. |
| Terminal still waiting after browser connected | Token poll hit a different `device_code` than the open browser tab | Run `npx mushi-mushi` again in the terminal you want to use. Approve in the fresh browser tab only. |
| `429 Too Many Requests` during token poll | Rate limit on `/device/token` | The CLI retries automatically. Wait a few seconds; do not click Approve again. |
| `408 Request Timeout` during token poll | Transient network blip | The CLI retries automatically. If it persists, check firewall/proxy rules. |

## Flutter quickstart

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/quickstart/flutter

---
title: Flutter quickstart
description: Add the Mushi Mushi Flutter SDK as a git dependency. Shake-to-report, a Material bottom sheet and an offline queue for iOS and Android. Not on pub.dev yet.
---

# Flutter quickstart

  **Preview, not on pub.dev yet.** A plain version constraint for `mushi_mushi`
  will not resolve until the package is published. Until then, depend on it straight from the
  repository with a `git:` dependency, as below. `npx mushi-mushi` does not set
  up Flutter projects.

## Install

```yaml filename="pubspec.yaml"
dependencies:
  mushi_mushi:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi.git
      path: packages/flutter
      ref: master
```

Then run `flutter pub get`. Pin `ref:` to a commit SHA if you want repeatable builds.

## Initialize

`endpoint` is required: use the hosted API below, or your own if you self-host.

```dart filename="lib/main.dart"
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:mushi_mushi/mushi_mushi.dart';

final mushiBoundary = GlobalKey();

void main() {
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();
  Mushi.instance.configure(const MushiConfig(
    projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
    apiKey: 'mushi_...',
    endpoint: 'https://dxptnwrhwsqckaftyymj.supabase.co/functions/v1/api',
    triggerMode: MushiTriggerMode.shake, // shake | button | both | none
  ));
  runApp(const MyApp());
}

class MyApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const MyApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // Screenshots are captured from this boundary.
    Mushi.instance.screenshotBoundaryKey = mushiBoundary;
    return MaterialApp(
      builder: (ctx, child) {
        Mushi.instance.rootContext = ctx;
        return RepaintBoundary(key: mushiBoundary, child: child);
      },
      home: const HomeScreen(),
    );
  }
}
```

## Open the widget or submit a report

```dart
// Present the bottom sheet from any screen
ElevatedButton(
  onPressed: () => Mushi.instance.showWidget(context),
  child: const Text('Report a bug'),
);

// File a report from code, no UI
await Mushi.instance.report(
  description: 'Bottom nav cuts off on iPhone SE',
  category: 'bug',
);

// Forward a caught error
try {
  await riskyCall();
} catch (e, st) {
  await Mushi.instance.captureError(e, st);
}
```

Full API: [`mushi_mushi` (Flutter)](/sdks/flutter).

## iOS (Swift) quickstart

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/quickstart/ios

---
title: iOS (Swift) quickstart
description: Add the Mushi Mushi Swift SDK to an iOS app with Swift Package Manager. Shake-to-report, offline queue and device context. A preview, not on CocoaPods yet.
---

# iOS quickstart

The `MushiMushi` Swift package ships shake-to-report, a file-backed offline
queue, automatic device context, a breadcrumb ring buffer and PII scrubbing.

  **Preview.** The Swift SDK is not published to CocoaPods and has no release
  tag yet, so a version rule like `from: "0.4.0"` cannot resolve. Install it
  from the repository's `master` branch as shown below. `npx mushi-mushi` does
  not set up native iOS projects.

## Install (Swift Package Manager)

In Xcode → **File → Add Package Dependencies**, enter the URL below and set the
dependency rule to **Branch → `master`**, then add the `MushiMushi` library to
your app target.

```
https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi
```

Or in a `Package.swift`:

```swift filename="Package.swift"
dependencies: [
  .package(url: "https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi.git", branch: "master"),
],
targets: [
  .target(name: "MyApp", dependencies: [
    .product(name: "MushiMushi", package: "mushi-mushi"),
  ]),
]
```

SwiftPM clones the whole monorepo the first time, so the initial resolve is
slower than a single-package repo. CocoaPods is not supported yet.

## Initialize

`endpoint` is required: use the hosted API below, or your own if you self-host.

```swift filename="MyApp.swift"
import SwiftUI
import MushiMushi

@main
struct MyApp: App {
  init() {
    Mushi.shared.configure(with: MushiConfig(
      projectId: "YOUR_PROJECT_ID",
      apiKey: "mushi_...",
      endpoint: "https://dxptnwrhwsqckaftyymj.supabase.co/functions/v1/api",
      triggerMode: .both // .shake | .button | .both | .none
    ))
  }

  var body: some Scene {
    WindowGroup { ContentView() }
  }
}
```

## Open the widget or submit a report

```swift
// Present the bottom-sheet widget
Button("Report a bug") { Mushi.shared.showWidget() }

// File a report from code, no UI
Mushi.shared.report(
  description: "Pull-to-refresh spinner never stops on Wi-Fi switch.",
  category: "bug"
)

// Forward a caught error
do { try riskyOperation() } catch { Mushi.shared.captureError(error) }
```

## Sentry

The Swift package has no Sentry bridge. Keep initialising Sentry in your app
and attach context to Mushi reports with `Mushi.shared.setMetadata(_:value:)`.

Full API: [`MushiMushi` (iOS)](/sdks/ios).

## Lovable or Bolt quickstart (no terminal)

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/quickstart/lovable-bolt

---
title: Lovable or Bolt quickstart (no terminal)
description: Add Mushi Mushi to a Lovable or Bolt app without a terminal. Paste one script tag through your prompt, then read each bug's plain-English cause and fix prompt.
---

# Mushi Mushi in Lovable or Bolt

Lovable and Bolt build your app from a chat, with no terminal, so `npx` is
not an option. You add Mushi the way you change anything else there: with a
prompt. It takes about five minutes.

- Sign up free and copy your script tag.
- Ask Lovable or Bolt to add it to your app.
- When a user reports a bug, Mushi tells you why and gives you a prompt that fixes it.

### Get your script tag

[Sign up free](https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/admin/signup?src=quickstart-lovable-bolt)
and create a project. On the setup page (**Set up** in the sidebar), open the
**Install widget** tab and, in **Configure & install the SDK**, pick the
**Script tag** tab. Your project ID is already in the tag. If the key still
reads `YOUR_SDK_KEY`, click **Generate API key** in the **Mint your API key**
box above it and the real key fills in. If there is no such box (a key was
already made for you and is no longer shown), click **Rotate** next to your key
in the same card: the new key fills in. Then copy the tag.

**You'll see:** a tag that starts with `

### Paste it into Lovable or Bolt

Send this prompt in your project's chat, with your tag from the step above in
place of the example tag:

```text
Add this script tag inside the <head> of index.html exactly as written, and change nothing else:
<script async src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@mushi-mushi/web@1/dist/mushi.loader.global.js" data-project="YOUR_PROJECT_ID" data-key="YOUR_API_KEY"></script>
```

If your project has no `index.html` (a Next.js app, for example), ask it to
add the same tag to the page `` of the root layout instead.

**You'll see:** a small report button in the corner of your app after it rebuilds.

### Publish and send a test report

Publish the app, open the live site, tap the report button and write one
sentence, for example "Testing Mushi".

**You'll see:** the report in your [Mushi console](https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/admin/reports) within seconds, with a title, how serious it is and the likely cause.

### Fix a real bug

When a user reports something, open the report in the console and click
**Copy fix prompt**. Paste it into Lovable or Bolt. The prompt says what
broke, why, where, and how to check the fix.

**You'll see:** Lovable or Bolt make a change aimed at the cause. Check it in the preview before you publish.

Not sure what a diagnosis looks like? [Read a sample](/demo/diagnosis): a
user's complaint, what the widget captured, the cause and the fix prompt.

## Read reports inside Lovable

You can also connect Mushi to Lovable's chat, so you can ask "what did users
report today?" and get the diagnosis without opening the console. See
[Mushi as a Lovable connector](/quickstart/lovable-mcp).

## Where the key goes, and is it safe?

The key in the tag is an SDK key. It can only send reports to your project
(`report:write`); it cannot read reports, change settings or see other
projects. That is why it can sit in your page's HTML, like any analytics or
chat-widget key.

  Paste only the tag from the **Script tag** tab. Every Mushi key starts with
  `mushi_`, so the prefix does not tell them apart: never put a key you made
  for an editor or the MCP server into your app, because those keys can read
  your reports.

## Change how the button looks

The tag takes a few `data-*` settings, such as `data-position` and
`data-theme`. The full list is on the
[script-tag reference](/quickstart/web#no-bundler-script-tag).

## If nothing shows up

- **No button:** ask Lovable or Bolt to show you the `` of
  `index.html` and check the tag is there, unchanged. Then publish again.
- **Button, but no report in the console:** check that `data-project` and
  `data-key` match the Script tag tab exactly, with no spaces.
- **Still stuck:** the [troubleshooting list](/quickstart#troubleshooting)
  covers the other cases.

## Ask Lovable why it broke

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/quickstart/lovable-mcp

---
title: Ask Lovable why it broke
description: Add Mushi Mushi to Lovable as an MCP connector in three steps; Lovable reads the plain-English diagnosis and fixes the bug. Claude Code and Cursor in one paste.
---

# Ask Lovable why it broke

A user says your app is broken. Ask Lovable *"what did my users report?"* and it
reads Mushi Mushi's diagnosis of each report, gets the fix prompt and fixes the code.
The same connection works in Claude Code and Cursor.

- Add Mushi to Lovable as a custom MCP server: one URL, sign in, approve.
- Ask in the Lovable chat: "what did my users report?"
- Lovable gets the report, the plain-English cause and a fix prompt, then fixes it.

You need a Mushi project that receives reports. A Lovable app gets the
reporting widget from one [script tag](/quickstart/web#no-bundler-script-tag).
No real report yet? Step 4 files a test one.

## Add Mushi to Lovable

Custom MCP servers are available on every Lovable plan
([Lovable docs](https://docs.lovable.dev/integrations/custom-mcp)).

### Open the custom MCP form

In Lovable, open [Connectors](https://lovable.dev/dashboard?connectors), select
**Add custom** at the top right, and choose **MCP server**.

If **MCP server** is greyed out, a workspace admin has turned off custom MCP
servers. Ask them to turn on **Custom MCP** under **Connectors → Admin settings**.

### Fill in the form

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| **Server name** | `Mushi` |
| **Connection** (shown only on some workspaces) | **Direct connection** |
| **Server URL** | `https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/hosted-mcp/?features=vibe` |
| **Authentication** | **OAuth** (the default) |

Click **Add & authorize**.

### Sign in and approve

A Mushi page opens. Sign in, choose which projects Lovable may see, and click
**Approve**. You never copy a key: the sign-in creates one for this connection,
and you can revoke it from the Mushi console at any time.

**You'll see:** Mushi in your list of chat connectors in Lovable.

### Ask Lovable

In a project chat, try:

```text
Using the Mushi connector, what did my users report this week?
```

```text
Get the Mushi fix context for the checkout report and fix it.
```

```text
That's deployed. Mark the report fixed in Mushi and tell the reporter.
```

No reports yet? Ask for a test one. Mushi diagnoses it like a real user report:

```text
Using Mushi, file a test report: "The Save button on the settings page does nothing."
```

**You'll see:** the report, the likely cause in plain English and the files to change, then Lovable's edit.

Lovable runs read-only tools without asking. Before a tool that changes
something (mark fixed, reply to the reporter, file a report) it shows an
approval card; choose **Always allow** to skip it next time.

## Claude Code: one paste

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http mushi "https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/hosted-mcp/?features=vibe"
```

Then run `/mcp` in a session, pick `mushi` and sign in in your browser. Ask:
*"What did my users report in Mushi? Fix the top one."*

## Cursor: one click

[Add Mushi to Cursor](cursor://anysphere.cursor-deeplink/mcp/install?name=mushi&config=eyJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2tlbnNhdXIudXMvbXVzaGktbXVzaGkvaG9zdGVkLW1jcC8%2FZmVhdHVyZXM9dmliZSJ9)
(opens Cursor), or paste this into `.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json filename=".cursor/mcp.json"
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mushi": {
      "url": "https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/hosted-mcp/?features=vibe"
    }
  }
}
```

Cursor asks you to sign in the first time the agent calls Mushi. Leave out any
`headers` block: a static `Authorization` header turns the sign-in off.

## Bolt

Bolt also accepts a custom MCP server under **Connectors (MCP) → Custom MCP
server** ([Bolt docs](https://support.bolt.new/integrations/mcp)). Use the same
URL. We have not tested Mushi in Bolt yet.

## What `?features=vibe` gives you

`?features=vibe` keeps the connection to the 12 tools this loop needs. Without
it the connection lists about 80. A chat assistant picks the right tool more
often from a short list, and some clients, Cursor among them, warn once all
their servers together pass about 40 tools.

| Tool | What it does | Changes anything? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `triage_next_steps` | What to fix first | No |
| `get_recent_reports` | The latest reports from your users | No |
| `search_reports` | Find reports by words ("checkout") | No |
| `get_report_detail` | One report: what the user saw, logs, screenshot, diagnosis | No |
| `get_fix_context` | The cause, the files to change and a ready fix prompt | No |
| `transition_status` | Mark a report fixed, or dismiss a duplicate | Yes |
| `reply_to_reporter` | Tell the user in your app that it's fixed | Yes |
| `file_report` | File a report yourself (or a test one) | Yes |
| `diagnose_setup` | Why reports aren't arriving, and the next step | No |
| `use_mushi` | Which tool to use for a task | No |
| `search_mushi_docs` / `get_mushi_doc` | Answers from these docs | No |

If you approved more than one app, the connection also lists `list_projects`
and `get_account_overview`, so Lovable can find the app you mean.

Want more? Drop `?features=vibe` for the default set (reports, fixes, app
inventory, setup, docs), or use `?features=all` for every tool. You can also
combine them, for example `?features=vibe,qa`.

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Sign-in fails with "404" | Use the `kensaur.us` URL above. Sign-in does not work on a `supabase.co` URL. |
| "tool … is not enabled for this connection" | The tool is outside `vibe`. Ask `use_mushi` which group it needs and add that group to `?features=`, or use `?features=all`. |
| Answers mix up your apps | Pin the connection to one app: add `&project=<project-id>` to the URL. |
| You can't use OAuth | Choose **Bearer token or API key** in Lovable and paste a Mushi API key with MCP access, minted on **Manage apps** in the Mushi console (preset **MCP read + write**). Sign-in is safer: its key is made for this one connection. |
| You want to disconnect | Remove the connector in Lovable, and revoke its key under **Editor agents → Account keys** in the Mushi console. |

  More on the sign-in, project scopes and other clients: [MCP server](/quickstart/mcp).
  The full fix loop from your editor: [Incident loop](/quickstart/incident-loop).

## React quickstart

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/quickstart/react

---
title: React quickstart
description: Add the Mushi Mushi React SDK in one command. npx mushi-mushi installs the bug-report widget, writes env vars, and offers to send a test report.
---

# React quickstart

Add the Mushi Mushi bug-report widget to a React app.

  **Coming from Create React App?** Migrate to Vite first: see
  the [CRA → Vite migration guide](/migrations/cra-to-vite). All Mushi React
  examples below assume Vite + React 19.

## Try it live

## 1. Install

```bash
pnpm add @mushi-mushi/react
# or: npm install @mushi-mushi/react
```

`@mushi-mushi/react` re-exports from `@mushi-mushi/core` and `@mushi-mushi/web`,
so you only need this one dependency.

## 2. Wrap your app

```tsx filename="src/main.tsx"
import { MushiProvider } from '@mushi-mushi/react'
import { App } from './App'

export function Root() {
  return (
    <MushiProvider
      config={{
        projectId: import.meta.env.VITE_MUSHI_PROJECT_ID,
        apiKey: import.meta.env.VITE_MUSHI_API_KEY,
      }}
    >
      <App />
    </MushiProvider>
  )
}
```

### Next.js App Router

`` uses React context, so it goes in a client component, not
straight into `app/layout.tsx`:

```tsx filename="app/providers.tsx"
'use client'
import { MushiProvider } from '@mushi-mushi/react'

export function Providers({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <MushiProvider
      config={{
        projectId: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_MUSHI_PROJECT_ID!,
        apiKey: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_MUSHI_API_KEY!,
      }}
    >
      {children}
    </MushiProvider>
  )
}
```

```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx"
import { Providers } from './providers'

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <Providers>{children}</Providers>
      </body>
    </html>
  )
}
```

`npx mushi-mushi` writes this `providers.tsx` for you when it detects Next.js.
Keep callbacks such as `beforeSend` inside `providers.tsx`, because a Server
Component cannot pass functions to a client one.

  The web SDK uses your **public** API key (safe to bundle). All sensitive
  operations are gated server-side by RLS + the gateway. Never ship your
  service-role key to the browser.

## 3. Trigger reports

Add a hook anywhere in your tree to capture programmatic reports:

```tsx filename="src/components/CrashFallback.tsx"
import { useMushiSdk } from '@mushi-mushi/react'

export function CrashFallback({ error }: { error: Error }) {
  const mushi = useMushiSdk()
  return (
    <div role="alert">
      <p>Something broke.</p>
      <button onClick={() => void mushi?.captureException(error, { severity: 'high' })}>
        Send a bug report
      </button>
    </div>
  )
}
```

`useMushiSdk()` returns `null` until the provider has initialised, hence the
`?.`. To open the report widget from a button instead, use
`const { report } = useMushi()` and call `report()`.

Or rely on the built-in widget, with no extra code. The launcher mounts as
soon as `` initialises.

## 4. Verify

Open your admin console at [kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/admin](https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/admin) (or your self-hosted
instance). Your first report appears on the **Bugs** page within seconds, and
its AI diagnosis follows shortly after.

- [Concepts → Classification pipeline](/concepts/classification)
- [SDK reference → @mushi-mushi/react](/sdks/react)
- [Plugins → Receive a webhook in your own service](/plugins/building)

## React Native quickstart

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/quickstart/react-native

---
title: React Native quickstart
description: Add Mushi Mushi shake-to-report to a React Native or Expo app with @mushi-mushi/react-native. Install, mount the provider, and check the first report.
---

# React Native quickstart

Add Mushi Mushi's shake-to-report and floating bug button to your iOS or
Android app.

Works for **bare React Native CLI** apps and **Expo** apps (managed-with-dev-client
or bare). Peer dependency is React Native **≥ 0.72**; this quickstart targets
**0.82+** with the New Architecture as the recommended baseline.

## 1. Install

```bash
# React Native CLI
npm install @mushi-mushi/react-native @react-native-async-storage/async-storage
cd ios && bundle exec pod install && cd ..

# Expo
npx expo install @mushi-mushi/react-native @react-native-async-storage/async-storage
```

To enable **shake-to-report**, also install `expo-sensors`. On a bare RN CLI
project, wire up Expo modules first (one-time):

```bash
# Bare RN CLI only — Expo apps already have this
npx install-expo-modules@latest
npm install expo-sensors
cd ios && bundle exec pod install && cd ..

# Expo
npx expo install expo-sensors
```

## 2. Mount the provider

```tsx filename="App.tsx"
import { MushiProvider } from '@mushi-mushi/react-native'

export default function App() {
  return (
    <MushiProvider
      projectId="YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
      apiKey="YOUR_PUBLIC_API_KEY"
      config={{
        widget: { trigger: 'both' },        // 'shake' | 'button' | 'both' | 'manual'
        capture: { console: true, network: true },
      }}
    >
      <RootNavigator />
    </MushiProvider>
  )
}
```

`` mounts the floating bug button automatically (unless you
set `trigger: 'manual'`), opens the bottom-sheet report form on tap or
shake, and attaches the last 100 console logs and last 50 network requests
to every report.

### Optional native modules

Three packages are optional. The SDK picks each one up when it is installed:

| Package | What it adds |
| --- | --- |
| `expo-sensors` | Shake to report |
| `react-native-view-shot` | A screenshot attached to the report |
| `@react-native-community/netinfo` | Queued reports resend as soon as the network is back |

The SDK loads them with a plain `require()` inside `try/catch`, which Metro
treats as optional (`transformer.allowOptionalDependencies`, on in Expo and
React Native's default Metro config). If your Metro config turns that off, or
you would rather the SDK never load anything itself, pass the modules in:

```tsx filename="App.tsx"
import type { ReactNode } from 'react'
import { MushiProvider } from '@mushi-mushi/react-native'
import NetInfo from '@react-native-community/netinfo'
import * as ViewShot from 'react-native-view-shot'
import * as ExpoSensors from 'expo-sensors'

export function AppWithMushi({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <MushiProvider
      projectId="YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
      apiKey="YOUR_PUBLIC_API_KEY"
      netInfo={NetInfo}
      viewShot={ViewShot}
      expoSensors={ExpoSensors}
    >
      {children}
    </MushiProvider>
  )
}
```

A module you pass in always wins. Versions 0.21–0.23 needed a postinstall
patch for these (`__require` errors in Metro); releases with this fix need none.

## 3. Verify

Run your app on a simulator or a device, tap the bug button, type a
description, and submit. The report should appear in the Mushi admin console
within a couple of seconds, showing the SDK that sent it
(`@mushi-mushi/react-native` and its version).

If nothing arrives:

- Confirm `apiKey` is a Mushi project key (it starts with `mushi_`, like every
  Mushi key) with the `report:write` scope, not the Supabase service-role key.
- Confirm `` is at the **root** of the component tree, above
  any `NavigationContainer`.
- iOS release builds must use HTTPS for the Mushi endpoint (the default).

  Pure-native shells should use the [iOS](/quickstart/ios) or
  [Android](/quickstart/android) SDKs directly. Capacitor / Ionic apps have
  their own [plugin](/quickstart/capacitor); a step-by-step
  [Capacitor → React Native migration guide](/migrations/capacitor-to-react-native)
  covers porting an existing Capacitor app.

## Vanilla JS quickstart

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/quickstart/web

---
title: Vanilla JS quickstart
description: Add the Mushi Mushi browser SDK to any site without a framework. Install @mushi-mushi/web, call Mushi.init, and file reports from your buttons or the widget.
---

# Vanilla JS quickstart

For non-React apps (or any framework you'd rather drive imperatively).

## Try it live

## 1. Install

```bash
pnpm add @mushi-mushi/web
```

## 2. Initialize

```ts filename="src/mushi.ts"
import { Mushi } from '@mushi-mushi/web'

export const mushi = Mushi.init({
  projectId: import.meta.env.VITE_MUSHI_PROJECT_ID,
  apiKey: import.meta.env.VITE_MUSHI_API_KEY,
})
```

## 3. Submit

```ts filename="src/report-button.ts"
import { mushi } from './mushi'

document.querySelector('#report-bug')?.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  await mushi.captureEvent({
    description: 'Login button does nothing on mobile Safari.',
    severity: 'medium',
  })
})
```

`captureEvent` files the report without opening any UI. To open the widget
instead, call `mushi.report()`.

The widget launcher mounts automatically on `Mushi.init`. Set
`widget: { trigger: 'hidden' }` to keep it out of sight and open it only
from your own buttons.

## No bundler: script tag

On a site with no build step (plain HTML, Rails or Django templates,
WordPress, Webflow), paste one tag into `` instead of installing the
package:

```html filename="index.html"
<script async
  src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@mushi-mushi/web@1/dist/mushi.loader.global.js"
  data-project="YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
  data-key="YOUR_API_KEY"
></script>
```

The file is the loader that `@mushi-mushi/web` publishes to npm, served by
jsDelivr and pinned to major version 1, so minor and patch releases reach
you without editing the tag. It reads its settings from its own `data-*`
attributes and calls `Mushi.init` once; including the tag twice does not
start a second copy. With no `data-project` and `data-key` it does nothing.

| Attribute | Maps to |
| --- | --- |
| `data-project` | `projectId` (required) |
| `data-key` | `apiKey` (required; an SDK key with the `report:write` scope) |
| `data-trigger` | `widget.trigger` |
| `data-theme` | `widget.theme` |
| `data-position` | `widget.position` |
| `data-trigger-text` | `widget.triggerText` |
| `data-banner-variant` | `widget.bannerConfig.variant` (`neon`, `brand` or `subtle`) |
| `data-banner-position` | `widget.bannerConfig.position` (`top` or `bottom`) |
| `data-endpoint` | `apiEndpoint`, for a self-hosted server |
| `data-debug` | `debug` when set to `"true"` |

Anything else (capture options, `beforeSend`, `captureEvent` from your own
code) needs the npm package above. The console's **Script tag** install tab
prints this tag with your project ID and key filled in.

  See [SDK reference → @mushi-mushi/web](/sdks/web) for the full config
  surface (PII scrubbing, rate limits, custom triggers, on-device pre-filter).

## Pricing: Free, Builder, Studio and self-host

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/pricing

---
title: "Pricing: Free, Builder, Studio and self-host"
description: Mushi Mushi pricing. Free for one app and 100 AI bug diagnoses a month. Builder $29/mo for 3 apps, Studio $79/mo for 10. Free to self-host.
---

# Pricing

## Plans

A plan is the number of **apps** Mushi Mushi watches for your team: one on Free, three on Builder, ten on Studio. Diagnoses are the allowance under it. Reports are always captured and are never billed.

Installing plugins from the Marketplace (PagerDuty, Zapier, the Cursor and Claude Code agents, Linear Sync, Sentry Mirror) needs Builder or above. The Integrations page (Sentry, Slack, GitHub, Linear) works on every plan.

  **Annual billing saves two months.** Pay for 10 months, get 12: Builder is $290 a year, Studio $790. Annual plans have no pay-as-you-go overage: they include the plan's diagnoses each month and pause new diagnoses at that limit. Pick annual at checkout, or switch an existing plan with **Change plan** on the Billing page. For Enterprise commits, contact us.

  **Overage is capped.** Builder and Studio include a default cap on overage spend ($50 and $200 a month, on top of the base fee). You can lower or raise it in the console. At the cap, Mushi pauses new diagnoses and says so, instead of sending a bigger invoice. Email alerts fire at **50%, 80%, and 100%** of your included diagnoses.

  **Free has a hard stop**, not a soft limit. At 100 diagnoses Mushi stops diagnosing new reports until the next calendar month. No card, no charge, no bill shock.

## What counts as a diagnosis

One diagnosis = one completed classification pass. Specifically:

- The report passes the fast noise filter (not spam or incomplete junk).
- It is not a duplicate of an existing group already classified this period.
- The classifier finishes and writes a plain-English root cause + severity + fix hint.

Under the hood that is a two-stage pipeline (Haiku fast-filter → Sonnet structured output). Classification, deduplication, knowledge-graph writes, and MCP tool calls are **not** counted separately: they are included in the per-diagnosis price. Fix PRs and agent runs are not counted as diagnoses; with your own AI key (see [below](#your-own-ai-key-and-the-self-host-path)), their tokens are billed by that vendor.

**What does NOT count:**

- Reports filtered by the fast-filter (noise, spam, incomplete submissions).
- Reports deduplicated to an existing group (same broken button, same stack trace: they collapse, you only pay once).
- Inbound adapter events (Sentry alerts, Datadog webhooks) that don't complete a fresh diagnosis.
- MCP `get_fix_context` calls, fix dispatch, or any read-only operation.

## Pricing estimator

Use the slider below to model your bill. Toggle **Annual** to see the effective monthly base fee. When you hit a tier limit, the estimator suggests the next plan.

## Example bills

Monthly plans, default caps, for a billing period that lines up with the calendar month (overage metered on top of the base fee; the cap limits the overage, not the total):

```
Builder: $29 + min(max(0, diagnoses − 1,000) × $0.03, $50)
Studio:  $79 + min(max(0, diagnoses − 3,000) × $0.03, $200)
```

| Diagnoses / mo | Builder | Studio |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 100 | $29.00 | $79.00 |
| 500 | $29.00 | $79.00 |
| 1,000 | $29.00 | $79.00 |
| 1,500 | $44.00 | $79.00 |
| 2,000 | $59.00 | $79.00 |
| 3,000 | $79.00 *(cap)* | $79.00 |
| 5,000 | $79.00 *(cap)* | $139.00 |
| 8,000 | $79.00 *(cap)* | $229.00 |

The cap is checked per calendar month (UTC) of usage: at the cap, new diagnoses pause until the 1st. Builder reaches its default cap at about 2,667 diagnoses in a month, Studio at about 9,667. Reports past that point are kept, not diagnosed.

## Why apps, not reports?

Reports are noisy: one broken button can send fifty, and a busy week is hard to predict. The number of apps you ship is something you already know, and it grows with what you get out of Mushi. So a plan is sized by apps watched, diagnoses are a generous allowance under it, and reports are never billed at all.

## Why diagnoses, not events

Sentry meters errors. We meter diagnoses: one per plain-English root cause and paste-ready fix, a unit you can predict. Duplicate errors from the same broken button collapse to one diagnosis. You pay once.

## Your own AI key and the self-host path

On every Cloud plan, Free included, you can add your own Anthropic, OpenAI or Cursor key under **Settings → API keys**. Mushi then uses it for fix PRs and agent work; you pay those vendors directly at list rate, and we never mark up tokens.

When self-hosting, Mushi uses **your** keys for everything. For a sense of scale: on Mushi's own key, a diagnosis cost about $0.017–0.022 in LLM tokens over the 30 days to 2026-10-28, so 1,000 diagnoses is roughly $20. Fix PRs and reviews are extra and depend on the model you pick.

The self-host path is free, and always will be: [see the guide](/self-hosting).

## Compared to Sentry + Seer

| | Sentry Team + Seer | Mushi Builder |
|---|---|---|
| Base plan | Team: $26 / mo billed annually, $29 monthly | $29 / mo for 3 apps ($290 a year) |
| AI diagnosis | Seer add-on: + $40 / active contributor / mo | Included |
| Solo dev total | **$66–69 / mo** plus any pay-as-you-go | **$29 / mo** |
| Catches non-crash friction | Via its User Feedback widget and Session Replay | Yes: a report widget (shake on mobile) with screenshot and console/network tail, then a diagnosis |
| Bugs in your editor | Sentry MCP server: issues and Seer analysis in Cursor / Claude Code | Mushi MCP server: diagnosis, fix prompt and lessons; no second LLM key |

Sentry prices from [sentry.io/pricing](https://sentry.io/pricing/) and [Sentry's pricing docs](https://docs.sentry.io/pricing/), checked 2026-10-29. Seer is an add-on to the Team or Business plan, billed as its own monthly charge. An active contributor is anyone who opens two or more pull requests in a month to a Seer-enabled repo; the $66–69 total assumes one of them. Seer is not available in self-hosted Sentry ([self-hosted docs](https://develop.sentry.dev/self-hosted/)).

Sentry + Seer is strong at code-thrown errors, tracing, breadcrumbs and session replay, and Seer is an AI debugging agent for those issues. Mushi starts from user-felt friction that never triggers an error, ingests Sentry's errors too, and turns each into a plain-English diagnosis and a paste-ready fix prompt in your editor. A diagnosis is an LLM's reading and can be wrong; check it before you merge.

## Frequently asked questions

### What happens when I hit my diagnosis limit?

**Free:** New plain-English diagnoses pause until the next calendar month. Reports are still captured.

**Builder / Studio (monthly):** You can keep diagnosing into overage until your **spend cap** stops new classification runs. Reports are never dropped.

**Builder / Studio (annual):** New diagnoses pause at the included amount until the next calendar month. Reports are never dropped. Switch to monthly (pay-as-you-go overage) or to Studio from **Change plan**.

### What happens when I add one app too many?

The console says how many apps your plan watches and how many your team has, and offers the plans. Nothing already running stops: your existing apps keep their reports and diagnoses. Move up a plan, or remove an app you no longer use.

### Can I use my own AI key on Free?

Yes. Bring-your-own-key works on every plan, Free included. Add an Anthropic, OpenAI or Cursor key under **Settings → API keys** and Mushi can open fix PRs with it, so you see the whole loop on your first app before paying anything.

### When does my quota reset?

Diagnoses are counted per calendar month (UTC) on every plan, so the count starts again on the 1st. Paid plans are invoiced on your Stripe billing period, which can start on a different day.

### Can I change my spend cap?

Yes. Open **Billing → Spending cap** on your project card. Set any USD cap on overage from $0–100,000 or clear it to use the plan default ($50 Builder, $200 Studio).

### Who receives usage alert emails?

By default, the **project owner**. Override the address under **Usage alert email** on the same card. Alerts fire once per threshold (50%, 80%, 100%) per billing month.

### Is usage per app or per team?

**Diagnoses are per app; the app limit is per team.** Each app you connect has its own diagnosis counter and spend cap, and the plan's app limit counts the apps in your team.

### Can I downgrade mid-cycle?

Change plans in the console with **Change plan** on the Billing page (Builder ↔ Studio, monthly ↔ annual). The change applies immediately and is pro-rated: unused time is credited and the new plan is charged for the rest of the period. Moving between monthly and annual starts a new billing period that day. Stripe's customer portal (**Manage**) handles your card, invoices and cancellation.

### Do annual plans include overage?

No. Annual plans include the plan's diagnoses every month (1,000 on Builder, 3,000 on Studio) and pause new diagnoses at that limit until the next month, so an annual invoice never grows. If you need more, switch to monthly for pay-as-you-go overage or upgrade to Studio from **Change plan**.

### What does Enterprise cost?

From $499 a month, billed annually: unlimited apps, SAML SSO, the SOC 2 readiness pack, self-host support and up to 365 days of history. [Contact us](mailto:kensaurus@gmail.com?subject=Mushi%20Enterprise%20inquiry) for a quote.

### How do I estimate before signing up?

## Jam vs Mushi Mushi

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/compare/jam-vs-mushi

---
title: Jam vs Mushi Mushi
description: Jam.dev vs Mushi Mushi in 2026. A teammate recording a bug in the Jam extension versus a user reporting from your app, MCP handoff and free tiers.
---

# Jam vs Mushi Mushi

Jam and Mushi Mushi both put console and network logs next to a bug so nobody has
to ask "can you reproduce that?". The difference is who presses the button.
With Jam, a person on or near your team records the bug in Chrome. With
Mushi, the user who hit the bug reports it from inside your production app,
and the report arrives with a diagnosis already written.

## What each one is

## Side by side

## Where they overlap

Both attach the technical context a developer needs: console output, network
requests, device details and the sequence of user actions. Both expose that
context to a coding agent over MCP, and Jam's "Debug Jams via MCP" is on the
free tier, which is a fair point in its favour for a team that already uses
Jam for QA.

## Where they do not

Jam is a recording tool. The unit is a Jam: a video a human made, sent to a
tracker such as Jira or Linear. Reading the video is still your job, and
Recording Links are the way to get one from someone outside the workspace.

Mushi is a reporting SDK plus a diagnosis. The unit is a report: the user's
sentence, a screenshot, the console/network tail, the route and a timeline of
what they did before. Mushi reads that against your repo and writes what
broke and why. Repeat reports collapse into one row, and each fix becomes a
lesson your editor sees next time.

## Using both

Sensible, and common: Jam for internal QA passes and support-desk recordings,
Mushi for reports from real users in production and for the fix loop in
Cursor or Claude Code. There is no direct integration between the two today;
if you want a Jam link on a Mushi report, put it in the report's metadata.

## Pick Jam if

- Your bugs are found by teammates, testers or support agents who can run a
  Chrome extension.
- A video is the artefact your tracker workflow expects.

## Pick Mushi if

- Your bugs are found by end users on devices you do not control, including
  mobile (React Native, Capacitor, Flutter, iOS, Android).
- You want the first thing you read to be the diagnosis, not the recording.
- You want the report and fix context inside Cursor or Claude Code.

## PostHog session replay vs Mushi Mushi

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/compare/posthog-session-replay-vs-mushi

---
title: PostHog session replay vs Mushi Mushi
description: PostHog session replay vs Mushi Mushi in 2026. Every session recorded versus the one a user flagged as broken, free tiers, and why teams run both.
---

# PostHog session replay vs Mushi Mushi

PostHog records every session and every exception, and gives you product
analytics on top. Mushi Mushi records the moment a user says something is wrong,
attaches the screen they were looking at and the console/network tail, and
writes the diagnosis. They answer different questions, and this page is
mostly about which question you have.

Both now use AI on bugs. PostHog puts a "Fix with AI" prompt on every
error-tracking issue, and its Self-driving beta opens a draft pull request
for recurring high-impact errors, with a small free allowance each month and
a price per PR after that (both in the table below). That path starts from
the exceptions PostHog captured. Mushi starts from what a user reported and
the screen they were on, writes a plain-English diagnosis on every plan, and
hands the fix context to Cursor or Claude Code over MCP.

## What each one is

## Side by side

## They work alongside each other

Nothing here conflicts in the browser: the PostHog snippet and the Mushi SDK
run side by side. There is no PostHog plugin for Mushi today, so a Mushi
report will not deep-link to the matching replay. If you want that, add the
PostHog session id to Mushi's metadata when you initialise the SDK and the
report will carry it.

Mushi also ships a basic product-analytics surface of its own, `Mushi.track()`
with funnels, paths, people and retention in the same console. It exists so a
solo builder does not need a second tool to see a signup funnel; it is not a
PostHog replacement and does not try to be. See the
[SDK analytics reference](/sdks/analytics).

## Pick PostHog if

- You want replay for every session, not only reported ones, and product
  analytics, flags and surveys in the same place.
- Your bugs are found by watching replays rather than by users telling you.
- You want AI fix prompts, and beta draft pull requests, on the exceptions
  PostHog already captures.

## Pick Mushi if

- You want the bug to start from what the user said and saw, and to arrive
  explained, with the screenshot and a fix prompt.
- You fix bugs in Cursor or Claude Code and want the report in the editor.
- You want the diagnosis on every plan, including self-hosted with your own
  LLM key.
