## @mushi-mushi/ux

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/sdks/ux

---
title: '@mushi-mushi/ux'
description: '@mushi-mushi/ux, the Mushi Mushi UX tool, runs your coding agent over each screen, measures every change and keeps only what helps, on a branch you review.'
---

# `@mushi-mushi/ux`

The Mushi Mushi UX tool finds the UX problems on every screen of your app before
your users do, and lets the coding agent you already pay for fix them one screen at a time.
Every change is measured. Only the ones that help are kept, on a branch you
review. It runs on your machine.

## Quick start

```bash
mushi ux ui                    # through the Mushi CLI: passes your login, so runs show in the console
npx @mushi-mushi/ux ui         # or standalone
mushi ux run --dev "pnpm dev --port {port}" --agent cursor --model <id> --skill enhance-mobile-native-feel
```

The package installs a `mushi-ux` command; `mushi ux …` in
[`@mushi-mushi/cli`](/sdks/cli#ux-pass-over-every-screen) runs the same
thing and passes your Mushi login along. Your app must run locally, inside
a git repository. In `--dev`, `{port}` is replaced with a spare port.

Signed-in app? Run `mushi-ux login --url http://localhost:5173` once and
sign in by hand in the window that opens; later runs reuse that session
with `--login-url`.

## From studio to merge

1. **Studio (your computer).** `mushi ux ui` opens a page on 127.0.0.1.
   Pick the agent, model, skill and pages, then watch each attempt live.
2. **Console (mirror and review).** With sync on, the run is mirrored to
   the console's [UX runs](/admin/ux-runs) page as it goes. The studio
   offers sync when you are signed in with the Mushi CLI; from the
   terminal, add `--sync`.
3. **Merge.** Open the kept changes as a draft PR from the studio, then
   merge it from the console (after a confirmation) or on GitHub. Nothing
   is merged for you.

## What a run does

1. Checks the agent can start and read a file (about a minute), so a
   signed-out agent fails before anything slow.
2. Creates a git worktree on a new branch, `mushi-ux/`, and starts
   your dev server there. Your own checkout is never touched.
3. Maps the app: every page, plus the tabs, dialogs and menus each one
   opens.
4. For each screen: screenshots it at phone and desktop width and measures
   accessibility (axe), sideways scrolling, tap targets under 24×24 px,
   console errors and layout shift. The agent gets the screenshots, the
   problems and your design tokens.
5. After each attempt it measures again. The edit is **kept** as a commit
   if nothing got worse and something changed, otherwise **rolled back**
   with the reason for one more try. Screens already done are checked
   again, and any that moved are marked **regressed**.
6. Optionally, a second model compares each changed screen before and
   after. Its review is advisory and never keeps or reverts anything.

With `--steps` (on by default in the studio) the agent first plans 2–5
small changes per screen, then makes one per attempt. A stopped run (closed
laptop, Stop, crash) shows **Resume** in the studio, or continue it from
the first unfinished screen with `mushi-ux run --resume `.

## Safety

- **Exploring never writes.** Every non-GET request is blocked, forms are
  never submitted, and buttons like Delete, Pay, Send and Log out are never
  clicked. If your app reads with POST (Supabase `rpc`, GraphQL), allow it:
  `--allow "POST /rest/v1/rpc/*"`.
- **The agent never sees your session or keys.** Credentials are stripped
  from its environment except its own model key. Claude Code runs with no
  shell and only the worktree's files.
- **Your dev server** runs without this tool's keys (`CURSOR_API_KEY`,
  `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `MUSHI_*`). Put app
  secrets in the app's ignored `.env` files; those are copied into the
  worktree.
- **What reaches the console:** phase, screens, scores, problem counts,
  screenshots, and the names of files read or edited. The agent's words,
  its commands and their output stay in `.mushi/ux//agent/`.
- Use a test account if your dev server talks to production data.

## Agents

| `--agent` | Needs | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `claude-code` (default) | `claude` on PATH | Verified on Windows |
| `cursor` | Cursor CLI (`agent`), signed in with `agent login` | Verified on Windows |
| `codex` | `codex` on PATH | Unverified |
| `cursor-cloud` | `CURSOR_API_KEY` and an `origin` on GitHub | Unverified |

`mushi-ux models --agent ` lists the models your account can use.
`--skill` takes a skill name (`mushi-ux skills` lists them; they come from
`npm:@kensaurus/skills` unless you pass `--skills-repo`), several names
comma-separated to chain them, or a path to a skill folder. Without one,
the agent gets built-in UX guidance.

On Windows, start runs from PowerShell or cmd: a Claude Code hook that
fails under Git Bash makes the Cursor CLI refuse every file read, and the
start-up check says so.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `mushi-ux ui` | The studio: start runs and watch them |
| `mushi-ux run --dev ""` | Run the loop from the terminal |
| `mushi-ux discover --url ` | List the screens, change nothing |
| `mushi-ux audit --url  --profile-dir ` | Find UX bugs on signed-in screens and file them as Mushi reports |
| `mushi-ux explore --url  --profile-dir ` | Let a model use the signed-in app like a careless user; file the errors a replay confirms |
| `mushi-ux login --url ` | Sign in once, in a visible browser |
| `mushi-ux models` / `mushi-ux skills` | What `--model` and `--skill` accept |
| `mushi-ux open ` | The local dashboard for a past run |

Common `run` options:

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--max-surfaces` / `--iterations` / `--timeout` | 10 / 2 / 10 min | Screens, attempts per screen, minutes per attempt |
| `--base ` | `HEAD` | Branch from this ref, e.g. `origin/main` |
| `--path ` | — | Work only on these pages (repeatable) |
| `--ignore ` | — | Not your UI (a dev badge): hidden and skipped. Or mark it `data-mushi-ux-ignore` |
| `--install ` | from the lockfile | Install command for the worktree; `none` skips it |
| `--sync` | off | Mirror the run to the console (`mushi ux` passes your login) |
| `--no-judge` / `--no-preflight` / `--no-dashboard` | — | Skip the review, the agent check, or the local dashboard |

`mushi-ux run --help` lists the rest. Run state and screenshots live in
`.mushi/ux//`. The run adds its folders to `.git/info/exclude`, so
`git status` stays clean. `--sync` refuses a run whose app reports to a
different Mushi project than your login.

## Audit and explore signed-in screens

`mushi-ux audit` checks the live app the way a signed-in user sees it and
files what is wrong as Mushi reports, so the fix loop picks them up. It
never edits code and never opens a fresh browser: point it at a cached,
signed-in browser profile.

```bash
mushi-ux audit --url https://example.com/admin \
  --profile-dir ~/.playwright-cli-profiles/example \
  --review claude-code --file --dry-run
```

- It maps the screens under the URL's path (`--max-pages`, default 15;
  `--states N` also opens up to N dialogs or tabs a page) and captures each
  on desktop (1440×900) and phone (390×844).
- It files measured problems: serious accessibility rules, a page that
  scrolls sideways, console errors, content that jumps while loading.
  `--review` adds visual defects a model finds (`claude-code`,
  `anthropic-api` or `cursor`).
- `--file` files at most 15 reports a run, one per screen and problem, and
  skips one filed in the last 14 days or still open. It needs
  `MUSHI_API_KEY` and `MUSHI_PROJECT_ID`. `--dry-run` files nothing.

`mushi-ux explore` runs short sessions where a model picks what a curious
or careless user would do next (forms with odd input, back and reload
mid-task, double-clicks, filters that match nothing), in the same read-only
browser and profile. The model only chooses actions; code decides what is a
bug. A finding is filed only when replaying the steps without the model
shows it again.

```bash
mushi-ux explore --url https://example.com/admin \
  --profile-dir ~/.playwright-cli-profiles/example \
  --charter forms --charter filters --steps 30 --file --dry-run
```

## On GitHub Actions

Copy
[`docs/templates/mushi-ux.yml`](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/blob/master/docs/templates/mushi-ux.yml)
to `.github/workflows/mushi-ux.yml` and set its `dev-command`. Start it from
the Actions tab, or with **Run in the cloud** on the console's
[UX runs](/admin/ux-runs) page. It uses `cursor-cloud`, sees the app signed
out, and opens one draft PR. Its pushes go to `mushi-ux/**`, so add
`branches-ignore: ['mushi-ux/**']` to any CI that runs on every push.

## @mushi-mushi/vue

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/sdks/vue

---
title: '@mushi-mushi/vue'
description: Mushi Mushi for Vue 3, @mushi-mushi/vue. MushiPlugin, the useMushi, useMushiReport and useMushiWidget composables, user identity and submitting reports.
---

# `@mushi-mushi/vue`

The Mushi Mushi Vue 3 plugin and composables over [`@mushi-mushi/web`](/sdks/web). Shared wrapper
notes: [Framework wrappers](/sdks/framework-wrappers).

```bash
npm install @mushi-mushi/vue
```

  **Still on Vue 2?** This adapter requires Vue 3. See the [Vue 2 → Vue 3 migration guide](/migrations/vue-2-to-vue-3), which walks through the bridge build and the Mushi-specific bits.

See [Quickstart → Vue](/quickstart/vue) for the full setup walkthrough.

## API surface

```ts
import { MushiPlugin, useMushi, useMushiReport, useMushiWidget } from '@mushi-mushi/vue'
```

| Export | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `MushiPlugin` | `app.use(MushiPlugin, config)` installs the plugin and boots the SDK (browser only; it does nothing during SSR) |
| `useMushi()` | Returns the SDK instance, or `undefined` outside the plugin |
| `useMushiReport()` | Returns `{ submitReport({ description, category }) }`; sends a report from code without opening the widget. Both fields are required |
| `useMushiWidget()` | Returns `{ isOpen, open, close }` to control the widget |

The plugin also chains onto `app.config.errorHandler`: your existing handler
still runs, and the error is sent with `captureException()`.

## Setup (Vite / Vue 3)

```ts
// main.ts
import { createApp } from 'vue'
import { MushiPlugin } from '@mushi-mushi/vue'
import App from './App.vue'

createApp(App)
  .use(MushiPlugin, {
    projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
    apiKey: 'mushi_...',
  })
  .mount('#app')
```

## Identifying users

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { watch } from 'vue'
import { useMushi } from '@mushi-mushi/vue'
import { useAuth } from './auth'

const mushi = useMushi()
const { user } = useAuth()

watch(user, (u) => {
  if (u) mushi?.identify(u.id, { email: u.email, name: u.name })
})
</script>
```

## Submitting a report

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { useMushiReport } from '@mushi-mushi/vue'

const { submitReport } = useMushiReport()
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="submitReport({ description: 'Something feels off', category: 'bug' })">
    Report issue
  </button>
</template>
```

## @mushi-mushi/wasm-classifier

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/sdks/wasm-classifier

---
title: '@mushi-mushi/wasm-classifier'
description: "@mushi-mushi/wasm-classifier filters junk bug reports in the browser, before they reach the server or your LLM."
---

# `@mushi-mushi/wasm-classifier`

Optional on-device junk filter for bug reports. It stops empty or nonsense
reports ("hi", "asdf") in the browser, before they are sent. The default
backend is a heuristic with no dependencies; an optional ONNX backend runs a
model you host, through `onnxruntime-web`.

```bash
pnpm add @mushi-mushi/wasm-classifier
# Optional, only for the ONNX backend:
pnpm add onnxruntime-web
```

## Use it with the web SDK

The web SDK does not load the classifier on its own. Pass it in
`preFilter.wasmClassifier`:

```ts
import { Mushi } from '@mushi-mushi/web'
import { createHeuristicClassifier } from '@mushi-mushi/wasm-classifier'

Mushi.init({
  projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
  apiKey: 'mushi_...',
  preFilter: { wasmClassifier: createHeuristicClassifier() },
})
```

It runs after the SDK's built-in pattern filter. A `block` verdict stops the
report on the device; `pass` and `unsure` send it, and the server does the
full classification.

## Call it directly

```ts
import { createHeuristicClassifier } from '@mushi-mushi/wasm-classifier'

const classifier = createHeuristicClassifier({ blockThreshold: 0.2, passThreshold: 0.55 })
const result = await classifier.classify({ description: 'asdf qwer' })
// → { verdict: 'pass' | 'block' | 'unsure', confidence, reason, modelId: 'heuristic-v1', durationMs }
```

`classify()` also takes the signals the web SDK passes: `category`, `url`,
`hasScreenshot`, `hasSelectedElement`, `hasNetworkErrors`,
`hasConsoleErrors` and `proactiveTrigger`.

## ONNX backend (experimental)

```ts
import { createOnnxClassifier } from '@mushi-mushi/wasm-classifier'

const classifier = await createOnnxClassifier({
  modelUrl: 'https://cdn.your-app.com/mushi/model.onnx',
  cacheKey: 'model-v1',
  preload: true,
  classifyTimeoutMs: 750,
})
```

If `onnxruntime-web` is missing, the model fetch fails, or a call exceeds
`classifyTimeoutMs`, it falls back to the heuristic backend. The package does
not ship a model.

  Model inference is not implemented yet. The ONNX backend loads the runtime
  and downloads your model, then still returns heuristic verdicts (`modelId:
  'heuristic-fallback'`, a reason starting "ONNX inference is not
  implemented yet", and one console warning). Use
  `createHeuristicClassifier()` until that changes.

## JavaScript bug reporting SDK for the browser

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/sdks/web

---
title: JavaScript bug reporting SDK for the browser
description: Reference for @mushi-mushi/web, the Mushi Mushi browser SDK. Screenshots, console and network capture, the Shadow DOM widget, sampling, beforeSend and privacy.
---

# `@mushi-mushi/web`

The Mushi Mushi browser SDK: screenshots, console logs, network breadcrumbs, and a
report widget in a Shadow DOM so your CSS never leaks in or out.

  **Migrating from another bug-capture tool?** We have step-by-step guides
  for [Instabug / Luciq](/migrations/instabug-to-mushi),
  [Shake](/migrations/shake-to-mushi),
  [LogRocket Feedback](/migrations/logrocket-feedback-to-mushi),
  [BugHerd](/migrations/bugherd-to-mushi), and
  [Pendo Feedback](/migrations/pendo-feedback-to-mushi). Each maps the
  competitor's API to the Mushi Mushi equivalent and includes an interactive
  checklist.

See [Quickstart → Vanilla JS](/quickstart/web) for setup. Notable extras:

- **XHR + fetch network capture.** The SDK patches both `XMLHttpRequest` and
  `window.fetch` globally at `init()`. Every network request (including legacy
  jQuery/axios XHR calls) is captured as a `MushiNetworkEntry` and appears in
  the Network breadcrumbs tab. Calling `destroy()` removes the patches; if
  another APM tool (Sentry, Datadog) has since wrapped the same globals, the
  SDK detects the unsafe state and leaves the native references alone.
- **`runtimeConfig: 'auto'`** fetches console settings from `GET /v1/sdk/config`
  and merges them over host init. Host-wired banner and capture flags win over
  console defaults. See [Runtime config](/concepts/runtime-config).
- **`proactive: { rageClick, errorBoundary, longTask, apiCascade, pageDwell, firstSession, cooldown }`**:
  friction detectors that open the reporter contextually (rage clicks, error
  boundaries, long tasks, API cascades, page dwell, first session). Subscribe
  with `mushi.on('proactive:triggered', ({ data }) => …)` (`proactive:dismissed`
  fires on close) and cap frequency with `cooldown`.
- **`beforeSend((report) => report | null)`**: last-mile transform after
  built-in PII scrub. Return `null` to drop the report client-side. Prefer
  this over the deprecated `beforeSendFeedback` (feedback-only).
- **`sampleRate` / `replaySampleRate`**: probabilistic gates for automatic
  error reports and session replay (see below). User-initiated feedback is
  never sampled out.
- **Built-in PII scrubber**: always on; masks emails, phones, SSNs,
  credit-card-shaped strings, JWTs and vendor API keys (see the
  [pattern table](/sdks/core#pii-scrubbing-utilities-127)). It has no init option. To remove
  anything else, edit or drop the report in `beforeSend`.

---

## Sampling & `beforeSend`

High-traffic apps can thin automatic capture without turning off the widget:

```typescript
Mushi.init({
  projectId: '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000',
  apiKey: 'mushi_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx',
  // Automatic (non-user) error reports only — feedback always sends
  sampleRate: 0.1,
  // Session replay: decision once at init; sampled-out sessions never load rrweb
  replaySampleRate: 0.2,
  beforeSend: (report) => {
    if (report.description?.includes('internal-only')) return null
    return report
  },
})
```

| Option | Default | Applies to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sampleRate` | `1` | Automatic error/exception reports. Range `0`–`1`. |
| `replaySampleRate` | `1` | Whether this session records replay. Independent of `sampleRate`. |
| `beforeSend` | — | Every report type after PII scrub. Async OK. |
| `beforeSendFeedback` | — | **Deprecated.** Feedback-only; ignored when `beforeSend` is set. |

Types live on `MushiConfig` in `@mushi-mushi/core`.

---

## Screenshot preview & consent (1.19+)

When screenshot capture is enabled (`capture.screenshot: 'on-report'` or
`'auto'`), the report screen shows a **visible preview** of the image that will
be attached, not just a "Screenshot attached ✓" label. Reporters can **Remove**
the screenshot before submit and optionally read a **privacy caption** beneath
the preview.

```typescript
Mushi.init({
  projectId: '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000', // UUID from Projects page
  apiKey: 'mushi_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx',        // report:write key
  widget: {
    // true  → localized default caption (en/es/ja/th/zh)
    // string → your compliance copy verbatim
    // false → hide caption (preview + Remove still show)
    screenshotSensitiveHint: true,
  },
  capture: { screenshot: 'on-report' },
})
```

Tune the caption from the admin console (**Projects → SDK install → Screenshot
privacy caption**) without rebuilding. It travels in `GET /v1/sdk/config` under
`widget.screenshotSensitiveHint`.

The preview stays in sync if the reporter uses **Mark up** (highlight, blur, arrow).
Keep `img-src data:` in your CSP when using screenshots on locked-down pages.
See the [Next.js App Router + CSP recipe](/sdks/nextjs-app-router-csp).

Maintainer deep-dive:
[SDK_SCREENSHOT_PREVIEW.md](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/blob/master/docs/SDK_SCREENSHOT_PREVIEW.md)

---

## Runtime config merge (Jul 2026+)

When `runtimeConfig` is `'auto'`, the SDK merges console settings from
`GET /v1/sdk/config` over your `init()` config. Explicit host wiring wins: if
you set `widget: { trigger: 'banner' }`, a console default of `launcher: 'auto'`
no longer hides the banner.

Capture flags merge key-by-key: only values the console explicitly configured
replace host values. Unconfigured console defaults are omitted so they cannot
clobber host init.

See [Runtime config](/concepts/runtime-config) for the setup default and
troubleshooting table. Maintainer deep-dive:
[SDK_RUNTIME_CONFIG.md](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/blob/master/docs/SDK_RUNTIME_CONFIG.md).

---

## Capture availability & errors

Screenshot and element-picker buttons hide when that capture mode is unavailable
(permission denied, unsupported browser, or disabled in config). When capture
fails at runtime, the widget shows a short inline error instead of a dead button.
The SDK sets this availability itself; there is no public method to call.

---

## Description draft persistence

Typed report text (description, email, follow-up reply) survives background panel
re-renders, for example when runtime config refreshes or the route changes.
Drafts clear on successful submit or when the reporter opens a new session.

## Identifying users & the Rewards program

Call `identify()` as soon as your auth state resolves. The SDK links all
subsequent reports and activity events to that user identity server-side.

```typescript
// On login / auth state change
const { user } = await supabase.auth.getUser()
if (user) {
  mushi.identify(user.id, {
    email: user.email,
    name: user.user_metadata?.full_name,
    provider: 'supabase',
  })
}
```

`identify()` is idempotent: calling it again with the same `userId` and traits
does nothing, and calling it with new traits updates them. Calling it with a
different `userId` switches the identity used for later reports and activity.

### Enabling the Rewards program

Add a `rewards` block to your `init()` config:

```typescript
import { Mushi } from '@mushi-mushi/web'

const mushi = Mushi.init({
  projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
  apiKey: 'YOUR_API_KEY',
  rewards: {
    enabled: true,
    trackActivity: true,        // auto-capture first route visits and [data-testid] clicks
    consentMode: 'explicit',    // 'explicit' | 'auto'
    showInWidget: true,         // show tier + points in the bug-report widget
    flushIntervalMs: 300_000,   // how often to POST activity (min 30s)
  },
})
```

`trackActivity: true` automatically captures:

| Action | Trigger |
|--------|---------|
| `screen_view_unique_per_day` | First visit to each route during the page session (`history.pushState`, `popstate`, or a DOM change under ``). Despite the name, the SDK remembers visited routes in memory only, so a reload counts them again |
| `element_selected` | Clicks on `[data-testid]` elements |

With rewards enabled, the SDK also records `session_minute` once a minute
while the page is open (up to 60 minutes a day), whether or not
`trackActivity` is on. Nothing is sent until the user has opted in and
`identify()` has been called.

For custom actions:

```typescript
mushi.recordActivity('lesson_complete', { lessonId: 'l_123', score: 0.9 })
```

### Querying points & tier

```typescript
// Current user's points
const points = await mushi.getReputation()
// → { totalPoints, points30d, reputation, confirmedBugs, totalReports }

// Current tier
const tier = await mushi.getTier()
// → { id, slug, displayName, pointsThreshold, perks } | null
```

See [Concepts → Rewards & contributor identity](/concepts/rewards) for the
full data model, anti-gaming integration, and webhook reference.

## Reporter API

Let reporters see and follow up on their own submissions without a login. Every
method is keyed to the persistent anonymous `reporterToken` the SDK stores in
`localStorage`, so no auth wiring is required.

```typescript
// The reporter's own report history (newest first)
const reports = await mushi.listMyReports()
// → MushiReporterReport[]  (each carries `unread_count` for a badge)

// The comment thread on one of their reports
const comments = await mushi.listMyComments(reportId)
// → MushiReporterComment[]  (their comments + team replies)

// Post a follow-up comment on their own report
const comment = await mushi.replyToReport(reportId, 'Still happening on iOS 18')
// → MushiReporterComment | null

// The project's public contributor leaderboard
const leaders = await mushi.getHallOfFame(10)
// → MushiHallOfFameEntry[]  (display_name, tier_name, points_30d, total_points)
```

All four methods fail soft: they return `[]` / `null` (never throw) when the
network is down or no reporter token exists yet, so they're safe to call on
first render.

### React

The same methods are exposed on the `useMushi()` hook, memoised so they're
stable across renders:

```tsx
import { useMushi } from '@mushi-mushi/react'

function MyReports() {
  const { listMyReports, replyToReport } = useMushi()
  // ... call inside an effect or event handler
}
```

`useMushi()` returns no-op fallbacks (`() => Promise.resolve([])`) before the
SDK finishes initialising, so you never need to null-check the instance.

---

## Hash-routed SPAs (e.g. React Router ``, Backbone, legacy apps)

Hash-routed SPAs navigate via `location.hash` changes (`#/login`, `#/article/my-post`).
The Mushi Mushi web SDK subscribes to `hashchange` automatically, so every navigation is
captured as a timeline entry. To group parametric routes in the **Inventory**,
supply `/#/`-prefixed route templates:

```typescript
Mushi.init({
  projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
  apiKey: 'YOUR_API_KEY',
  capture: {
    discoverInventory: {
      enabled: true,
      routeTemplates: [
        '/#/article/[slug]',   // matches #/article/my-post → /#/article/[slug]
        '/#/profile/[username]',
      ],
    },
  },
})
```

**Why the `/#/` prefix?** Hash fragments are not part of the pathname.
When a hash route is present Mushi stores `'/#' + hashPath` (the pathname is
dropped); otherwise it stores the plain pathname. History-based routes
(`/article/[slug]`) and hash routes (`/#/article/[slug]`) therefore stay
distinct in the Inventory and can be monitored independently.

**Filter params** (e.g. `#/?tag=elixir&offset=10`) are stripped before the route
template is matched; only the path segment after `#/` is matched.

**Without templates**, every unique hash path becomes its own Inventory row.
For slug-heavy apps (articles, profiles, products) this inflates the Inventory;
route templates collapse them to a manageable list.

**`mushi doctor --host-app`** detects hash-router usage in your source files and
warns when `/#/` route templates are missing from your Mushi init call.

## BugHerd → Mushi Mushi

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/migrations/bugherd-to-mushi

---
title: 'BugHerd → Mushi Mushi'
description: Move from BugHerd to Mushi Mushi. Map pin-to-element feedback to Mushi's element picker, screenshot markup and metadata capture, with an interactive checklist.
---

# BugHerd → Mushi Mushi

 

BugHerd's signature feature is **pixel-pin annotations**: clients click
on a part of a web page to attach a comment to that exact element. Mushi
Mushi gives similar element-level context: in the web widget the reporter
can pick an element, and the report records its tag, id / class, XPath
and position, next to a screenshot they can mark up.

  Mushi doesn't replicate BugHerd's Kanban task board. If your
  client-feedback workflow depends on the Kanban view, plan for a workflow
  change as well as a tool change.

## Why switch

- **Open source.** Mushi's SDKs are MIT; its server and admin console are
  AGPLv3.
- **Self-host.** Mushi runs on your own infrastructure.
- **AI triage.** Mushi categorises and prioritises reports automatically,
  which helps when client feedback is noisy.
- **Developer context.** Reports carry console and network logs, so a
  developer can often reproduce the bug without asking the client.

## API mapping

| BugHerd | Mushi |
|---------|-------|
| `` | `` mounting `Mushi.init({ projectId, apiKey })` |
| Sidebar widget (always visible) | The Mushi launcher (by default a floating button on desktop, an edge tab on phones), opens on click |
| Element click → annotation | User opens the widget → picks an element, marks up the screenshot |
| `window.BugHerdConfig = { reporter: { email } }` | `mushi.setUser({ id, email, name })` |
| Project task board | Mushi admin console, Reports page |
| Hiding sensitive content from screenshots | Add `data-mushi-redact` to the element (or list selectors in `privacy.redactSelectors`) |

## Before / After

```html
<!-- BEFORE — BugHerd -->
<script type="text/javascript">
  (function(d,t) {
    var bh = d.createElement(t); bh.async = true;
    bh.type = 'text/javascript';
    bh.src = 'https://www.bugherd.com/sidebarv2.js?apikey=YOUR_API_KEY';
    var s = d.getElementsByTagName(t)[0]; s.parentNode.insertBefore(bh, s);
  })(document, 'script');
</script>
```

```html
<!-- AFTER — Mushi (web) -->
<script type="module">
  import { Mushi } from 'https://esm.sh/@mushi-mushi/web'
  const mushi = Mushi.init({
    projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
    apiKey:    'YOUR_PUBLIC_KEY',
  })  // default launcher: floating button on desktop, edge tab on phones
  // later, once you know the client: mushi.setUser({ id, email, name })
</script>
```

For React / Vue / Svelte / Next, use the framework-specific SDK instead.

## Migration checklist

Sign in to the Mushi admin console; copy projectId + apiKey.</> },
    { id: 'install', label: 'Install or script-tag Mushi', content: {`# CDN, for the same script-tag setup BugHerd had:

  import { Mushi } from 'https://esm.sh/@mushi-mushi/web'
  Mushi.init({ projectId: '...', apiKey: '...' })

# Or via npm:
npm install @mushi-mushi/web`} },
    { id: 'mount-mushi', label: 'Add Mushi alongside BugHerd', content: <>Both can coexist for a few days while you train clients on the new UX.</> },
    { id: 'redact', label: 'Mark sensitive elements with data-mushi-redact', content: {`<!-- Blacked out in Mushi screenshots -->

<!-- Password inputs and autocomplete="cc-*" fields are always redacted -->`} },
    { id: 'identify-user', label: 'Wire client identity (mushi.setUser)', content: <>If you passed the reporter&apos;s email to BugHerd through BugHerdConfig.reporter, call {`mushi.setUser({ id, email, name })`} on the instance from Mushi.init(). Useful when the same client reports across several pages.</> },
    { id: 'client-comms', label: 'Tell clients about the new widget', content: <>The biggest difference: BugHerd's sidebar is always visible. Mushi's widget is a floating button (an edge tab on phones) that opens on click. Send clients a one-line note so they know what to look for.</> },
    { id: 'verify', label: 'Submit a test report from a real page', content: <>Open the widget, pick an element, write a description, and confirm the screenshot and element details are attached and the report lands in the Mushi admin console.</> },
    { id: 'remove-bugherd', label: 'Remove the BugHerd script + revoke the API key', content: <>Once clients are on Mushi for ≥ a week, pull the script tag and revoke BugHerd's API key in their dashboard.</> },

/>

## Feature parity

| Capability | BugHerd | Mushi |
|------------|---------|-------|
| User-triggered report | ✅ | ✅ |
| Screenshot capture | ✅ | ✅ |
| Element context | ✅ (pixel pin) | ✅ (picked element: tag, id / class, XPath, position) |
| Console + network capture | not checked | ✅ |
| Sidebar / always-visible | ✅ | ❌ (floating button) |
| Project Kanban board | ✅ | ❌ (report inbox + filters) |
| Client guest accounts | ✅ | ❌ (anonymous reports OK; named clients via `setUser`) |
| Visual annotations on screenshot | ✅ | ✅ (highlight, blur, arrow; web) |
| Self-host | not checked | ✅ |
| AI triage | not checked | ✅ |

If pinning comments to exact spots on the page is central to your client
workflow, BugHerd is built around that and may suit you better.

## Migration: Capacitor → React Native

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/migrations/capacitor-to-react-native

---
title: 'Migration: Capacitor → React Native'
description: Port an Ionic or Capacitor app to React Native. A full plan with a Mushi Mushi API map and CI/CD recipes for Expo EAS or React Native CLI with Fastlane.
---

# Capacitor → React Native

 

A porting plan for Ionic / Capacitor apps that want to move to React
Native, with **two** end-to-end CI/CD options: Expo + EAS Build (the
easy, paid path) and React Native CLI + GitHub Actions + Fastlane (the
cost-sensitive path). Mushi Mushi bug reporting keeps working throughout.

  The full plan (ready-to-paste GitHub Actions YAML for Android and iOS,
  the Fastlane match recipe, the Capacitor → RN plugin map, the Mushi SDK
  API mapping, the 6-week timeline, and the go/no-go checklist) lives in
  the repo at
  [`docs/migrations/capacitor-to-react-native.md`](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/blob/master/docs/migrations/capacitor-to-react-native.md).
  This page is the public summary; the linked file is the contract.

## TL;DR

| Path | Cost / month | Speed to first build | Maintenance | Recommended for |
|------|--------------|----------------------|-------------|-----------------|
| **A: Expo + EAS Build** | EAS Starter $19 or Production $199, plus usage | Hours | Lowest | Teams that want zero CI ops |
| **B: React Native CLI + GitHub Actions + Fastlane** | $0 + GH Actions minutes (or $0 on a self-hosted Mac mini) | 2–3 days | Medium | Cost-sensitive, GitHub-Actions-native teams |

The repo plan was written for Expo SDK 55 and React Native 0.83. Current
releases are Expo SDK 58 and React Native 0.88 (npm, 2026-10-29); check
each tool's upgrade notes before you start. Both paths use the New
Architecture (Fabric / Bridgeless). EAS prices from
[expo.dev/pricing](https://expo.dev/pricing), 2026-10-29.

## Web strategy

You have three options for the **web** experience after porting the native app:

1. **Keep Next.js, port only mobile.** Suits SEO-sensitive marketing sites.
2. **RN Web for the app shell + Next.js for marketing.** One app, two surfaces.
3. **Full RN Web.** Single codebase, with SEO trade-offs.

Option 1 is usually the simplest. You can run `@mushi-mushi/web` on the
marketing site and `@mushi-mushi/react-native` in the new app against the
same project ID and API key at the same time.

## Mushi Mushi during the migration

The single most important property: **you do not change anything on the
Mushi side.** Same project, same API key, same admin console. Reports from
the Capacitor build and the React Native build land in the same inbox.

### API mapping at a glance

| Capacitor (`Mushi.*`) | React Native | Notes |
|-----------------------|--------------|-------|
| `Mushi.configure({ projectId, apiKey })` | `` | Provider replaces the imperative call |
| `Mushi.report({ description, category })` | `useMushiReport().submitReport(...)` hook | Returns `{ submitReport }`, which takes `{ description, category }` |
| `Mushi.showWidget()` | `useMushiWidget().open()` | Same effect |
| `Mushi.setUser({ user: { id, email } })` | `useMushi().setUser({ id, email })` | RN takes the user object directly |
| `Mushi.setMetadata({ key, value })` | `useMushi().setMetadata(key, value)` | Two arguments |
| `Mushi.flushQueue()` | _Automatic_ | The provider flushes its offline queue on mount and when the network comes back; there is no manual flush |
| `triggerMode: 'shake'` | `config.widget.trigger: 'shake'` | Same vocabulary; needs the `expo-sensors` peer |
| `captureScreenshot: boolean` | `config.capture.screenshot: boolean` | Needs the `react-native-view-shot` peer |

### Before / after

```ts
// BEFORE — Capacitor
import { Mushi } from '@mushi-mushi/capacitor'

await Mushi.configure({
  projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
  apiKey:    process.env.PUBLIC_MUSHI_KEY,
  triggerMode: 'shake',
  captureScreenshot: true,
})
```

```tsx
// AFTER — React Native
import { MushiProvider } from '@mushi-mushi/react-native'

export default function App() {
  return (
    <MushiProvider
      projectId="YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
      apiKey={process.env.EXPO_PUBLIC_MUSHI_KEY!}
      config={{
        widget:  { trigger: 'shake' },   // npx expo install expo-sensors
        capture: { screenshot: true },   // npx expo install react-native-view-shot
      }}
    >
      <RootNavigator />
    </MushiProvider>
  )
}
```

### Get the snippet from the admin console

The **Install SDK** card in the admin console (Onboarding, Projects → your
project, Settings → SDK & connection) has **React Native**, **Expo**, and
**Capacitor** tabs alongside React / Vue / Svelte / Vanilla. The snippets
are populated with your real project ID and (right after a key mint) your
real API key.

The mobile trigger settings additionally persist to the project's runtime
SDK config, so future builds pick them up without a redeploy.

### Or use the CLI

```bash
cd your-rn-app
npx mushi-mushi init
```

The CLI auto-detects `react-native`, `expo`, and `@capacitor/core` and
writes the matching boilerplate. Capacitor users get `Mushi.configure(...)`
(`Mushi.init(...)` is an alias for it).

The full plan in
[`docs/migrations/capacitor-to-react-native.md`](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/blob/master/docs/migrations/capacitor-to-react-native.md)

1. Decision matrix: should you migrate at all?

## Cordova → Capacitor

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/migrations/cordova-to-capacitor

---
title: 'Cordova → Capacitor'
description: Migrate a Cordova app to Capacitor in place (same web code, a new native shell) and add Mushi Mushi bug reporting with @mushi-mushi/capacitor.
---

# Cordova → Capacitor

 

Capacitor, built by the Ionic team, is a successor to Cordova. This guide
migrates an existing Cordova app to Capacitor in place (same web codebase,
new native shell) and mounts Mushi Mushi with the `@mushi-mushi/capacitor`
plugin.

The official upstream guide is [capacitorjs.com/cordova](https://capacitorjs.com/cordova);
this page is the Mushi-aware companion to it.

## Why migrate

- Check whether the Cordova plugins you depend on are still maintained;
  most common ones have an official Capacitor counterpart (table below).
- Capacitor's native projects are first-class (`ios/`, `android/`): you
  commit them and edit them like any other Xcode / Android Studio project.
- Mushi has a Capacitor plugin ([`@mushi-mushi/capacitor`](/sdks/capacitor))
  with native shake-to-report and screenshot capture. There is no Mushi
  Cordova plugin; in a Cordova app you would have run `@mushi-mushi/web`
  inside the WebView.

## Prerequisites

- Working Cordova app that builds for at least one platform.
- For Capacitor 8: Node 22+, Xcode 26+ for iOS, Android Studio 2025.2.1+
  for Android ([environment setup](https://capacitorjs.com/docs/getting-started/environment-setup)).
- A Mushi project. If you already use `@mushi-mushi/web` in the Cordova
  app, keep the same `projectId` and `apiKey`.

## API mapping (Cordova plugins → Capacitor)

Most popular Cordova plugins have a 1:1 Capacitor counterpart:

| Cordova plugin | Capacitor equivalent |
|----------------|----------------------|
| `cordova-plugin-camera` | `@capacitor/camera` |
| `cordova-plugin-geolocation` | `@capacitor/geolocation` |
| `cordova-plugin-statusbar` | `@capacitor/status-bar` |
| `cordova-plugin-splashscreen` | `@capacitor/splash-screen` |
| `cordova-plugin-network-information` | `@capacitor/network` |
| `cordova-plugin-device` | `@capacitor/device` |
| `cordova-plugin-file` | `@capacitor/filesystem` |
| `cordova-plugin-inappbrowser` | `@capacitor/browser` |
| `cordova-plugin-clipboard` | `@capacitor/clipboard` |
| `cordova-plugin-vibration` | `@capacitor/haptics` |
| `cordova-plugin-share` | `@capacitor/share` |
| `cordova-plugin-firebase-messaging` | `@capacitor/push-notifications` + `@capacitor-firebase/messaging` |
| `cordova-sqlite-storage` | `@capacitor-community/sqlite` |
| `@mushi-mushi/web` in the WebView | `@mushi-mushi/capacitor` (adds native shake and screenshots) |

For anything not listed, search the [Capacitor Plugins](https://capacitorjs.com/docs/plugins)
catalog or the [Capawesome community plugins](https://capawesome.io/plugins/).

## Common gotchas

- **iOS scheme defaults changed.** Capacitor uses `capacitor://` by default
  on iOS. If your app stores anything under origin-bound web APIs
  (LocalStorage, cookies, IndexedDB), set `server.iosScheme: "ionic"` in
  `capacitor.config.json` to keep the origin Cordova used and avoid
  losing user data.
- **Splash hide timing.** `@capacitor/splash-screen` hides itself after
  `launchShowDuration` by default (`launchAutoHide: true`). To hide it
  when your app is ready instead, set `launchAutoHide: false` and call
  `SplashScreen.hide()` once your app is mounted.
- **`whitelist` plugin gone.** Capacitor uses native ATS (iOS) and
  `usesCleartextTraffic` (Android) instead of Cordova's whitelist. Add your
  Mushi endpoint and any other API hosts to those if you allow non-HTTPS.

## Rollback

You branched in step 1, so:

```bash
git checkout main
# Capacitor's ios/ and android/ projects were committed on the migration
# branch only, so main still has the Cordova app.
```

If you committed and pushed before discovering a regression, revert the
merge commit; Cordova builds will start working again immediately.

## Cordova → React Native

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/migrations/cordova-to-react-native

---
title: 'Cordova → React Native'
description: Move a Cordova app to React Native in two hops (stabilise on Capacitor first, then port screen by screen) without losing Mushi Mushi bug reporting.
---

# Cordova → React Native

 

A two-hop migration: stabilise on Capacitor first, then port screen-by-screen
to React Native. This is the safest path if your Cordova app is non-trivial,
because it lets you ship features the whole time instead of feature-freezing
for a full rewrite.

If your app is small (a handful of screens, no deep native plugin
dependencies) you can skip the Capacitor stop and port directly to RN.
See **Path B** below.

  This guide composes two existing guides. Read them in order:
  [Cordova → Capacitor](/migrations/cordova-to-capacitor) first, then
  [Capacitor → React Native](/migrations/capacitor-to-react-native).
  Mushi Mushi stays on the same project the whole way through.

## Why migrate

You're on Cordova and want to end up on React Native because:

- **Performance.** WebView-based shells can struggle with long scrolling
  lists, chat views and animations. React Native renders native views.
- **Native API access.** Newer iOS / Android APIs (App Intents,
  WidgetKit, Health, etc.) are often reachable through Expo modules or
  community libraries.
- **Hiring.** React Native engineers are usually easier to find than
  Cordova ones.

You should NOT migrate if:

- You ship daily and cannot afford a feature freeze on the mobile surface.
- Your differentiator is web-first SEO (RN Web is OK, but Next.js is better).
- Your app is mostly a thin wrapper around a great mobile web experience.

## Two paths

### Path A: Cordova → Capacitor → React Native (recommended)

Lower-risk because you stay shippable at every step.

1. **Week 1-2.** Migrate Cordova → Capacitor following
   [that guide](/migrations/cordova-to-capacitor). Ship to production. This
   alone is a meaningful win (better debugging, modern WebView, modern
   plugin ecosystem).
2. **Week 3-8.** Migrate Capacitor → React Native following
   [that guide](/migrations/capacitor-to-react-native). Dual-ship for a
   couple of weeks before sunsetting the Capacitor build.

This is what we recommend for any app with > ~10 screens or > 5 native
plugins.

### Path B: Direct Cordova → React Native

Faster end-to-end, riskier mid-migration. Use only when:

- Your app has a small surface area (≤ 10 screens, ≤ 5 native plugins).
- You're comfortable feature-freezing the mobile surface for the full
  migration window.
- Your React/JS code is already well-isolated from Cordova plugin calls
  (you can swap call sites to RN equivalents directly).

## Mushi Mushi during the migration

Identical to [§ 7 of the Capacitor → React Native plan](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/blob/master/docs/migrations/capacitor-to-react-native.md#7-mushi-mushi-during-the-migration):
same project, same `apiKey`, dual-ship Cordova/Capacitor and RN at the
same time, sunset the legacy build only after the RN one has been stable for
a week in beta.

You'll touch the Mushi SDK exactly once per hop:

- **Hop 1 (Cordova → Capacitor):** replace `@mushi-mushi/web` in the
  WebView (if you used it) with [`@mushi-mushi/capacitor`](/sdks/capacitor)
  and call `Mushi.configure({ projectId, apiKey })`.
- **Hop 2 (Capacitor → React Native):** swap that for
  [`@mushi-mushi/react-native`](/sdks/react-native) and mount
  `` at the app root.

## Migration checklist (Path A)

Walk the plugin list once at the start. Anything without a Capacitor or RN equivalent is the long pole — budget time for a TurboModule wrapper.</> },

## Verification

- The Mushi Reports page shows reports from `@mushi-mushi/react-native`
  sent from a real device.
- Cold start on a mid-range Android device is no slower than the Cordova
  baseline (measure both; results vary by app).
- The crash rate in beta is no worse than the Cordova build's.

## Rollback

The strength of Path A is that **rollback is trivial at any step**: if the
RN build hits a wall in week 5, you simply keep shipping the Capacitor build
and pause RN work. The Cordova build is also still in your git history if
hop 1 itself goes sideways (rare but possible).

## Create React App → Vite

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/migrations/cra-to-vite

# Create React App → Vite

 

The React team deprecated Create React App on February 14, 2025: it has
no active maintainers and stays in maintenance mode
([React blog](https://react.dev/blog/2025/02/14/sunsetting-create-react-app)).
The same post lists Vite as one of the build tools to move to.

A community codemod handles much of the mechanical work:

```bash
npx migrate-to-vite@latest cra
```

This guide walks the rest.

  **Mushi Mushi keeps working** through this migration. The SDK doesn't
  care which bundler ships your app; only the env-var prefix changes
  (`REACT_APP_*` → `VITE_*`).

## Prerequisites

- A working CRA app (`react-scripts` ≥ 5).
- A Node version the current Vite supports (check the
  [Vite guide](https://vite.dev/guide/)).
- Mushi web SDK or React adapter already installed.

## Migration checklist

The codemod rewrites package.json, the entry HTML, and config files. Branch first so you can diff.</> },

## Common gotchas

- **`process.env`**. Vite doesn't inject `process.env` at build time. The
  codemod rewrites `process.env` to `import.meta.env`; grep for
  `REACT_APP_` to catch names that still need the `VITE_` prefix.
- **Absolute imports without aliases**. CRA had implicit absolute imports
  via `jsconfig.json` / `tsconfig.json` `baseUrl`. Vite respects
  `tsconfig.json` paths only through a plugin such as `vite-tsconfig-paths`
  or a `resolve.alias` entry; add one yourself.
- **Worker imports**. CRA used a webpack-specific `Worker` loader; Vite
  uses native `?worker` URL imports. The codemod won't migrate workers
  for you.
- **`@craco/craco` users.** If you used craco for custom webpack config,
  port those overrides to `vite.config.ts` plugins manually.

## Rollback

Branched in step 1, so a `git checkout main` reverts cleanly. If you've
already merged and found an issue after deploying, revert the merge. CRA
still builds; it is deprecated, not removed.

## Mushi Mushi compatibility

The Mushi web SDK and React adapter work the same on CRA and Vite. With
Vite, `MushiProvider` can also read `VITE_MUSHI_PROJECT_ID` and
`VITE_MUSHI_API_KEY` by itself when you don't pass `config`.

## Instabug (Luciq) → Mushi Mushi

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/migrations/instabug-to-mushi

---
title: 'Instabug (Luciq) → Mushi Mushi'
description: Replace Instabug (now Luciq) with Mushi Mushi for in-app bug reporting in React Native. Config mapping, shake-to-report, a beta validation pass and a checklist.
---

# Instabug (Luciq) → Mushi Mushi

 

  Instabug now ships as Luciq. Both it and Mushi Mushi do in-app bug
  capture, so the config maps closely. Luciq's SDKs are mobile (iOS,
  Android, React Native, Flutter, KMP); this page covers React Native. For
  native iOS / Android, see the [iOS](/sdks/ios) and [Android](/sdks/android)
  SDK pages.

## Why switch

- **Open source and price.** Mushi SDKs are MIT and the server is AGPLv3.
  Self-hosting is free; the cloud is free for one app and 100 diagnoses a
  month. Compare with your Luciq contract.
- **AI triage.** Mushi ships a built-in two-stage classifier
  (fast-filter + classify-report) that turns raw user reports into
  triaged tickets without manual review.
- **Self-host.** Mushi can run on your own Supabase / Postgres.

## API mapping

The calls on the right are on the instance from `useMushi()`
(`@mushi-mushi/react-native`).

| Instabug / Luciq (React Native) | Mushi Mushi |
|------------------|-------|
| `Luciq.init({ token, invocationEvents })` (older Instabug SDKs: `Instabug.init` / `Instabug.start`) | `` at the app root |
| `Luciq.show()` | `mushi.open()` |
| `Luciq.identifyUser(email, name, id)` | `mushi.setUser({ id, email, name })` |
| `Luciq.setUserAttribute(k, v)` | `mushi.setMetadata(k, v)` |
| Custom logs | Console, network and navigation are captured automatically; add your own with `mushi.addBreadcrumb({ category: 'custom', level: 'info', message })` |
| `invocationEvents: [InvocationEvent.shake]` | `config.widget.trigger: 'shake'` (needs `expo-sensors`) |
| `invocationEvents: [InvocationEvent.floatingButton]` | `config.widget.trigger: 'button'` (the default) |
| `invocationEvents: [shake, floatingButton]` | `config.widget.trigger: 'both'` |
| Repro steps | Captured automatically (console + network + navigation) |
| Crash reporting | **Stays where it is.** Mushi works next to Sentry / Crashlytics; it doesn't replace them. |

## Before / After (React Native)

```ts
// BEFORE: Luciq React Native
import Luciq, { InvocationEvent } from '@luciq/react-native'
Luciq.init({
  token: 'YOUR_TOKEN',
  invocationEvents: [InvocationEvent.shake],
})
Luciq.identifyUser('user@example.com', 'Jane Doe', 'user-42')
```

```tsx
// AFTER: Mushi Mushi React Native
import { MushiProvider } from '@mushi-mushi/react-native'

export default function App() {
  return (
    <MushiProvider
      projectId="YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
      apiKey="YOUR_PUBLIC_KEY"
      config={{ widget: { trigger: 'shake' } }}
    >
      <RootNavigator />
    </MushiProvider>
  )
}

// Inside any screen:
import { useEffect } from 'react'
import { useMushi } from '@mushi-mushi/react-native'
function ProfileScreen() {
  const mushi = useMushi()
  useEffect(() => {
    mushi.setUser({ id: 'user-42', email: 'user@example.com', name: 'Jane Doe' })
  }, [mushi])
  // ...
}
```

## Feature parity at a glance

| Capability | Instabug / Luciq | Mushi |
|------------|------------------|-------|
| Shake to report | ✅ | ✅ (`widget.trigger: 'shake'`, needs `expo-sensors`) |
| Floating button | ✅ | ✅ (`widget.trigger: 'button'`) |
| Screenshot on report | ✅ | ✅ (`capture.screenshot: true`, needs `react-native-view-shot`) |
| Console + network capture | ✅ | ✅ (default on) |
| Repro steps timeline | ✅ | ✅ (auto from console + network + navigation) |
| Crash reporting | ✅ | ❌ (keep Sentry / Crashlytics for crashes) |
| Surveys / NPS | ✅ | ❌ (out of scope) |

Mushi can also be self-hosted, its SDKs and server are open source, and it
runs AI triage on every report by default.

If you use Luciq's surveys, keep them on Luciq after moving bug capture
to Mushi.

## Rollback

If Mushi doesn't fit, remove the Mushi package and re-add the Luciq SDK.
Because this guide has you dual-ship for at least 3 days before removing
Luciq, you have both sets of reports to compare.

## LogRocket Feedback → Mushi Mushi

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/migrations/logrocket-feedback-to-mushi

---
title: 'LogRocket Feedback → Mushi Mushi'
description: Collect bug reports with Mushi Mushi while keeping LogRocket for session replay. Both SDKs run side by side, with a step-by-step checklist.
---

# LogRocket Feedback → Mushi Mushi

 

LogRocket is mainly session replay and product analytics. Its feedback
features are in-app Surveys (a paid add-on you configure in the LogRocket
dashboard, which can show a persistent rating and comment tab) and a
Feedback view that pulls in feedback from tools like Intercom, Zendesk and
the app stores. This guide moves in-app bug reporting to Mushi Mushi while
you keep LogRocket for session replay.

  **You can run both SDKs side by side indefinitely.** LogRocket records
  the session; Mushi captures the user's report. Mushi can attach a
  LogRocket session URL to every report via metadata, so triagers get
  one-click access to the replay.

## Why switch (the bug-report piece)

- **Bug reports, not ratings.** A Mushi report carries the user's
  description, a screenshot they can mark up, console and network logs,
  and (on the web) the page element they picked.
- **AI triage.** Mushi's two-stage classifier and judge loop turn raw
  reports into triaged tickets without a human pass.
- **Open-source server.** Mushi's server and console are AGPLv3, so you can
  self-host them for free. (LogRocket also offers self-hosting, as part of
  its paid plans.)
- **Privacy.** Mushi captures on user trigger, one report at a time. If
  LogRocket keeps recording sessions, keep using LogRocket's privacy
  controls too.

## API mapping

`const mushi = Mushi.init({...})` returns the instance used below.

| LogRocket | Mushi Mushi |
|-----------|-------|
| `LogRocket.init('app/id')` | `const mushi = Mushi.init({ projectId, apiKey })` (mounted separately) |
| `LogRocket.identify(uid, traits)` | `mushi.identify(uid, traits)` |
| `LogRocket.captureMessage(msg)` | `mushi.captureEvent({ description: msg })`, or let the user submit through the widget |
| `LogRocket.captureException(err)` | `mushi.captureException(err)` |
| `LogRocket.track(name, props)` | For repro context on the next report: `mushi.addBreadcrumb({ category: 'custom', level: 'info', message: name })`. For product analytics: `mushi.track(name, props)` (names must be `snake_case`; not attached to reports) |
| In-app survey / feedback tab | The Mushi widget (by default a floating button on desktop, an edge tab on phones), or your own button calling `mushi.open()` |
| `LogRocket.getSessionURL(cb)` | Attach the URL as metadata on Mushi reports (below) |

## Linking LogRocket session URLs into Mushi Mushi reports

With this, each Mushi report carries the LogRocket session URL, so
triagers can open the replay from the report.

```ts
import LogRocket from 'logrocket'
import { Mushi } from '@mushi-mushi/web'

LogRocket.init('your-app/id')
const mushi = Mushi.init({ projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID', apiKey: 'YOUR_PUBLIC_KEY' })

// LogRocket calls this again when a new session starts.
LogRocket.getSessionURL((sessionUrl) => {
  mushi.setMetadata('logrocketSession', sessionUrl)
})

LogRocket.identify('user-42', { email: 'jane@example.com' })
mushi.identify('user-42', { email: 'jane@example.com' })
```

Every Mushi report now carries the LogRocket session URL in its metadata.

    { id: 'mount-mushi', label: 'Mount Mushi (LogRocket stays as-is)', content: {`import LogRocket from 'logrocket'

const mushi = Mushi.init({ projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID', apiKey: 'YOUR_PUBLIC_KEY' })`} },

## Feature parity (feedback only; replay is its own product)

| Capability | LogRocket Feedback | Mushi |
|------------|-------------------|-------|
| User-triggered feedback in the app | ✅ (Surveys add-on: rating + comment) | ✅ (bug report widget) |
| Screenshot in the report | Session replay instead | ✅ (with markup on web) |
| Console + network capture | ✅ (in the replay) | ✅ |
| Self-host | ✅ (paid plans) | ✅ (free) |
| Open-source server | ❌ (SDK is MIT) | ✅ |
| Session replay | ✅ | Opt-in, sampled (`capture.replay`); keep LogRocket if replay is central |
| Heatmaps | ✅ | ❌ |
| Funnels / analytics | ✅ | ✅ (basic, from `mushi.track()`) |

The takeaway: **Mushi replaces in-app bug reporting, not the replay**.
Keep LogRocket for replay; use Mushi for bug reports that arrive with
context, an AI diagnosis and a ready fix.

## Mushi Mushi SDK upgrades (0.x → 1.x)

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/migrations/mushi-sdk-upgrade

---
title: 'Mushi Mushi SDK upgrades (0.x → 1.x)'
description: Upgrade @mushi-mushi packages from 0.x to the current 1.x releases. The real breaking changes by package, the version-bump command, and the current versions.
---

# Mushi Mushi SDK upgrades (0.x → 1.x)

 

  **Most packages are on 1.x.** `@mushi-mushi/core` 1.33.4, `web` and
  `react` 1.33.3, `node` 1.3.4, `capacitor` 1.1.4, `vue` / `svelte` /
  `angular` 1.0.4 (npm, 2026-10-29). `@mushi-mushi/react-native` is still
  0.x (0.24.4). The native iOS and Android SDKs are 0.4.0 and are not on
  npm. Read each package&apos;s CHANGELOG, then run `npx mushi-mushi upgrade`
  to bump versions.

## Breaking changes from 0.x

Taken from the 1.0.0 entries in each package&apos;s `CHANGELOG.md`, except the React Native `endpoint` row, which comes from the SDK source (React Native is still 0.x):

| Package | What changed at 1.0 | What you do |
|---------|---------------------|-------------|
| `@mushi-mushi/core`, `web`, `react` | No breaking changes from 0.9. 1.0 added `identify`, `setTag` / `setTags` / `clearTag`, `addBreadcrumb` and structured `captureException`. | Bump the version. |
| `@mushi-mushi/vue` | `MushiPlugin` calls `Mushi.init()` itself and depends on `@mushi-mushi/web`. | Remove your own `Mushi.init(config)` call and the separate `@mushi-mushi/web` install. |
| `@mushi-mushi/svelte` | `initMushi()` calls `Mushi.init()` itself. | Remove your own `Mushi.init(config)` call. |
| `@mushi-mushi/angular` | `provideMushi()` calls `Mushi.init()` itself. | Remove your own `Mushi.init(config)` call. |
| `@mushi-mushi/capacitor` | `Mushi.configure()` is the init call (`Mushi.init()` is now an alias for it). API keys use the `mushi_*` format. | Check your key starts with `mushi_`. |
| `@mushi-mushi/node` | Stable 1.0 API, no functional changes from 0.x. | Bump the version. |
| `@mushi-mushi/react-native` (still 0.x) | `MushiProvider` accepts a `config` object as well as bare props, and reads env vars when neither is set. `endpoint` is deprecated in favour of `apiEndpoint`. | Rename `endpoint` to `apiEndpoint`. |

## What stays stable

Within 1.x, these are meant not to break:

- The `Mushi.init({ projectId, apiKey })` shape and the instance it returns.
- Instance methods such as `setUser`, `setMetadata`, `captureEvent`,
  `captureException`, `open` and `report({ category })`.
- The `` component in React (and the framework equivalents).
- Wire-format API endpoints (`/v1/reports`, `/v1/admin/*`).
- The MCP server protocol.

Check the CHANGELOG before bumping for:

- Internal capture types exported via `@mushi-mushi/core`.
- Bundled-CSS export paths and default privacy-redaction lists.

If you build only against the documented public API (everything under
`/sdks/*` in these docs), most upgrades are a single version bump.

## Migration checklist

Each package ships its own CHANGELOG.md in the GitHub repo (e.g. @mushi-mushi/web). Skim the latest entry for breaking changes.</> },

## Native iOS / Android → Hybrid

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/migrations/native-to-hybrid

---
title: 'Native iOS / Android → Hybrid'
description: Should you wrap a native iOS or Android app in Capacitor or React Native? When it pays off, how to do it, and where the Mushi Mushi SDKs fit either way.
---

# Native iOS / Android → Hybrid

 

When (and how) to wrap an existing pure-native iOS / Android app with
**Capacitor** or **React Native**, keeping the platform Mushi Mushi SDKs in
place.

This is a strategic guide more than a tactical one. Many apps that get
this far don't need to migrate, so read "Should you migrate?" first.

## Should you migrate?

Migrate if **two or more** of these are true:

- ☐ You're shipping the same feature twice in Swift and Kotlin and the
  parity work is eating > 30 % of your engineering time.
- ☐ You have an existing web app whose UI you'd like to share with mobile.
- ☐ Your app's core surface is forms / lists / chat / dashboards (high JS
  affinity); not games, AR, video editors, or audio DSP.
- ☐ You're losing native engineers and can hire React engineers more
  easily.

DON'T migrate if:

- Your app's value is performance-bound native (camera, GL, audio, VPN).
- Your team is happy and ships steadily on native.
- You can't afford a 6–12 month parallel-track migration.

If you proceed, the realistic outcome is **hybrid**: most of your screens
in JS, a handful of performance-critical surfaces left in Swift / Kotlin,
bridged to JS via TurboModules (RN) or Capacitor plugins.

## Pick a target shell

| | Capacitor | React Native |
|---|-----------|--------------|
| **Reuse web codebase** | Yes (it IS the web app, in a WebView) | Mostly — RN uses React but not DOM components |
| **Native fidelity** | WebView ceiling | ~Native, with effort |
| **Migration size** | Smaller (you can wrap a static export) | Larger (every screen is rewritten) |
| **Team profile** | Web devs only | React devs + some native fluency |
| **Mushi support** | [`@mushi-mushi/capacitor`](/sdks/capacitor) + [`@mushi-mushi/web`](/sdks/web) for the WebView | [`@mushi-mushi/react-native`](/sdks/react-native) |

Pick **Capacitor** if you already have a strong web product and just need
a native shell. Pick **React Native** if you want to ship native UX from
JS and you don't have a meaningful web app.

## Migration checklist

List every screen, native module, and platform integration. Mark each as: port to JS, keep native + bridge, or delete. Anything performance-critical (camera, AR, audio) usually stays native.</> },
    { id: 'spike', label: 'Run a 2-week spike on the most complex screen', content: <>Don't commit to a 12-month migration based on the easy screens. Pick the worst one (most native code, most edge cases) and port it first. If it takes &gt; 2 weeks, recalibrate the timeline upward.</> },
    { id: 'shell', label: 'Pick the shell: Capacitor or React Native', content: <>Use the table above. The earlier you commit, the better; switching mid-migration costs 2-3x.</> },
    { id: 'design-system', label: 'Port the design system', content: <>Tokens (colors, type scale, spacing) come over first. Components follow. Aim for visual parity within ± 2 px before porting any screens.</> },
    { id: 'pilot', label: 'Pilot one user-facing flow end-to-end', content: <>Pick a low-risk flow (e.g., Settings). Ship it as a hybrid screen embedded in the existing native app — your shell can host both worlds during the migration.</> },
    { id: 'mushi', label: 'Wire Mushi: keep the native SDK AND add the JS one', content: <>If you're wrapping the native app with Capacitor, you can keep your native iOS / Android Mushi SDKs and add @mushi-mushi/capacitor (or @mushi-mushi/web for WebView-only surfaces). Both report to the same project; filter Reports by SDK to tell them apart.</> },
    { id: 'screen-rollout', label: 'Roll out screen-by-screen behind a feature flag', content: <>Each screen flips from native to hybrid behind a flag. Monitor crash + complaint rate per flag, roll back individual screens when needed.</> },
    { id: 'sunset', label: 'Sunset native screens once their hybrid versions are stable', content: <>Delete the Swift / Kotlin code only after the hybrid version has been at 100 % rollout for ≥ 30 days.</> },

/>

## Mushi Mushi during the migration

You'll have **two** Mushi SDKs running side by side for the migration window:

- The existing native [**iOS**](/sdks/ios) (`MushiMushi`, Swift) and / or
  [**Android**](/sdks/android) (`dev.mushimushi:mushi-android`, Kotlin)
  SDKs, mounted in the native shell. Both are 0.4.0 previews: they are not
  on CocoaPods trunk, SwiftPM tags or Maven Central yet, so they are built
  from source as their SDK pages describe.
- The **shell-specific JS SDK** —
  [`@mushi-mushi/capacitor`](/sdks/capacitor) (for Capacitor shells) or
  [`@mushi-mushi/react-native`](/sdks/react-native) (for RN shells).

Both **must use the same `projectId`**. Reports from each land in the same
inbox, and each report records which SDK sent it, so you can filter
Reports by SDK.

```swift
// Native iOS — stays as-is during the migration
import MushiMushi

Mushi.shared.configure(with: MushiConfig(
    projectId: "YOUR_PROJECT_ID",
    apiKey: "YOUR_PUBLIC_KEY",
    endpoint: "https://dxptnwrhwsqckaftyymj.supabase.co/functions/v1/api"
))
```

```ts
// JS shell — added on top
import { Mushi } from '@mushi-mushi/capacitor'
await Mushi.configure({ projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID', apiKey: 'YOUR_PUBLIC_KEY' })
```

When the migration completes and you remove the native shell entirely, you
also remove the native Mushi SDK; the JS one carries on alone.

## Verification

- Both SDKs land reports under the same project.
- Filtering Reports by SDK shows reports from both surfaces during the
  migration window.
- The crash rate on the hybrid surfaces moves toward the native surface's
  rate over the first weeks. Set your own threshold before you start.

## References

- [Capacitor docs](https://capacitorjs.com/)
- [React Native docs](https://reactnative.dev/)
- [Mushi iOS SDK](/sdks/ios) and [Mushi Android SDK](/sdks/android) reference
- [`@mushi-mushi/capacitor`](/sdks/capacitor) and [`@mushi-mushi/react-native`](/sdks/react-native) reference

## Next.js Pages → App Router

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/migrations/nextjs-pages-to-app-router

---
title: 'Next.js Pages → App Router'
description: Move a Next.js app from the Pages Router to the App Router step by step. Where to mount Mushi Mushi, CSP for static export, and client component boundaries.
---

# Next.js Pages → App Router

 

Move a Next.js Pages-Router app to the App Router incrementally. The two
routers can run in the same app, one route at a time, so you don't need a
flag day. A given URL can live in only one of them.

This guide focuses on the **Mushi Mushi** bits: provider placement, CSP
for static export, and server-component vs client-component boundaries.
For the framework-level migration mechanics see the
[official Next.js migration guide](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/migrating/app-router-migration).

  **Same Mushi project, same API key.** App routes get the provider from
  `app/providers.tsx`; routes still in `pages/` keep getting it from
  `pages/_app.tsx` until you move them. Everything downstream works the
  same.

## API mapping (Pages → App)

| Pages Router | App Router |
|--------------|------------|
| `pages/_app.tsx` (`` mounted here) | `app/providers.tsx` (client component) imported in `app/layout.tsx` |
| `pages/_document.tsx` | `app/layout.tsx` |
| `getServerSideProps` | Server Component fetch |
| `getStaticProps` / `getStaticPaths` | `generateStaticParams` + Server Component fetch |
| `useRouter().query` | `useSearchParams()` + `useParams()` |
| `next/head` | `metadata` export OR `` in layout |

## Migration checklist

Most major libraries (Next-Auth, SWR, react-query, framer-motion) are App Router-ready in 2026. The exceptions are anything that monkey-patches Next's internals.</> },

## Where to put `` (the most asked question)

**At the root of your tree, in a `'use client'` component, mounted by the
root layout.** This means:

- ✅ `app/providers.tsx` (client component) imported into `app/layout.tsx`
- ❌ Inside an individual page (loses provider context across navigations)
- ❌ As a Server Component (the SDK uses React state — must be client)

The cost of one client boundary at the root is minimal (the rest of your
tree can still be server-rendered) and it matches how Next-Auth's
`SessionProvider`, react-query's `QueryClientProvider`, and similar libs
are placed.

## Server Components and `useMushi()`

`useMushi()`, `useMushiReport()`, and the visual widget all require a
client component. That's expected: Mushi captures user-side context
(console, network, screenshot) which only exists in the browser.

If you need user-facing context inside a Server Component (e.g. to
pre-render a "Report a problem with this article" button with a
contextual route), pass the data down as props and let the client child
call Mushi:

```tsx
// app/articles/[slug]/page.tsx (Server Component)
export default async function Page({ params }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string }> }) {
  const { slug } = await params   // params is a Promise in Next.js 15+
  const article = await fetchArticle(slug)
  return <ArticleReportButton articleId={article.id} />
}

// app/articles/[slug]/ArticleReportButton.tsx (Client Component)
'use client'
import { useMushiSdk } from '@mushi-mushi/react'
export function ArticleReportButton({ articleId }: { articleId: string }) {
  const mushi = useMushiSdk()
  return <button onClick={() => void mushi?.captureEvent({ description: 'Article issue', metadata: { articleId } })}>Report</button>
}
```

## Common gotchas

- **Deleting `pages/_app.tsx` too early.** Routes still in `pages/` lose
  their providers, including Mushi's. Delete `_app` only after the last
  `pages/` route has moved.
- **Navigating between the two routers is a full page load.** The Mushi
  SDK starts again on the other side; nothing else to do.
- **`useMushi()` in a Server Component.** Build error. Add `'use client'`
  to the file or move the hook into a child client component.
- **Env vars.** Only `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` variables reach the browser, in
  both routers. If a Pages app passed a server-only `MUSHI_*` value down
  through `getServerSideProps`, rename it to `NEXT_PUBLIC_MUSHI_*` and
  read it in the client provider.

## Pendo Feedback → Mushi Mushi

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/migrations/pendo-feedback-to-mushi

---
title: 'Pendo Feedback → Mushi Mushi'
description: Pendo retired classic Feedback on 2026-08-01. Move in-app feedback and bug reports to Mushi Mushi while keeping Pendo for analytics and guides.
---

# Pendo Feedback → Mushi Mushi

 

  **Pendo retired classic Feedback on August 1, 2026.** Its replacement is
  Pendo Listen. Pendo's notice says classic Feedback data could be
  retrieved until **November 1, 2026** and is permanently deleted after
  that; export it from Pendo settings if you still can. See
  [Pendo&apos;s retirement notice](https://support.pendo.io/hc/en-us/articles/5092218184475-Overview-of-Pendo-classic-Feedback).

Pendo also covers **product analytics**, **in-app guides** and **NPS
surveys**. This guide moves in-app feedback and bug reports to Mushi Mushi
while you keep Pendo for the rest. The two tools share user identity
through one identify function.

## Why switch (the feedback piece)

- **AI triage built in.** Mushi's two-stage classifier categorises and
  prioritises each report.
- **Reproduction context.** Mushi captures console, network, a screenshot
  and a DOM summary with each report, so you aren't relying on the user's
  description alone.
- **Self-host and open source.** Mushi SDKs are MIT and the server is
  AGPLv3.
- **Built for developers.** Mushi's console is for triaging and fixing
  bugs; it also has a feature board where reporters vote on ideas.

## API mapping

`const mushi = Mushi.init({...})` returns the instance used below.

| Pendo | Mushi Mushi |
|-------|-------|
| `pendo.initialize({ visitor: { id, email } })` | `const mushi = Mushi.init({ projectId, apiKey })` + `mushi.setUser({ id, email })` |
| `pendo.identify(visitor, account)` | `mushi.setUser({ id, email, name })` + `mushi.setMetadata('accountId', account.id)` |
| `pendo.track('event', props)` | For repro context on the next report: `mushi.addBreadcrumb({ category: 'custom', level: 'info', message: 'event' })`. For product analytics: `mushi.track('event_name', props)` (names must be `snake_case`; not attached to reports) |
| A button that opened classic Feedback | `mushi.open()`, or the Mushi launcher (a floating button on desktop, an edge tab on phones) |
| Feedback ideas board | Mushi [feature board](/admin/feature-board) (reporters vote), or Reports filtered to feature requests |

## Recipe: keep Pendo for analytics + guides; use Mushi Mushi for feedback

```ts
import { Mushi } from '@mushi-mushi/web'

// 1. Initialise both
window.pendo.initialize({
  visitor: { id: 'user-42', email: 'jane@example.com' },
  account: { id: 'acme-corp' },
})

const mushi = Mushi.init({
  projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
  apiKey:    'YOUR_PUBLIC_KEY',
})

// 2. Mirror identity
mushi.setUser({ id: 'user-42', email: 'jane@example.com' })
mushi.setMetadata('accountId', 'acme-corp')
```

Now Pendo handles analytics and product guides; Mushi handles feedback
intake and triage.

## Migration checklist

Sign in to the Mushi admin console; copy projectId + apiKey.</> },

# Or @mushi-mushi/react if you're on React`} },

## Feature parity

|------------|---------------|-------|

## Hybrid (the third option, often the right one)

You can run a fully bare React Native CLI app AND consume select Expo SDK
packages without the Expo CLI:

```bash

npm install expo-haptics expo-secure-store expo-image-picker expo-sensors
cd ios && bundle exec pod install
```

You get the Expo packages you picked, your CI stays on Fastlane + GitHub
Actions, and Mushi runs the same way it does everywhere. The
[Capacitor → React Native guide](/migrations/capacitor-to-react-native)
uses this setup.

After either direction, smoke-test:

1. App boots, opens, shows the Mushi widget on tap or shake.
2. A test report appears on the Reports page of the Mushi admin console.
3. Native modules (camera, secure storage, etc.) work on a real device.

## Sentry + Mushi Mushi (enrich or standalone)

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/migrations/sentry-to-mushi

---
title: 'Sentry + Mushi Mushi (enrich or standalone)'
description: Add Mushi Mushi alongside Sentry or run it on its own. Three setups, the Sentry webhook for errors, and user bug reports with plain-English diagnoses.
---

# Sentry + Mushi Mushi (enrich or standalone)

 

**This is not a rip-out guide.** Sentry is good at exception tracking,
performance monitoring, and release health, so keep it. Mushi Mushi adds
user-triggered bug reports with a plain-English AI diagnosis and a
paste-ready fix you can hand to your editor's agent via MCP.

  **Three ways to run Mushi with Sentry:**
  1. **Route errors in (recommended).** Point a Sentry internal integration's
     webhook at `/v1/webhooks/sentry?projectId=<your-project>` (and import
     the issues you already have) and Sentry errors land
     in the same Mushi queue as user reports: deduped per issue, diagnosed in
     plain English, fix-dispatchable. Merging the fix resolves the Sentry issue;
     resolving in Sentry resolves the report; a repeat alert on a fixed report
     reopens it as a regression. See [the Sentry plugin page](/plugins/sentry)
     for the setup.
  2. **Enrich.** Keep Sentry as-is. Mushi captures user bug reports, and with
     `sentry` set in the Mushi config each report carries the active Sentry
     event, trace and replay IDs. (`@mushi-mushi/plugin-sentry` is the
     opposite direction: it copies Mushi reports into Sentry.)
  3. **Standalone.** Use Mushi on its own for capture, diagnosis and fix. You
     can add Sentry later (or never); nothing in Mushi assumes it.

## What each tool is for

| Job | Sentry | Mushi |
|-----|--------|-------|
| Unhandled exception capture | ✅ best-in-class | ✅ (basic) |
| Performance / tracing / release health | ✅ | ❌ (keep Sentry) |
| User-triggered bug reports (widget) | ✅ (User Feedback) | ✅ feedback-first (shake on the mobile SDKs) |
| Plain-English AI diagnosis per report | Seer (paid add-on, $40 per active contributor/mo) | ✅ included, BYOK on self-host |
| Paste-ready fix prompt via MCP | Sentry MCP: issue lookup, status updates, and Seer root cause + suggested fix (Seer add-on) | ✅ full fix-dispatch loop |
| Self-host | complex (Sentry self-hosted) | ✅ Supabase / Docker / Helm |
| Open source | FSL | MIT SDKs / AGPLv3 server |

## Option 1: Enrich (run both, link events)

Install Mushi alongside Sentry. The two SDKs don't interfere: Mushi's
widget is Shadow-DOM isolated.

```ts
import * as Sentry from '@sentry/react'
import { Mushi } from '@mushi-mushi/web'

Sentry.init({ dsn: 'YOUR_DSN' })

// Mushi looks for Sentry on globalThis. A bundled Sentry SDK isn't there
// by default, so expose it once:
;(globalThis as Record<string, unknown>).Sentry = Sentry

const mushi = Mushi.init({
  projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
  apiKey: 'YOUR_PUBLIC_KEY',
  // At submit time, attach the last Sentry event ID, scope, trace and
  // replay IDs to each report.
  sentry: {},
})
```

To also copy Mushi reports into Sentry, run
[`@mushi-mushi/plugin-sentry`](/plugins/sentry) on your server.

If you use Sentry Session Replay, see
[Sentry Replay coexistence](/sdks/sentry-replay-coexistence) for the
CSP + sampling configuration that lets both record cleanly.

## Option 2: Standalone

Run the wizard; it detects your framework and wires everything:

```bash
npx mushi-mushi
```

Mushi captures unhandled exceptions too (via `window.onerror` /
`unhandledrejection` and the Node handler), so a small app can skip
Sentry. If you outgrow it on the monitoring side, add Sentry then. The
SDKs coexist.

## API mapping (for code you already have)

`Mushi.init()` returns the SDK instance; the methods below are called on
it (`const mushi = Mushi.init({...})`). In React, get it with
`useMushiSdk()` from `@mushi-mushi/react`.

| Sentry | Mushi Mushi |
|--------|-------|
| `Sentry.init({ dsn })` | `const mushi = Mushi.init({ projectId, apiKey })` |
| `Sentry.setUser({ id, email })` | `mushi.setUser({ id, email })` |
| `Sentry.setTag(k, v)` | `mushi.setTag(k, v)` |
| `Sentry.setContext(name, ctx)` | `mushi.setMetadata(name, ctx)` |
| `Sentry.captureException(err)` | `mushi.captureException(err)` (or keep sending to Sentry) |
| `Sentry.captureMessage(msg)` | `mushi.captureEvent({ description: msg })` |
| `Sentry.addBreadcrumb(...)` | `mushi.addBreadcrumb(...)`; clicks, navigation, console and network are recorded automatically |
| User Feedback widget | The Mushi widget (by default a floating button on desktop, an edge tab on phones), or open it yourself with `mushi.open()` |

## Migration checklist

Run npx mushi-mushi. It handles browser sign-in, project pick, SDK install, and env vars.</> },
    { id: 'install', label: 'Install Mushi alongside Sentry (do not remove Sentry)', content: {`npm install @mushi-mushi/web
# or @mushi-mushi/react on React. Sentry stays in package.json`} },
    { id: 'mount-both', label: 'Mount both SDKs, with Sentry linking on', content: {`Sentry.init({ dsn: 'YOUR_DSN' })
;(globalThis as Record<string, unknown>).Sentry = Sentry
const mushi = Mushi.init({
  projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
  apiKey: 'YOUR_PUBLIC_KEY',
  sentry: {},
})`} },
    { id: 'mirror-identify', label: 'Mirror Sentry.setUser into mushi.setUser', content: {`function identifyEverywhere(user: { id: string; email?: string; name?: string }) {
  Sentry.setUser(user)
  mushi.setUser(user)
}`} },
    { id: 'wire-mcp', label: 'Wire the Mushi MCP server into your editor', content: <>Run npx mushi-mushi setup --ide cursor (or claude / continue / zed). Now get_fix_context returns a paste-ready fix for every diagnosed report.</> },
    { id: 'verify', label: 'Submit a test report and check the Sentry link', content: <>Trigger an error, submit a Mushi report, and confirm the report shows the Sentry event ID of that error.</> },

/>

## When would you actually drop Sentry?

Only if you never used its monitoring depth. If a small app adopted
Sentry only for error emails, Mushi's capture and diagnosis may cover it.
That's a side effect, not the goal. If you rely on tracing,
release health, or alerting rules, **keep Sentry**; Mushi is built to sit
next to it.
