## From "this is broken" to a draft PR: building Mushi Mushi

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/blog/auto-fix-loop

---
title: 'From "this is broken" to a draft PR: building Mushi Mushi'
description: How Mushi Mushi turns a one-sentence user complaint into a classified, deduped, AI-judged draft PR, and why the human stays in the loop the whole way.
---

# From "this is broken" to a draft PR: building Mushi Mushi

*Kenji Sakuramoto*

---

  **Correction, 2026-10-29.** This post first promised "60 seconds" from report
  to draft PR. We never measured that, so the number is gone. What we do
  measure is on the [proof page](/proof): where the owner's bugs came from
  (almost all from the owner's own checks, very few from users), fixes merged,
  and the median time from bug found to fix merged. The pipeline details below are corrected to match the code, and
  an unsourced judge-accuracy figure was removed. Since this post, Mushi Mushi
  added an [AI review of every agent PR](/concepts/agent-pr-review) and is
  building verified merge ([roadmap](/roadmap)): an agent PR merging without a
  click, only when you switch it on (off by default) and the PR passes a
  fail-then-pass test and two AI reviews.

> Sentry sees what your code throws. Mushi sees what your users *feel*.

This is the post I would have wanted to read a year ago, when I was staring at a Sentry dashboard that was perfectly green while three people in a row told me the login button on iPad Safari "did nothing." No exception. No 5xx. No console error. Just a user, frustrated.

That gap — between **errors that throw** and **bugs that users feel** — is what [Mushi Mushi (虫虫)](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi) tries to close.

This post walks through the loop end-to-end, what each stage actually does, and why we kept a human in the loop for the parts that should not be automated.

## The loop

A user opens our SDK widget on the site they're frustrated with. They type one sentence: *"login button does nothing on my iPad."* They hit send.

What happens next, in order, every time:

1. **Plan** — the report lands in Mushi's `reports` table with the user's text, the page URL, the viewport, the browser, the console + network tail, and, if the app turned replay on, a short session-replay snippet. We attach a screenshot if the user opted in.
2. **Plan, classified** — a fast Haiku model filters the report for spam. Real reports get a Sonnet classification (the model is a setting; the default is Sonnet 5.5 today): category, severity, component path, summary, and a confidence score. The component path is grounded against the project's repo embeddings so it points at *real* files (`apps/web/src/login/SignInButton.tsx:42`), not invented ones.
3. **Plan, deduped** — every classified report is embedded and similarity-searched against existing reports. A close enough match joins the existing cluster instead of creating noise. The cluster grows a `blast_radius` counter so triage prioritises bugs hitting the most users first.
4. **Do** — the operator clicks **Dispatch fix**. A worker spins up an agent against the repo, gets the classified report + the embeddings of the relevant files as context, drafts a change, and opens a draft PR. We log every LLM call to Langfuse so you can see exactly what the agent thought.
5. **Check** — an LLM-as-Judge re-scores the original classification on four dimensions (category accuracy, severity, component, repro steps) and records whether it agrees overall. The scores are stored on the report and feed prompt tuning; a low score is a signal for the operator, not an automatic status change.
6. **Act** — the operator merges the PR (or doesn't). Mushi notes the merge, links the original report to the merge commit, and the report's PDCA receipt closes its final stamp. The user who reported the bug gets a one-line "we fixed this" note if they opted in.

## Why we kept the human in the loop

The full PDCA loop *could* be fully autonomous. The agent has the context, the judge has the receipts, and a draft PR is technically reversible.

We chose not to do that, for two reasons.

### 1. The judge is good. The judge is not infallible.

Our LLM-as-Judge mostly agrees with the classifier. Mostly is not "auto-merge" good. The disagreements include the exact cases that an autonomous loop would silently ship wrong fixes for: ambiguous severity, mis-routed component paths, and duplicate-fix attempts that mask the real bug.

Keeping the operator as the merge gate means the loop *gets faster* (one click instead of three) without removing the safety net.

### 2. The user's trust is the moat.

A user who reports a bug and watches the team respond — even with a one-line "we shipped this" — develops a kind of operational trust that tells them "this app is alive." That trust survives outages and slow weeks. It does not survive an automated reply that ships the wrong fix and silently breaks something else.

So the human stays in the loop. The loop just gets shorter.

## What's actually open source

The admin console and every SDK (web, React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, React Native, Capacitor and Node on npm, all MIT; iOS, Android and Flutter as previews in the repo) are on [github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi). The backend (Supabase Edge Functions + Postgres + pgvector for the embeddings) is AGPLv3 — true OSI open source: self-host it free, fork it, modify it for your own org. Offer a modified server as a hosted service and you publish your changes (§13) or take a commercial license.

It's open-core: the core is open source (AGPLv3), and the only paid boundary is a small source-available enterprise edition (SSO, audit export, retention policies, region pinning) that a solo builder never needs.

## Try it

If you'd rather see than read:

- **Sample diagnosis** (no signup): [kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/demo/diagnosis](https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/demo/diagnosis)
- **One-command install** (any web framework):
  ```bash
  npx mushi-mushi
  ```
- **Source + self-host docs**: [github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi)

If Mushi's voice — slightly Japanese, slightly bug-themed, *very* opinionated about the difference between an error and a bug — clicks for you, the easiest way to support the project is to [star the repo](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/stargazers). The next dev who needs this finds it that way.

# Launch Week 1 — five features, five days

*Jun 17, 2026 · Kenji Sakuramoto*

---

  **Correction, 2026-09-21.** The five features below shipped. The public
  posts this article promised (Show HN, Product Hunt, Reddit, a Friday retro)
  never went out, and the GitHub OAuth provider stayed switched off in
  production until September. The post is kept as written; the current launch
  plan and its gate are on the [launch page](/launch-week), and the numbers
  are in [9 signups in 5 months](/blog/nine-signups-what-the-data-said).
  Correction, 2026-10-29: the Friday item named `mushimushi.dev`, a domain this
  project never owned. `mushi login` opens the console at
  `kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/admin` and you approve a code there; no key paste.

Mushi has been shipping quietly for a year. This week we stop doing that.

Five real features, five days, all announced publicly. The model is Supabase's Launch Week — not a PR stunt, just a concentrated shipping cadence with enough momentum for the GitHub Trending algorithm to notice.

## The five

**Monday — open-source relicense.** The server goes from BSL "source-available" to true OSI open source under **AGPLv3**. [Read the post →](/blog/agplv3-relicense)

**Tuesday — One-click MCP install.** `mushi setup` writes `.cursor/mcp.json` (or `.claude/`, `.continue/`, or Zed's `settings.json`) in one command. No UUID paste.

```bash
mushi setup               # wires Cursor by default
mushi setup --ide claude  # wires Claude Code
mushi setup --ide zed     # wires Zed
```

**Wednesday — Zero-config SDK init.** `` needs no props if `NEXT_PUBLIC_MUSHI_*` (or `VITE_MUSHI_*`, `EXPO_PUBLIC_MUSHI_*`, etc.) are in your `.env`. The snippet in the wizard now reads exactly what was written to the file.

```tsx
// Before: <MushiProvider config={{ projectId: '...', apiKey: '...' }}>
// After:  <MushiProvider>  ← reads from env automatically
```

**Thursday — GitHub OAuth + onboarding.** Signup with one GitHub click. New users land on `/onboarding` instead of an empty dashboard. Self-hosters get `MUSHI_INIT_*` env vars for headless bootstrapping.

**Friday — `mushi login`.** The CLI now opens the console in your browser, waits for you to approve the sign-in there, and verifies it. No more copying Project UUIDs from the dashboard.

```bash
mushi login   # opens browser → approve → verified
```

## Why now

The install path had two activation-blocking bugs:
1. The "Add to Cursor" button on `/connect` was 404ing against a non-existent endpoint.
2. The CLI wizard's printed snippet used hardcoded literal keys instead of `process.env.*` — paste it and it broke.

Both are fixed. Launch Week is the announcement.

## Numbers on Friday

Friday's retro post will include: GitHub stars gained during the week, new signups, reports captured, and one honest "this didn't go as planned" item. No rounding. No "we're thrilled with the response."

## I shipped a bug tool for 5 months and got 9 signups. Here's what the data said.

---
title: "I shipped a bug tool for 5 months and got 9 signups. Here's what the data said."

date: 2026-09-21
---

# I shipped a bug tool for 5 months and got 9 signups. Here's what the data said.

*Sep 21, 2026 · Kenji Sakuramoto*

---

The repo went public on 16 April 2026. On 20 September I ran the queries I
should have been running every Monday. Here is what came back, and then what
I think it means.

## The numbers

- **9** console signups, all time. Three in April, five in May, one in June,
  zero in July, August and September.
- **4** external projects created by those signups. **0** of them ever sent
  a report. The API keys were minted on day one and never seen again.
- **16** bug reports in the database, all from my own apps.
- **26,000** end-user sessions, all on my own apps.
- **3** GitHub stars.
- **100** repository views from **25** unique visitors in the last 14 days.
- **0** issues from anyone but me. **1** external pull request.

Against that: **30** published npm packages, and an MCP server listed in the
official registry, Glama, mcp.so, Smithery, cursor.directory and
awesome-mcp-servers.

I had built every surface a launch is supposed to land on. Nothing had landed
on them.

## Three things I found when I looked

**The launch never ran.** In June I wrote a five-day launch runbook: Show HN
on Tuesday, Product Hunt on Wednesday, Reddit across the week, a retro on
Friday. The five features it was built around shipped on schedule. The posts
did not. There is no Show HN, no Product Hunt listing and no Reddit thread
for this project anywhere. The public launch page said otherwise until this
week; it now says this.

**GitHub OAuth was off the whole time.** The console has a "Continue with
GitHub" button for a developer audience. The provider was never enabled in
the auth settings of the live project, so the button never rendered, and
every one of the nine signups used email and password. I found out by
reading the live auth config, not from any dashboard.

**The console was not measuring itself.** Mushi's own console is supposed to
run the Mushi SDK, so that "did the owner open the diagnosis" is a number.
The deployed console had never been given its own SDK key. The build pipeline
did not pass it. Dogfooding was silently off, and every funnel cell between
"signed up" and "paid" was blank.

## What the data said

Put together, the three findings are one sentence: I built distribution
surfaces, never ran the distribution, and could not see the funnel. The
registries and packages were real work, and I would do them again. But they
are where people arrive, not why they come, and without measurement I could
not tell the difference between "nobody came" and "people came and left".

The four external projects are the part that stings. Four strangers signed
up, created a project and got a key. None of them installed the SDK, or if
they did, it never sent anything. I do not know which, because the step
between "key minted" and "first report" was not instrumented.

## What changed

**One number.** The goal is now activated external projects per week: a
project owned by someone who is not me receives its first real bug report,
and the owner opens the diagnosis. Not signups (nine people did that and
none came back), not stars, not downloads.

**Measured with our own SDK.** The SDK grew a `track()` call and the console
grew a Users & Funnels page, and Mushi's own landing, docs and console emit
events through it. The company funnel is a query now. Zero is a value it
returns; "unmeasured" is not.

**First run rebuilt.** A new signup should see a diagnosis of a realistic
report in under a minute, before installing anything, and then be walked to
the install. That is the step the four external projects fell through, so it
is the step that got rebuilt first.

## What happens next

A Show HN, once a public gate list is true: the demo loads with no signup in a
private window, a fresh app reaches a diagnosis in under five minutes on
camera, the docs search returns no dead links, the legal pages exist, and the
activation query returns a number. The [launch page](/launch-week) lists the
gate so anyone can check it.

Whatever the numbers are afterwards, they go in the next post. If you have
shipped an app mostly written by an AI editor and hear about bugs from users,
I would like to know what you actually do with those messages. The
[Discussions board](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/discussions) is
the place; I reply on weekdays.

---

# Launch Week

  **Correction, 2026-09-21.** This page used to say Launch Week 1 ran in June
  2026 with posts on Show HN, Product Hunt and Reddit. The five features did
  ship. The posts did not: no Show HN, no Product Hunt listing and no Reddit
  thread for Mushi Mushi ever went out. We are keeping the shipped list below
  and replacing the rest of the page with what actually happens next.

  **Update, 2026-10-29.** The first public posts went out today: a thread on
  Reddit r/SideProject, a post on X and a post on LinkedIn. The Show HN did not
  post: Hacker News is restricting Show HNs from new accounts, and we will not
  resubmit it as a plain story to get around that. The numbers in those posts
  come from the live [proof page](/proof).

## What shipped in June 2026

| Day | Feature | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Mon | **Open-source relicense** — the server moved to AGPLv3 ([the post](/blog/agplv3-relicense)) | shipped |
| Tue | **One-click MCP install** — `mushi setup` wires Cursor, Claude Code, Continue and Zed | shipped |
| Wed | **Zero-config SDK init** — `` reads its env vars, no props | shipped |
| Thu | **GitHub OAuth + onboarding** — built; the provider stayed switched off in production until September | shipped, mis-configured |
| Fri | **`mushi login`** — browser-guided credential setup, no UUID paste | shipped |

Nobody outside the project was told. That is the honest summary, and it is
why the launch model changed.

## How we launch now: one post per release

A five-day blast assumes an audience that is already watching. We do not have
one yet. So each release gets one public post on one channel, and the next
release does not launch until the previous one has been measured. The number
we publish after each is not stars; it is **activated external projects per
week**, meaning a project owned by someone who is not us received its first
real bug report and its owner opened the diagnosis.

| Release | Ships | The post | What we publish afterwards |
|---|---|---|---|
| **R1 "Proof"** | The no-signup demo verified in a private window; `npx mushi-mushi` on a fresh app reaching a first diagnosis in under five minutes, filmed; docs search returning no dead links; privacy policy and terms live; a first-reply promise on issues | **Show HN**, one Tuesday, 12:00–17:00 UTC. The URL is the demo, never the repo. | A blog post with the real numbers from that week, whatever they are: referrers, signups, activated projects. |
| **R2 "Found"** | The five [comparison and how-to pages](/compare); the Mushi setup skill audited for Cursor and Claude Code; the Cursor plugin submitted | **Product Hunt**, plus value threads in r/cursor and r/ClaudeAI over the following two weeks (a thread first, the link in the comments) and a pitch to two developer newsletters carrying the HN numbers | Journey post #2: what N visitors did on a no-signup demo. |
| **R3 "Loop"** | A "Bug reports by Mushi" mark on the widget with a one-click opt-out; the events that let us measure whether it refers anyone; GitHub Discussions as the community home | A normal HN submission of journey post #3 (not a Show HN) and a dev.to cross-post | Journey posts #3 and #4, and the loop's referral rate. |

## The gate before R1

R1 does not post until every line here is true. The list is public so that
if you read the Show HN and find one of these false, you can say so.

- The [sample diagnosis](/demo/diagnosis) and the [free site check](/check)
  load in a private window with no signup.
- `npx mushi-mushi` on a fresh Next.js app reaches a first report and
  diagnosis in under five minutes, screen-recorded.
- The two hero GIF slots on the landing page show that recording.
- The docs search tool our MCP server exposes returns zero dead links.
- The VS Code extension is either published or marked "deferred" in the
  distribution notes, and is not mentioned on HN until it is published.
- The privacy policy and terms of service return 200.
- `CONTRIBUTING.md` promises a first reply on issues within 24 hours on
  weekdays.
- This page tells the truth (done 2026-09-21, updated 2026-10-29).
- The site's structured data lists only accounts that exist.
- The Bluesky queue has no items scheduled in the past.
- The activation query returns a number, even if that number is zero.

## What we will not do

- Post the same text to two places.
- Buy upvotes, hunters or ads.
- Resubmit a Show HN that fell off the front page.
- Claim a launch happened when it did not.

## Operating (maintainers)

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/operating

---
title: Operating (maintainers)
description: Runbooks for maintainers running Mushi Mushi Cloud or publishing the open-source packages (deployment, releases and status). Not needed to use the SDK.

# Operating Mushi Mushi

This section is for **maintainers** running Mushi Mushi Cloud or shipping the
open-source SDK packages, not for app developers integrating the SDK. If you are
integrating Mushi into your app, start at [Quickstart](/quickstart) instead.

  Mushi is **OSS-first**: the hosted product runs the same code as this repo, plus its own
  tuning data (prompts and scoring weights kept as configuration).
  Self-hosters can reuse every deploy path described here. See [Self-hosting](/self-hosting).

## What lives here

| Page | Audience | Covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Deployment & releases](/operating/deployment) | Maintainers | npm SDK publish (Changesets + OIDC), edge functions, admin SPA, docs, DB migrations |
| [CI runners](/operating/ci-runners) | Anyone running GitHub Actions | Where your tests run and why a fix waits, a broken fix vs a stopped test machine, and `mushi runner add` |
| [Local workers](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/blob/master/docs/operators/local-workers.md) | Anyone fixing reports on their own machine | `mushi work --daemon` as a service, its guards and key, and the console's Pipeline → Workers tab |

## The independent deploy paths

Mushi Mushi has **six** delivery pipelines that ship independently, so a change
to one never blocks the others:

1. **npm SDK packages**: `release.yml` (Changesets version PR → merge → OIDC publish).
2. **Supabase Edge Functions**: `deploy-edge-functions.yml` (path-filtered push to `master`, plus a nightly full deploy).
3. **Admin console SPA**: `deploy-admin.yml` (S3 + CloudFront).
4. **Docs site**: `deploy-docs.yml` (S3 + CloudFront).
5. **Mushi Bounties marketplace**: `deploy-testers.yml` (S3 + CloudFront at `/testers`).
6. **Hosted MCP proxy**: `deploy-hosted-mcp.yml` (CloudFront route and OAuth discovery documents for `/hosted-mcp`).

**Database migrations are manual** (`supabase db push`) and are never run by CI.

See [Deployment & releases](/operating/deployment) for the full runbook.

## CI runners

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/operating/ci-runners

---
title: CI runners
description: See where your tests run and why a Mushi Mushi fix waits. Tell a broken fix from a stopped test machine, and add your own machine as a runner safely.
---

# CI runners

Your agent opened a fix. The check went red. Was the fix wrong, or did the test
machine stop? This page covers how Mushi tells the two apart, how to see where
your tests run and why they wait, and how to add your own machine as a runner.

Everything here is optional. Without it, Mushi still reads job times and
runner names from GitHub.

## Your fix failed, or the test machine stopped

Mushi reads every CI job of a fix's pull request and gives it one verdict:

| Verdict | What happened | Counts as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `passed`, `skipped`, `running` | What it says | — |
| `queued` | Waiting a short time for a runner | — |
| `waiting_for_runner` | Waiting 10 minutes or more on a self-hosted label (30 on a hosted one) | Test machine |
| `runner_lost` | The runner stopped mid-job: out of memory, a reboot, a lost connection | Test machine |
| `queue_expired` | No runner picked the job up, so GitHub cancelled it | Test machine |
| `cancelled` | Someone, or a newer push, cancelled it | Neither |
| `code_failure` | A step failed on a working runner | Your code |

A test-machine verdict means **your fix was not tested**. The fix page says so
and offers **Re-run tests**. The Opus review never holds a merge for it, and no
agent is sent to "fix" CI that never ran.

## The CI view

The console's **CI** page, `mushi runner status` and the MCP tool
`get_ci_overview` show the same thing:

- **Machines** that send a heartbeat: memory, swap, load, free disk.
- **Runners**: online, busy or offline, memory used against the limit, and out-of-memory kills.
- **Wait and run times**: how long half of jobs, and 95% of jobs, waited for a runner and ran.
- **Failures**: how many were the test machine and how many were code.
- **Advice**, each with the numbers behind it: jobs wait too long, memory is near the cap, a runner was killed for memory, swap is busy, `cancel-in-progress` is missing, draft PRs run full CI, no dependency cache, the slowest steps, one runner serving a busy repo.

```bash
mushi runner status            # this project, last 7 days
mushi runner status --refresh  # read GitHub now instead of the last 10-minute sync
mushi runner status --all      # every project your account key can read
mushi runner status --json
```

### GitHub permissions

| Permission | Needed for |
| --- | --- |
| Actions: read | Jobs, their times, runner names and why a job was cancelled |
| Administration: read (optional) | The runner list: online, offline, busy, labels |
| Metadata: read | Whether a repo is public or private (read once a day): it decides what GitHub-hosted minutes cost |
| Variables: read and write (optional) | Changing where CI runs: Mushi reads and writes only `LINUX_RUNNER` and `RUNNER_`, with the GitHub token stored in the project's settings (or, without one, the organization's). Never the Mushi GitHub App, which does not have this permission, and never Mushi's own token |

Without Administration: read, Mushi shows the runners it saw in jobs and says
so.

## What CI costs, and where it should run

The **Cost and speed** section of the CI page, `mushi runner compare` and the
MCP tool `get_ci_costs` compare GitHub-hosted runners with your own machines,
per repo. Nothing here changes where your CI runs.

```bash
mushi runner compare           # this project, last 30 days
mushi runner compare --all     # every project your account key can read
mushi runner compare --json
```

For each repo and each place its jobs ran (GitHub-hosted, one of your
machines, or never picked up) you see:

| Figure | Measured or estimated |
| --- | --- |
| Wait p95, run time p50, pull-request pass rate, jobs | Measured from GitHub's job times |
| Minutes billed | Estimated: each job rounded up to a whole minute, as GitHub bills |
| Cost per month | Estimated: GitHub's list price after your included minutes, or your machine's electricity and wear |
| Busy time of your machines | Measured: parallel jobs count once |
| Speed, your machine vs GitHub | Measured only on jobs that passed on both, at least 5 times each; the sample size is shown |

Money is always an estimate. GitHub's bill is the real figure.

### Why it costs what it costs

- **Public repositories run GitHub-hosted minutes free.** Private ones pay
  after the plan's included minutes (Free 2,000, Pro and Team 3,000 a month),
  which every private repo of the same GitHub account shares.
- **Every job bills at least one whole minute.** Twenty 7-second checks bill
  20 minutes; run them as steps of one job instead.
- **macOS costs about 10× Linux** a minute (Linux $0.006, Windows $0.010,
  macOS $0.062; Mushi shows the date it read GitHub's price list).
- **Re-runs bill again on GitHub**, and cost only electricity on your machine.
- **Jobs pinned to GitHub stay there.** A job that names
  `runs-on: ubuntu-latest # pixel baselines are captured on hosted` does not
  move with a runner variable; Mushi shows the comment as the reason.
- **Main-branch and Dependabot runs often always use GitHub**, when the
  workflow checks `github.ref` or `github.actor` before reading the variable.
- **GitHub gives private repos smaller machines** (2 CPUs, 8 GB) than public
  ones (4 CPUs, 16 GB), which is often why your own machine is faster.
- **A job no runner picks up expires after 24 hours.** It costs nothing, and
  the fix it was testing was never tested.

### Your figures

**Settings → General → CI cost** holds the figures behind the estimates, per
organization: your GitHub plan, the idle and under-load watts of your
machines, your price per kWh and currency, an optional wear cost per busy
hour, and which runners share one physical machine (`Alienware: aw-,
alienware-`). Until you save them, Mushi uses example figures and says so.
On WSL2, `mushi runner heartbeat` sends a hash of the VM's boot id, so
distros on one PC count as one machine without any setting.

### Advice

Cost advice comes with the numbers behind it: a private repo paying for
GitHub minutes while your runner sits idle, a public repo queueing on your
machine when GitHub would run it free, a workflow reading `vars.LINUX_RUNNER`
in a repo with no such variable (every job falls back to GitHub), jobs pinned
to GitHub and what they cost, many tiny jobs, and a public repo running on your
own machine (a pull request from a fork can run code there).

## Change where CI runs

Most workflows that can run on your own machine pick their runner from a repo
variable:

```yaml
runs-on: ${{ (github.actor != 'dependabot[bot]' && github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' && vars.LINUX_RUNNER) || 'ubuntu-latest' }}
```

The **Where CI runs** section of the CI page shows, for each repo, which jobs
read `LINUX_RUNNER` (or a `RUNNER_` variable) and where they run
now. You can move them between GitHub-hosted runners and one of your runner
labels. Mushi changes only that variable: never runner labels, registrations,
runner groups, or another tool's dispatcher.

Every change goes through four steps:

1. **Preview.** Nothing changes. You see the jobs that move and the ones that
   stay, with the reason: pinned to GitHub in the workflow (the comment next to
   `runs-on`), main-branch and Dependabot runs, or a different variable. You
   also see how many runners with the target label are online, how long jobs
   wait there, the estimated cost change, and warnings, such as no online
   runner for the label (jobs would wait, then expire after 24 hours) or a
   public repo where a pull request from a fork could run code on your
   machine.
2. **Request.** Anyone who is not a viewer can ask, in the console, with
   `mushi runner placement request`, or with the MCP tool
   `request_ci_placement_change`. Mushi builds the change itself from the
   preview, including the variable's current value.
3. **Approve.** A team owner or admin approves exactly that change in the
   console. An API key can never approve. The approval lasts an hour.
4. **Run.** The owner or admin runs it from the console. If the variable
   changed since the preview, Mushi refuses with `VARIABLE_MOVED` and you
   preview again.

After a change, Mushi watches the next 10 jobs that read the variable. It
raises an alert if one lands on another runner or waits more than 30
minutes. **Ask to revert** requests the reverse change, which goes through the
same approval.

```bash
mushi runner placement show
mushi runner placement preview --repo you/your-app --value my-runner-label
mushi runner placement request --repo you/your-app --value my-runner-label --reason "save paid minutes"
mushi runner placement preview --repo you/your-app --remove     # back to GitHub-hosted
```

### Your CI agreement

**Settings → General → CI policy** records the rules Mushi checks at the
request and again when the change runs. Mushi fills in nothing for you:

- **No paid GitHub-hosted minutes on private repos**, with a list of repos
  allowed anyway. Only an owner can turn this rule off.
- **External controllers**: another tool that decides where some repos run
  (for example a dispatcher that flips runner labels). Mushi shows those
  repos read-only and never competes with it.
- **Standby runners**: runner names or labels that are only a fallback
  (`kensaurus-local-*`). They are never a target.

## Machine health: heartbeat and job hooks

GitHub does not report a runner's memory or CPU. To see them, run a small
reporter on the machine.

### The runner key

The reporter sends with a **runner key**: a key that can only report runner
health. CI jobs run as the same user as the job hooks, so a pull request's code
could read the key file. If a job steals a runner key, all it can do is send
fake numbers. Your CLI key, which can merge pull requests, never goes on a
runner.

```bash
mushi runner key    # create one and save it to /etc/mushi/runner.key (root only); it is never printed
```

Creating a runner key needs a CLI key with `mcp:write` (`mushi login --upgrade-scope`).
`mushi runner hooks install` and `mushi runner add` create one for you unless
`MUSHI_RUNNER_KEY` is set. `mushi runner status` keeps using your CLI key; it
only reads.

**Heartbeat**, every 2 minutes:

```bash
mushi runner heartbeat --dry-run   # print what would be sent
mushi runner heartbeat --once      # send one (for a timer or cron)
mushi runner heartbeat             # send one every 2 minutes
```

It reads the runner key from `MUSHI_RUNNER_KEY`, the systemd credential that
`mushi runner add` sets up, or `/etc/mushi/runner.key`.

It finds GitHub runner services in systemd (`actions.runner.*`, and the ones
`mushi runner add` creates) and reads each one's memory use, memory limit and
out-of-memory kills from its cgroup. Linux and WSL2 are fully supported; macOS
reports the machine and its runner agents only.

**Job hooks**, once per job:

```bash
mushi runner hooks install --dir ~/actions-runner
```

This writes `job-started.sh` and `job-completed.sh` into `mushi-hooks/` and
turns them on in the runner's `.env` with GitHub's
[job hooks](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-runners/self-hosted-runners/run-scripts).
They send the job's memory peak, memory limit, out-of-memory kills, swap and
load. Restart the runner service afterwards. The hooks always exit 0, give up
after 5 seconds, and never fail a job. The runner key sits in `mushi-hooks/key`
with mode 0600; it is not in the scripts and never on a command line.

### What is sent, and what never is

| Sent | Never sent |
| --- | --- |
| Hostname, platform, CPU count, total memory | The raw machine id (only a SHA-256 hash of it) |
| Load, memory and swap in use, free disk | File contents, logs, `_diag` files |
| Runner names, repo names, unit names | Environment values or secrets |
| Per runner: running or not, restarts, memory use and limit, OOM kills | Process arguments |
| Per job: repo, run id, attempt, job id, memory peak, OOM kills | Anything from the job's workspace |

## Add your own machine as a runner

```bash
mushi runner add --repo you/your-app --dry-run   # read the whole plan first
mushi runner add --repo you/your-app
```

It prints every command before it runs, runs the ones that need root through
`sudo`, and registers the runner with **your own** `gh` login. Mushi's GitHub
App never registers runners.

### Is it worth it?

Self-hosted runners are free on GitHub in 2026: the planned per-minute charge
for them was
[postponed](https://github.blog/changelog/2025-12-16-coming-soon-simpler-pricing-and-a-better-experience-for-github-actions/).
GitHub-hosted Linux costs $0.006 a minute (2 cores) after your included
minutes: 2,000 a month on Free, 3,000 on Pro and Team. Public repos run free
anyway ([billing](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/concepts/product-billing/github-actions)).

So the savings are small. The reason to do it: when an agent opens many fix
PRs, your included minutes run out mid-month and the fixes stop being tested.
A machine you already own keeps them tested.

### The safe defaults, and why

| Default | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Private repos only.** A public repo is refused unless you pass `--allow-public`. | A pull request from a fork runs its code on your machine. GitHub: self-hosted runners "should almost never be used for public repositories" and "can be persistently compromised" ([secure use](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use)). |
| **One job per runner** (`--ephemeral`, the default). Before every job, a fresh one-job config is minted and the work folder is wiped. | One job cannot leave something behind for the next. `--persistent` keeps one long-lived runner. |
| **A dedicated user**, `gha-runner`, with a fixed uid, no login shell and no admin rights. Never your account, never root. The service cannot see `/home`. | A job cannot read your SSH keys, browser profile or other projects. |
| **A memory cap** (`--memory`, default 60% of RAM) in a systemd slice, with throttling before the hard limit. | A hungry build is stopped by its own limit instead of freezing the machine, and the CI view shows the out-of-memory kill. |
| **A label of its own**: `mushi-` (`--label` to change it). | Only workflows that ask for it run there. GitHub-hosted runners stay the fallback. |
| **Download checked**: the official `actions/runner` release, checked against the SHA-256 GitHub publishes in the release notes. | You run what GitHub shipped. |
| **Hooks and heartbeat** installed with it. | The CI view sees the machine from the first job. |
| **A runner key**, not your CLI key, on the machine. The heartbeat gets it from systemd; it is not in any unit file. | A job that reads it can only send fake numbers, not merge your pull requests. |

Before it registers, it also checks the repo's fork pull request approval
setting (it warns unless it is "Require approval for all external
contributors") and lists workflows that use `pull_request_target`, which run
with your secrets on fork pull requests.

Options:

| Flag | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `--block-lan` | Blocks the runner user from your LAN, tailnet and link-local addresses with nftables, in a table of its own. DNS stays open. It never flushes other rules. |
| `--wsl-isolate` | On WSL2: turns off Windows drives (`/mnt/c`) and starting Windows programs for that distro. |
| `--set-variable` | Sets the repo variable `LINUX_RUNNER` to the label. |
| `--persistent` | One long-lived runner instead of one per job. |

Then point a workflow at it:

```yaml
runs-on: ${{ vars.LINUX_RUNNER || 'ubuntu-latest' }}
# or: runs-on: [self-hosted, mushi-<host>]
```

  Cloud agents push branches inside your repo, so fork approval does not stop
  code an agent wrote from running on your runner. Keep the runner on private
  repos you trust, and review what your agents can push.

### WSL2

`mushi runner add` turns on systemd in `/etc/wsl.conf` (needed), then asks you
to run `wsl --shutdown` and run it again. WSL2 stops a distro about 15 seconds
after its last terminal closes, and the VM a minute later, so the runner goes
offline. To keep it up, add to `%USERPROFILE%\.wslconfig`:

```ini
[general]
instanceIdleTimeout=-1

[wsl2]
vmIdleTimeout=-1
```

Run `wsl --shutdown` once, then start the distro at logon (PowerShell):

```powershell
schtasks /Create /TN "mushi-runner-keepalive-Ubuntu" /SC ONLOGON /RL LIMITED /F /TR "wsl.exe -d Ubuntu -u root --exec sleep infinity"
```

See [WSL configuration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/wsl-config).

### macOS and Windows

- **macOS**: Mushi prints the steps instead of running them. Use a separate
  standard user and a user-session LaunchAgent (`./svc.sh install`), not a
  daemon, so jobs can reach the keychain and the iOS simulator.
- **Windows**: use WSL2 (`wsl --install`) and run `mushi runner add` inside it.

### One-job runners and your `gh` login

The one-job runner mints its config with your `gh` login before every job,
which needs **Administration: write** on the repo. If `gh` keeps its token in a
desktop keyring, a background service cannot read it. Then save a fine-grained
token with Administration: write on that one repo as
`/etc/mushi-runner/.gh-token` (root, mode 0600); the runner uses it
instead.

## What can go wrong

Self-hosted runners have been a real attack path:

- **Shai-Hulud 2.0** (November 2025) installed a rogue self-hosted runner named
  `SHA1HULUD` on developers' machines as a backdoor.
- **Nx "s1ngularity"** (August 2025) used a compromised package to steal tokens
  from developer machines.
- **tj-actions/changed-files** (CVE-2025-30066) leaked CI secrets from the
  workflows that used it.

Check your repos:

```bash
mushi runner audit --repo you/your-app
mushi runner audit --all
```

It lists every self-hosted runner, flags the ones Mushi did not set up (no
`mushi-` label and no heartbeat) and any named like `SHA1HULUD`, and shows the
fork approval setting and the `pull_request_target` workflows.

The stronger option is a fresh container for every job. `mushi runner add`
does not set that up yet; until it does, keep runners on private repos you
trust.

## Deployment & releases

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/operating/deployment

---
title: Deployment & releases
description: How Mushi Mushi's maintainers ship the SDKs, edge functions, console and docs. A public summary of the release process; app developers never need to run it.
---

# Deployment & releases

A public summary of how Mushi ships. The full maintainer runbook lives in the
repo at [`docs/DEPLOYMENT.md`](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/blob/master/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md).

  Maintainers only. App developers integrating the SDK never need to run any of
  this — install from npm and follow the [Quickstart](/quickstart).

## Independent pipelines

| Pipeline | Trigger | Target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| npm SDK packages | Merge the Changesets version PR to `master` (often a manual `release.yml` dispatch) | npm registry |
| Edge Functions | Push to `master` touching `packages/server/supabase/functions/**`, plus a nightly full deploy | Supabase Edge (Deno) |
| Admin console SPA | Push to `master` touching `apps/admin/**` | S3 + CloudFront |
| Docs site | Push to `master` touching `apps/docs/**` | S3 + CloudFront |
| Bounties marketplace | Push to `master` touching `apps/testers/**` | S3 + CloudFront |
| Hosted MCP proxy | Push to `master` touching the hosted-MCP scripts, or manual dispatch | CloudFront |
| DB migrations | **Manual**: `supabase db push` | Postgres |

## npm SDK release (Changesets + OIDC)

The SDK packages (`core`, `web`, `react`, `vue`, `svelte`, `angular`,
`react-native`, `capacitor`, `cli`, `mcp`, `node`, plugins, …) publish through
[Changesets](https://github.com/changesets/changesets) with **OIDC Trusted
Publishers** and Sigstore provenance — no long-lived npm token in the hot path.

### Add a changeset on your PR

Any PR that modifies a published package must include a changeset:

```bash
pnpm changeset
```

Pick the affected packages and the semver bump, then commit the generated
`.changeset/*.md` file with your PR.

### Merge to `master`

`release.yml` opens (or updates) a **"chore: version packages"** PR that bumps
versions, rolls up changelogs, and deletes consumed changesets.

### Merge the version PR

This is what publishes to npm. The publish job runs on **Node 24** (npm ≥ 11.5.1
for the OIDC handshake), verifies every published tarball contains no
`workspace:*` specifiers, and audits package signatures.

### Dispatch the release if it does not auto-start

Squash-merges attributed to `github-actions[bot]` usually suppress the `push`
trigger, so a manual dispatch is the normal path:

```bash
gh workflow run release.yml --ref master
```

  **Brand-new packages** need a one-time bootstrap publish (no provenance) so the
  package exists on the registry before a Trusted Publisher rule can be attached.
  See the repo runbook for the `pnpm bootstrap:new-package` flow.

## Edge Functions, admin & docs

These deploy automatically on a path-filtered push to `master` and do not wait
on the npm release. Self-hosters reuse the same scripts; see
[Self-hosting → Edge Functions](/self-hosting/edge-functions) and
[Self-hosting → Admin SPA](/self-hosting/admin-spa).

## Database migrations

Migrations are **never** run by CI. A maintainer applies them deliberately:

```bash
supabase db push
```

Run this **before** deploying any edge function or SDK release that depends on
the new schema, so the live backend is never behind the code that calls it.

---
description: Mushi Mushi Cloud status. The live status page for the API, hosted MCP, console and docs, what it checks, and what is and is not promised about uptime.
---

# Status & Uptime

  **Status page:** [updown.io/p/b6lod](https://updown.io/p/b6lod) shows live
  availability and history for the Mushi Mushi API, hosted MCP, console, and
  docs.

## What we monitor

The status page runs four HTTPS checks, each every 5 minutes. A check passes
when the endpoint answers and its TLS certificate is valid.

| Check | What it covers |
|-------|---------------|
| **Mushi API (ingest edge function)** | The Supabase edge function that receives reports |
| **Mushi hosted MCP** | The hosted MCP endpoint your editor connects to |
| **Mushi console** | The admin console at `kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/admin` |
| **Mushi docs** | This docs site |

The status page does not measure queue depth, latency percentiles, the
diagnosis pipeline or CLI sign-in. Those show up in the console, not here.

## Uptime commitment

Mushi Mushi Cloud has **no uptime SLA** on the Free, Builder or Studio plans.
It is run on a reasonable-efforts basis. Enterprise terms,
including any SLA, are set in a separate order form (see
[Terms §8](/legal/terms)). Ask at `kensaurus@gmail.com`.

## Incident communication

1. The status page reflects an outage as soon as a check fails.
2. Known incidents may also be posted in
   [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/discussions).

## Reporting availability issues

If you observe degradation not reflected on the status page, email
`kensaurus@gmail.com` with subject `[availability]` or open a thread in
[GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/discussions).
For security incidents, use `kensaurus@gmail.com` instead (see
[Security Policy](/security)).

# Open metrics

# What else Mushi Mushi does

The main job is simple: a user says your app is broken, and Mushi Mushi tells you
why and hands your AI editor the fix. But most bugs never get reported. People
just leave.

On my own apps that is exactly what happened. In 60 days people reported 32 bugs.
More than a thousand came from my own side: checks like the ones below, AI code
audits, Sentry errors and bugs I filed myself. Only one of the fixes that merged
started from a user's report. The [live numbers](/proof) count the two separately.

Each card says the problem it solves, what it does, and what it needs. Most are
off until you switch them on, and some need your own key (Firecrawl, Cursor or
Anthropic) or a paid plan; the console tells you before you switch one on.

  prompt, no sign-up needed.

## Who Mushi Mushi is for

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/who-its-for

---
title: Who Mushi Mushi is for
description: "Solo builders who make apps with AI, developers who own their code, and teams: the pains each has and what Mushi Mushi does about them."
---

# Who Mushi Mushi is for

Mushi Mushi was built for one person first: someone who makes apps with AI tools
and then has to deal with the bugs. Two other groups get just as much from it.
Find yours below.

## You build apps with AI, mostly on your own

You use Lovable, Bolt, Cursor or Claude Code. Your app has real users. You did
not write most of the code by hand, and you don't always know how it works.

**What hurts**

- A user writes "it's broken" and you have no idea where to start.
- You ask the AI to fix it, the fix looks fine, and something else breaks.
- You can't watch your app all day, so you hear about problems late, or never:
  most people who hit a bug just leave.

**What Mushi Mushi does**

- Your app gets a report button. Each report comes with a picture of the screen,
  the page and what the person tapped, and Mushi Mushi explains the likely cause
  in plain English.
- Your AI editor gets a ready fix prompt. In Cursor or Claude Code you ask "get
  the latest Mushi report and fix it"; in Lovable or Bolt you paste the prompt.
- It also looks for bugs nobody reports: [a first-time user test](/what-it-does#first-user-test),
  [a watch on your live site](/what-it-does#site-watch), and
  [a check for known security holes](/what-it-does#vulnerabilities).

**Start here:** the install box on the [home page](/) (one command for Claude
Code, one click for Cursor, a script tag for [Lovable or Bolt](/quickstart/lovable-bolt)).
The free plan covers one app with 100 diagnoses a month, no card and no AI key.

## You're a developer and you own your code

You read the diffs. You might already run Sentry. You use AI agents, but you
don't merge what they write without checking it.

**What hurts**

- Error tools tell you what the code threw, not what the person on the other end
  saw. Triage still eats your mornings.
- Agent-written pull requests pile up, and each one needs a careful read.
- CI is slow or expensive, and when it fails you can't tell whether it was your
  code or the machine.

**What Mushi Mushi does**

- Every report and every Sentry error lands in one list, with duplicates merged
  and a diagnosis that names the files and the steps to reproduce it.
- Agents can open fix pull requests, and [a second AI reviews each one](/what-it-does#ai-review)
  against the original report before anything merges. When you choose "Merge when
  ready", approved fixes land one at a time, each branch updated and its tests
  passed first.
- [Your CI bill and runners](/what-it-does#ci-cost), explained: which workflows
  cost the most, what is wasted, and whether a failure was your code or the
  machine.
- It works where you work: an [MCP server](/sdks/mcp) for your editor, a
  [CLI](/sdks/cli), and SDKs for web, React Native, Capacitor and Node.
- It is open source (SDKs MIT, server AGPL), and you can
  [run all of it yourself](/self-hosting).

**Start here:** `npx mushi-mushi` in your app folder, then connect your editor
from the [connect page](/connect).

## You run a team or a company

Several people ship. Bug reports come from support tickets, Slack, app store
reviews and error monitoring, and nobody sees all of them.

**What hurts**

- Bug reports are scattered, and the same bug gets reported five ways.
- Tickets arrive without steps to reproduce, so engineers spend the first hour
  guessing.
- You need to know where the data goes, who can see it, and what it costs.

**What Mushi Mushi does**

- One list for every source: the in-app button, Sentry, low-star App Store and
  Google Play reviews, Slack, and a phone shortcut. Each report gets a diagnosis
  before anyone opens it.
- Sends issues to Linear, Jira or GitHub Issues and alerts to Slack or Discord,
  so nobody has to leave the tools they already use.
- Team seats and roles, an audit log, and a monthly spending cap you set.
- For companies: single sign-on, longer data retention, and the option to run it
  on your own servers. See [security](/security) and
  [data residency](/security/data-residency).

**Start here:** compare the plans on [pricing](/pricing). The Studio plan
includes 10 apps and 5 seats; Enterprise adds single sign-on and self-hosting
support.

## Not sure?

Try the [sample diagnosis](/demo/diagnosis): one real-shaped bug from report to
fix prompt, nothing to install. Or see [everything else it does](/what-it-does).

## User activity

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/activity

---
title: User activity
description: The User activity view on Home in the Mushi Mushi console shows an app's end-user sessions, top pages, and signed-in vs anonymous users over the last 30 days.
---

# User activity

**Route:** `/dashboard?view=users` (**Home → User activity**). The old `/activity` link
redirects there.

> **Scenario:** You want to know whether end users are actually opening sessions
> in this project, which routes they hit, and how many of them are identified
> versus anonymous — over the last 30 days.

User activity is the per-app engagement view in Mushi Mushi. It reads SDK session telemetry
(session start / heartbeat / end, page views, identity) and pairs it with report
counts for the same window.

---

## What you see

| Section | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| **Sessions (30d)** | Sessions in the window |
| **Unique devices (30d)** | Unique devices |
| **Avg page views** / **Avg session** | Page views per session and session length |
| **Daily Active Users — last 30d** | Daily active users for the window |
| **Who uses the app** (or **Sessions by sign-in**) | Identified vs anonymous traffic |
| **Open reports** | Open, Critical and High counts, each linking to the filtered bug list |
| **Top pages by views** | Routes ranked by page views |

The window is fixed at **30 days**.

---

## Data source

```
GET /v1/admin/activity?window=30
```

Requires a console JWT and the active project (`x-project-id` via `apiFetch`).
Backed by the `project_activity_summary` RPC.

If numbers are zero after a real install, confirm the SDK has `trackSessions`
enabled (default on) and that ingest is healthy under [SDK health](/admin/sdk-health).

## Unusual spikes

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/anomalies

---
title: Unusual spikes
description: The Unusual spikes view in the Mushi Mushi console runs statistical detectors on your metrics and files a bug report when a spike starts right after a release.
---

# Unusual spikes

**Route:** `/health?view=spikes` (**Mushi health → Unusual spikes**). The old `/anomalies`
link redirects there. Until October 2026 this was its own page, called Anomaly detection.

**First on the page:** one sentence on the spikes to confirm or dismiss. Once metrics
arrive, **Your metrics, with releases and spikes** draws each metric over time (those
with an open spike first, up to three) with a dashed line per release and a dot per
spike, and **Confirm** / **Dismiss** under the chart. With no metrics yet the page is
one **Add metrics** step. The detectors read **Sudden jump** (z-score), **Slow drift**
(Page-Hinkley) and **Started with a release**.

Mushi Mushi applies statistical detectors to the time-series metrics you send, every
hour and whenever you click **Check now**. When a metric behaves unexpectedly, it shows
up as a spike. A spike that starts right after a release also files a bug report.

---

## Tabs

The tabs are **Summary**, **Spikes** and **Metrics**.

### Spikes

The summary counts include **Spikes to review**, **After a release**, **High score**,
**Auto-reported**, **Metrics watched** and **Dismissed**.

The spike table shows:

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Metric** | The metric name the detector is watching |
| **Method** | Detection algorithm badge: `Page-Hinkley`, `Z-score`, or `release-regression` |
| **Score** | The anomaly score (higher = more anomalous) |
| **Value** | The observed metric value that triggered the alert |
| **Baseline** | The expected value based on history (mean) |
| **Detected** | Timestamp |

**Actions:**
- **Confirm**: marks the spike as real
- **Dismiss**: marks it as noise and removes it from the open list

### Metrics

Feed time-series data into the detection pipeline:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Metric name** | Identifier for the series (e.g. `checkout_errors`, `p95_latency`) |
| **Value** | Numeric measurement |
| **Timestamp** | Date and time (defaults to now) |

Click **Ingest** to store the value. After several data points, a **mini bar chart**
appears per metric showing up to 50 recent values with min/max range.

### Check now

The **Spikes** tab has a card to run a detection pass on demand:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Metric name** | Optional filter — leave blank to run on all metrics |
| **Lookback (hours)** | 1 to 720 hours of history to analyse (starts at 48) |

Click **Check now** to run the detection pass. The result shows the count of
new anomalies found.

---

## Detection methods

| Method (label in the chart) | Best for |
|--------|----------|
| **Page-Hinkley** (Slow drift) | Gradual drift in a running mean (e.g. slowly rising error rate) |
| **Z-score** (Sudden jump) | Sudden spikes above a rolling standard deviation band |
| **release-regression** (Started with a release) | Metrics that changed significantly right after a release |

---

## Auto-reporting

When a spike is a **release regression** (it started right after a release), Mushi
creates a bug report in **Bugs** with severity `high` and category `regression`, and
marks the spike confirmed. Other spikes wait for you to confirm or dismiss them.

---

## API

```bash
# List anomalies
GET /v1/admin/anomalies?project_id=<pid>&limit=100

# Ingest a metric data point
POST /v1/admin/metric-series
{ "project_id": "<pid>", "metric_name": "p95_latency", "value": 1240, "ts": "2026-05-19T12:00:00Z" }

# Run detection
POST /v1/admin/anomalies/detect
{ "project_id": "<pid>", "lookback_hours": 24 }

# Confirm / dismiss
PATCH /v1/admin/anomalies/<id>
{ "status": "confirmed" }
```

- [Releases](/admin/releases) — the releases drawn on each metric chart
- [Experiments](/admin/experiments) — A/B test changes that might affect your metrics

## Spam & abuse

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/anti-gaming

---
title: Spam & abuse
description: The Spam & abuse page in Mushi Mushi lists devices that send reports and flags any that look like one person with many accounts or a report flood, for review.
---

# Spam & abuse

**Route:** `/anti-gaming` (sidebar: **Spam & abuse**, under Bugs; the page was called Anti-gaming before October 2026)

Mushi Mushi tracks every device that sends reports to your project and flags the ones
whose pattern looks like abuse: many reporter accounts behind one device, or one reporter
sending a flood of reports. Review the flagged devices here and clear the ones that are fine.

---

## How detection works

Every incoming report runs three server-side checks. The thresholds are fixed in the
server code; there is no per-project setting for them.

| Check | Flags a device when |
|------|----------------|
| **Cross-account** | 5 or more reporter identities share one SDK fingerprint hash |
| **Multi-account** | More than 3 reporter tokens come from one device fingerprint (IP and User-Agent). When the User-Agent is a script (`node`, `curl`, …) the reason says so, because one server relaying many users' reports looks the same. |
| **Velocity** | One reporter sends more than 10 reports in 24 hours |

A flag never blocks a report. The report is still stored, triaged and fixed normally;
the flag only marks the device for review.

---

## The page

- **Tiles:** Tracked devices, Flagged, Cross-account, Total reports.
- **Device list:** switch between flagged and all tracked devices, group by **Flat**,
  **Date** or **Status** (Cross-account, Flagged, Tracked), and search by fingerprint,
  token, IP or reason. Open a row for its details.
- **Recent events:** the log of flags and unflags, filterable by type.
  `/anti-gaming?tab=events` opens it directly.
- **Withheld tester redemptions** (super-admin only, shown when there are any): gift-card
  redemptions paused by the tester anti-fraud checks, each with **Approve** or **Deny**
  (deny refunds the points).

---

## Actions

| Action | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Flag as suspicious** | Flag the device by hand, with a short reason |
| **Unflag device** | Clear the flag. Tokens already seen count as reviewed, so the device is not re-flagged by its very next report. |

Flagging a device does NOT delete its reports. When a flagged device belongs to a reporter,
the reporter is marked with an anti-fraud flag: they drop off the rewards leaderboard and
their reward payouts are withheld for review.

---

## API

```bash
GET  /v1/admin/anti-gaming/stats?project_id=<pid>
GET  /v1/admin/anti-gaming/devices
GET  /v1/admin/anti-gaming/events
POST /v1/admin/anti-gaming/devices/:id/flag     { "reason": "..." }
POST /v1/admin/anti-gaming/devices/:id/unflag
```

---

## Related pages

- [Reports](/admin/reports): the reports these devices sent
- [Rewards](/admin/rewards): the reward program that abuse targets

## Audit log

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/audit

---
title: Audit log
description: The Audit log in the Mushi Mushi console records admin actions and key events, like who minted or revoked an API key, changed settings or merged a pull request.
---

# Audit log

**Route:** `/team?view=audit` (**Team → Audit log**; the old `/audit` address redirects there)

> **Scenario 1:** A pull request was merged last night and you want to know who merged it.
>
> **Scenario 2:** Your security team wants to know who generated API keys in the last
> 30 days and whether any were revoked.

The Audit log in Mushi Mushi records actions taken by people, agents and scheduled jobs
on the active project. Each entry has a time, an actor, a resource and, when the action
stored one, a metadata payload you can expand. The view has three tabs: **Overview**,
**Log** and **Breakdown**.

The Audit log needs the `audit_log` entitlement (Builder, Studio and Enterprise). The
API also checks the Enterprise license and runs in evaluation mode without one.

---

## What's logged

Not every change writes an entry: the code logs a fixed list of actions. Most settings
changes, including SSO and storage changes, are recorded as `settings.updated` or
`settings.deleted` with the resource type telling you what changed. Examples from that list:

| Action | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `report.created` / `report.triaged` | A report was filed or triaged |
| `api_key.created` / `api_key.revoked` | An API key was minted or revoked |
| `settings.updated` / `settings.deleted` | A setting, SSO provider, storage config and so on changed |
| `fix.reviewed` / `pull_request.merged` | A fix was reviewed; a pull request was merged |
| `fix_dispatch.cancelled` | A fix dispatch was cancelled |
| `project.created` / `project.deleted` | A project was created or deleted |
| `org.member_role_changed`, `org.invite_revoked` | Team membership changes |
| `billing.plan_changed` | The plan changed |
| `mcp.tool_called` | An MCP tool call |

---

## Columns

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Time** | When it happened |
| **Action** | The action name; failure actions (`fix.failed`, `integration.disconnected`) and warning actions (`api_key.revoked`, `plugin.uninstalled`) are highlighted |
| **Actor** | Who did it |
| **Resource** | The type and short ID of the object the action affected |
| **▶** | Expand to see the metadata payload and the full resource ID |

---

## Snapshot

The strip at the top shows **Changes (24h)**, **Failures (24h)** and **All time**. The
Overview tab breaks the last day down by **Human actors**, **Agent actors** and
**System actors**, and names the most frequent action of the last 7 days.

---

## Filtering

| Filter | Options |
|--------|---------|
| **Action** | A fixed list of common action names |
| **Resource** | `report`, `fix`, `settings`, `integration`, `project`, `api_key`, `plugin`, `dsar`, `fine_tuning`, `prompt` |
| **Actor type** | Human / Agent (LLM) / System (cron / webhook) |
| **When** | Last hour / Last 24h / Last 7 days / Last 30 days / All time |
| **Actor email** | Filter to a specific person |
| **Search action / resource** | Free-text search on action and resource |

The **Failures (24h)** card also filters the log to failure or warning outcomes.

Active filters appear as chips in a rail below the toolbar. Click the **×** on any chip
to remove it, or **Clear all** to reset.

---

## Expanding a row

Click a row that has metadata to expand it and see the JSON payload the action stored,
plus the full resource ID. What the payload holds depends on the action; most do not
store a before/after copy.

---

## Export

Click **Export CSV** to download the entries currently loaded (one page, up to 50) with
Time, Action, Actor, Resource, Resource ID and the metadata JSON. Page through the log
to export more.

---

## Common tasks

### Finding who merged a pull request
1. Type `pull_request.merged` in **Search action / resource**.
2. Set **When** to **Last 24h**.
3. Expand the entry to see its metadata and the actor.

### Security review: who created API keys this month
1. Type `api_key.created` in **Search action / resource** (the Action dropdown lists `api_key.minted`, which the server does not write).
2. Set **When** to **Last 30 days**.
3. Set **Actor type** to **Human**.
4. Review the Actor column.
5. Repeat with `api_key.revoked`, then **Export CSV** each page to share.

### Finding out when a project was deleted
1. Set **Action** to `project.deleted`.
2. Expand the row to see the metadata the deletion stored and the actor.

---

## API

```bash
GET /v1/admin/audit?action=&outcome=&resource_type=&actor=&actor_type=&since=&q=&limit=50&offset=
GET /v1/admin/audit/stats
```

## Billing

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/billing

---
title: Billing
description: The Billing view shows your Mushi Mushi plan, diagnosis quota, usage alerts at 50% and 80%, your projected bill and your spend cap.
---

# Billing

**Route:** `/team?view=billing` (Team → **Billing**; the old `/billing` link opens it)

> **Scenario:** It's the 20th of the month. You get an email at 50% of your diagnosis quota, then again at 80%. You want to know when you'll hit the wall, what your projected bill is, and how to cap spend, without logging into Stripe.

Everything you need to manage your Mushi Mushi subscription is in this view, on three tabs: **Overview** (your project card with usage, controls and invoices), **Plans** (plan comparison) and **Support** (open a ticket).

---

## Reading your usage card

Each project has a billing card. The key element is the **usage bar**:

```
Diagnoses used: ████████░░░░  85%  (850 / 1,000)
```

Below the bar you will see:

| Element | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| **Forecast chip** | At current pace, when you'll hit your included quota, or "Quota resets in N days" |
| **Projected cost** | Estimated monthly bill at current pace (paid plans with overage; never shown on a complimentary account) |

**What happens at 100%?**

- **Free:** New reports are captured but **not diagnosed** until the period resets.
- **Builder / Studio (monthly):** Overage continues ($0.03 a diagnosis on Builder, $0.02 on Studio) until your **spend cap** pauses Stage-2 classification. No reports are lost.
- **Builder / Studio (annual):** No overage. Stage-2 classification pauses at the included diagnoses until the next calendar month. No reports are lost.

### Usage breakdown

| Meter | What it measures |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Diagnoses** | Completed Stage-2 classifications this billing period, against the plan's allowance |
| **Reports** | Reports received this period (no report limit on current plans) |
| **Seats** | Members plus pending invitations, against the plan's seats |
| **Spend cap** | Your hard USD ceiling on overage, or **Not set** |
| **Fixes merged** | Fix PRs from Mushi merged this period, from any agent |

The card also shows **Classifier tokens** for the period. A `past_due` subscription shows a banner asking you to update your card.

The **30-day sparkline** shows daily report volume, useful for spotting a spike that will push diagnoses over quota.

---

## Predictability controls

On each paid project card, **Predictability controls** let you:

1. **Monthly spend cap (USD)**: override the plan default ($50 Builder, $200 Studio). Diagnoses pause gracefully at the cap.
2. **Usage alert email**: where 50% / 80% / 100% quota alerts are sent (defaults to project owner).

Both settings save immediately via the Billing API. Leave the cap blank to revert to the plan default; leave the email blank to use the owner address.

  Alerts are deduplicated: at most **one email per threshold per billing month**. The usage-alerts cron runs hourly.

---

## Apps on your plan

A plan sets how many apps your team watches: **Free 1, Builder 3, Studio 10, Enterprise no limit**. Creating one more app than the plan allows stops with a message that names your plan, how many apps the team has, and the plan that fits, plus a **See plans** button that opens the Plans tab. Apps you already have keep working.

The **Plans** tab compares Free, Builder, Studio and Enterprise by apps, diagnoses, overage and history, and shows whether your team's apps and this period's diagnoses fit each plan.

## Upgrading your plan

1. Click **Upgrade** on the project card.
2. Pick **Monthly** or **Annual** (about two months free), then **Select** the plan you want
   (Builder $29/month or $290/year; Studio $79/month or $790/year).
3. Complete payment in **Stripe Checkout**.
4. Stripe sends you back to Billing, which shows the new plan as soon as Stripe confirms the payment.

## Changing plan

A project that already pays switches in the console, not in Checkout:

1. Click **Change plan** on the project card.
2. Choose Builder or Studio, monthly or annual. The current choice shows as **Current plan**.
3. The dialog shows what Stripe charges now (or credits) for the prorated difference. Click **Confirm change**.

The change applies immediately. Moving between monthly and annual starts a new billing period that day. If the card is declined, nothing changes. Annual plans have no overage and stop at the included diagnoses each month. Enterprise is arranged with our team: use **Contact us** on the Plans tab.

---

## Managing payment and invoices

Click **Manage** to open the **Stripe Billing Portal**. Plan changes happen in **Change plan** above; Stripe's portal cannot switch a subscription that has metered usage. Use the portal for:

- Updating your credit card
- Viewing upcoming invoices
- Cancelling a subscription
- Downloading invoice PDFs

The **Invoices table** on this page shows recent hosted invoice links.

---

## CLI parity

```bash
mushi usage              # diagnoses used / limit this period
mushi billing status     # plan, usage, cap, overage rate
mushi billing cap        # show current spend cap
mushi billing cap 100    # set $100/mo hard cap
mushi billing cap 0      # clear override → plan default
```

## Checks

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/checks

title: Checks
description: The Checks page in the Mushi Mushi console shows every automatic check on this app with its state, when it last ran and its open count, failing checks first.
---

# Checks

**Route:** `/checks` (sidebar: Checks)

Is my app OK, and which check is red? Every automatic check Mushi Mushi runs on this app, in one grid, failing checks first. A sentence at the top names the checks that need you, with one button to open the first.

Each card has a dot and a state:

| Dot | State | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Red | Failed | The last run failed or could not finish. |
| Amber | N findings | The check ran and found something to fix. |
| Green | Pass | A finished run was read and found nothing. Shown with when it last ran. |
| Grey | Not run yet, Not set up, Status unavailable | Never a pass. Not set up comes with a Set up link. |

An Upgrade pill means the check needs a higher plan. AI prompts and CI runners are Labs: their cards appear once you switch them on under Settings → Display & sidebar → Labs. While you are on Checks or one of its pages, the sidebar lists every check under Checks.

## The checks

### App checks

Is the app itself sound: scheduled tests, user stories, audits, its blueprint, design tokens and content, a first-time user test, plus Mushi’s own health.

| Card | Route | What it covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Scheduled tests](/admin/qa-coverage) | `/qa-coverage` | Browser tests of your user stories that run on a schedule and alert when one breaks. |
| [Mushi health](/admin/health) | `/health` | Is Mushi itself working: its AI calls and background jobs. Also your code size, schema changes and unusual spikes. |
| [CI runners](/admin/ci) | `/ci` | Where your tests run, how long they wait for a machine, and what slows your fixes down. |
| [Full-stack audit](/admin/fullstack-audit) | `/fullstack-audit` | An end-to-end audit across the frontend, the API and the database. |
| [User stories](/admin/inventory) | `/inventory` | The things users can do in your app, found by crawling it, and which ones broke. |
| App blueprint | `/recipe` | What this app is built from — database, design system, routes, CI, deploy, env and integrations — and what changed. |
| Design system | `/design` | Design tokens, contrast pairs, type scale and off-token code. Token and rule edits open a draft pull request. |
| [Content checks](/admin/content) | `/content` | AI-generated and user-submitted content flagged as wrong or low quality. |
| First-time user test | `/first-user-test` | An AI that has never seen your app tries to sign up and use it; where a new user gets stuck and how long it takes. See [UX runs](/admin/ux-runs#first-time-user-test). |

### AI quality

How good the AI's triage is: grading, lessons learned and the prompts behind it.

| Card | Route | What it covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Triage grading](/admin/judge) | `/judge` | A second AI grades how well each bug was triaged and flags where it disagrees with the first. |
| [Lessons](/admin/lessons) | `/lessons` | Patterns learned from past bugs and fixes. |
| [AI prompts](/admin/prompt-lab) | `/prompt-lab` | Edit and compare the prompts that turn bug reports into pull requests. |
