## CI runners

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/ci

---
title: CI runners
description: The CI runners page in the Mushi Mushi console shows where tests run, how long they wait for a machine, and whether a red check was your code or the machine.
---

# CI runners

**Route:** `/ci` (sidebar: Checks › CI runners. CI runners is a Lab: switch it on under **Settings → Display & sidebar → Labs** to keep it in the sidebar and on the Checks grid)

Every fix Mushi Mushi opens is tested by your CI before it can merge. This page shows the machines that run those tests, the jobs waiting for one, and why a fix takes as long as it does to land. **This app** follows the app you have open. **All apps** reads every project you can see.

The page reloads every 30 seconds while the tab is visible, and **Refresh** does the same. Each reload asks GitHub for queued and running jobs. The server does that live read at most once a minute per app.

## Spend less on CI

AI agents open a lot of pull requests, and every one runs your tests on GitHub Actions. This page keeps that bill small:

- **See what you really pay.** Your GitHub Actions bill per repo and per day, with public repos and free minutes shown as $0.
- **Find the waste.** Tests that run on drafts, schedules that run every hour, docs-only changes that run every test.
- **Fix it in one pull request.** Mushi opens a small workflow change for you to review, then shows the minutes saved after it merges.

Mushi's own fix pull requests run your tests only after a review says they are worth merging.

## How it reads your runs

A collector also runs every 10 minutes. It reads GitHub Actions runs updated in the last 2 hours, on every branch of each app's repositories, classifies each job, and deletes job rows and samples older than 30 days.

## Test machine or your code

A lost runner, a job still waiting for a runner, and a queue that expired are the test machine. They are never a code failure. The page labels them **Test machine stopped**. **Tests failed** means a step failed while a machine was running your code.

Re-run a job the test machine stopped. Open the fix for a job whose tests failed. The line at the top says what needs you: a job has been waiting a long time for a machine, most failures are the test machine, some jobs failed on the code, or every finished job passed.

## Queue and wait

**Queue** is every job, from waiting for a machine to finished.

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Waiting** | Waiting for a free test machine. A long column means too few machines. |
| **Running** | On a test machine now. |
| **Finished** | Finished in the last 2 hours. Filter to **Tests failed**, **Test machine stopped**, or **Passed**. |

Above the queue: how many are waiting now, how many are running, the typical wait for a machine, and the typical run time. The wait also names the slow tail, the 1 job in 20 that waits longer. A bar splits the jobs from the last 7 days into passed, tests failed, test machine stopped, and cancelled, skipped or still going.

**Timeline** is one row per test machine. Gaps are idle time. Striped bars are jobs waiting for a machine.

## Runner map

**Runner map** is your machines, the runners on them, the repositories they serve, and the jobs waiting or running now. Click a card for its health and recent jobs.

Runners that live for a single job, named as a label plus a number of seconds, are folded into that label. With **Administration: read** on the GitHub token, Mushi reads the repository runner list, including idle and offline runners. Without it, the page says it only sees runners through jobs. Without **Actions: read**, it cannot see the jobs at all.

## What would make fixes land sooner

**Speed it up** lists changes that would land your fixes sooner, each with the evidence and a copy-ready fix.

**Slow jobs** is the jobs and steps that take the longest.

**Stopped by the test machine** lists jobs that never finished testing. Re-run them.

## Your real bill

The rest of the cost section estimates money from job times. **Your real bill**, at the top of it, shows what GitHub actually charged, read from GitHub's billing:

- this month's net charge so far, in large type;
- the gross price beside it, because public repos and your plan's included minutes are free and show up as a discount;
- the net per repository over the last 30 days, and the net per day;
- the change against the 30 days before, shown only when Mushi holds the whole earlier period;
- how much of your paid GitHub-hosted minutes ran on Mushi's own agent branches. This share is estimated from the jobs Mushi recorded.

Mushi reads the bill once a day for each GitHub account or organization your repositories belong to. It uses only the GitHub token saved in the project's settings, never the GitHub App. The token needs billing access:

| Account | Fine-grained token permission |
| --- | --- |
| Personal account | **Plan: read** |
| Organization | **Administration: read** (owners and billing managers) |

If the token can't read the bill, the card says so and shows how to connect one. Instead of a token, you can upload the bill from a machine where `gh` is signed in as the paying account:

```bash
gh auth refresh -s user   # once: a gh login has no billing access by default
mushi runner bill --push
```

A classic token, which is what `gh auth login` makes, reads a personal account's bill only with the `user` scope. Without it, GitHub answers 404 and `mushi runner bill` tells you to run the refresh above.

`mushi runner bill` without `--push` prints the same bill in the terminal. Your token stays on your machine.

### Cost advice that reads your workflows

Each item of **Cost advice** gives its evidence and a saving per month. The saving is the billed minutes Mushi recorded over the window, at GitHub's list price. It is zero for public repos and self-hosted runners, which GitHub doesn't charge for. An item with an **Open fix PR** button can open a pull request that makes the change.

| Advice | When it appears | One-click fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scheduled workflow runs too often | A `schedule` runs more often than weekly, and its runs billed minutes | Yes: weekly |
| Documentation-only pull requests run CI | A pull request workflow has no `paths` or `paths-ignore` filter, and pull requests that changed only docs ran it | Yes: ignore docs paths |
| Checks run again after the merge | Jobs that ran on the pull request ran again on the push to `main` | No: use a merge queue or release trains |
| The same check runs twice | Two jobs on the same event run the same command | No |
| Every package builds on each pull request | A turbo or nx monorepo runs all tasks on pull requests, without `--affected` or `--filter` | No. The minutes at stake are shown, but not priced. |
| Pull requests nobody merged | Minutes billed to pull requests closed without merging | No |
| macOS on pull requests | GitHub-hosted macOS jobs on pull requests, at about ten times the Linux price | No |
| Old runs keep going | A push or pull request workflow doesn't cancel the run it replaces | Yes, when it has no concurrency group yet |
| Draft pull requests run the full CI | A pull request workflow doesn't skip drafts | Yes: skip drafts |

Advice that needs data Mushi doesn't have yet stays hidden. It never guesses.

## Fix it in one PR

Some advice is one edit to one workflow file. Those cards have an **Open fix PR** button for each workflow they found:

| Fix | What changes in the workflow |
| --- | --- |
| Cancel superseded runs | A `concurrency` group. A new push to a pull request cancels the run it replaces. Pushes, manual and scheduled runs always finish. Mushi refuses on a workflow that deploys or releases. |
| Skip drafts | `ready_for_review` is added to the `pull_request` types, and every job skips draft pull requests. A job whose check your branch requires keeps running and fails at a first step named "Draft PRs run no CI": a skipped required check reads as passing, and a draft must never merge untested. |
| Run the schedule weekly | A schedule that runs more than once a week runs once a week, at the same hour. Mushi refuses on a workflow that deploys or releases, because some daily schedules roll out releases on purpose. |
| Skip docs-only changes | `paths-ignore` for Markdown files, `docs/`, the license and issue templates on `pull_request` and `push`. Mushi refuses when the workflow produces a required check, or a job looks like one: a skipped workflow never reports, so the pull request could not merge. It also refuses when a trigger already lists `paths`. |

Mushi reads which checks your default branch requires (branch protection and rulesets). When it cannot, it refuses the draft and docs fixes rather than guess.

Mushi asks you to confirm first. It then edits only that file, keeps your comments, and opens a **draft** pull request titled `ci: …`. Nothing changes until you review it, mark it ready and merge it. The card shows the job's progress and the link. If the workflow already has the fix, it says so and opens nothing.

After the merge, the card shows the saving Mushi measured. That is the workflow's billed minutes per day after the merge, against the 14 days before. Like every number on this page, it is estimated from job times.

Writing a workflow file needs the GitHub App's **Workflows: Read and write** permission, or a token with the `workflow` scope. Without it, the card says so. You can still copy the fix and commit it yourself.

From the terminal, run `mushi runner fix --repo <owner/repo> --workflow .github/workflows/ci.yml --kind skip_drafts`, and follow it with `mushi runner fix-status`. In your editor, use the MCP tool `open_ci_cost_fix`.

## Apply to every app

Every pull request runs CI once, and each run costs minutes. So when a repo has several fixes, it's cheaper to open them as **one** pull request. **Apply to every app**, next to the advice list, does that for all your apps at once:

1. **Preview.** Mushi lists every fix it can open in the apps you may change, grouped by repo, with the estimated saving per fix and per repo. A fix whose pull request is still open, or is being opened, can't be picked again. Mushi can't price every fix: those say "not priced", never $0. A repo where Mushi already knows its GitHub access can't edit workflow files starts unticked, with the reason. Mushi knows this from the setup check or the last attempt.
2. **Pick and confirm.** Tick the fixes you want, then confirm once. Mushi opens at most 10 repos at a time and 20 fixes per repo. Each repo counts once against its app's 10 CI fix pull requests an hour.
3. **Results.** Each repo gets **one draft pull request** with a `ci:` title. The body lists every change with what it changed and why, plus the workflow's minutes over the last 14 days. Each fix keeps the refusals above. A fix Mushi refused is listed in the pull request and in the result, never dropped. When Mushi refuses every fix in a repo, it opens no pull request there and says why.

Before opening anything, Mushi rebuilds the advice. It opens only fixes it still advises, so a stale preview can't open something the advice no longer says.

After the merge, Mushi measures each changed workflow once, even when two fixes changed the same file. The saving isn't counted twice.

From the terminal, run `mushi runner fix --all` to preview and `mushi runner fix --all --apply` to open. Follow each repo with `mushi runner fix-status --bundle `. In your editor, use the MCP tools `preview_ci_cost_fix_rollout`, `apply_ci_cost_fix_rollout` and `get_ci_cost_fix_bundle`.

## When nothing has reported in

The page stays empty until GitHub reports a job for this app's repositories, or a machine that runs your tests reports in. On that machine, run:

```bash
mushi runner key
mushi runner hooks install --dir <runner dir>
```

Host health arrives through `mushi runner heartbeat` and the job hooks, as `POST /v1/ingest/runner` with a `runner:write` key only. The setup steps are in [CI runners](/operating/ci-runners).

## CLI device auth

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/cli-auth

---
title: CLI device auth
description: The Mushi Mushi console page that mushi login opens so you can approve a CLI device code while signed in, and how the device authorization flow works.
---

# CLI device auth

**Route:** `/cli-auth?code=XXXX-XXXX`

> **Scenario:** You ran `mushi login` in a terminal. The CLI opened this page
> so you can approve the device code while signed into the console.

The page is titled **Connect your CLI**. It uses the RFC 8628 device authorization
grant for the Mushi Mushi CLI:

1. CLI starts `POST /v1/cli/auth/device/start` and opens this URL with the user code.
2. Sign in to the console if needed (`ProtectedRoute` returns you here).
3. Check that the code matches what your terminal printed. **Do not paste or type this
   code into your terminal.**
4. Click **Approve CLI connection** → `POST /v1/cli/auth/device/approve`. **Deny**
   rejects the code (`POST /v1/cli/auth/device/reject`).
5. The page polls `GET /v1/cli/auth/device/status` until the CLI claims the token
   (`cli_token_claimed_at`), then shows **CLI connected!**. The terminal wizard waits up
   to 10 minutes; if it does not continue, the tab may belong to an older run, so run
   `mushi login` again.

Operator deep-dive: [SDK reliability overhaul](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/blob/master/docs/operators/sdk-reliability-overhaul.md) · public guide: [CLI ↔ console loop](/quickstart/cli-console-loop).

## Code size

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/code-health

---
title: Code size
description: The Code size view in the Mushi Mushi console charts bundle size and oversized files from your CI over time, so you see an app getting heavier before users do.
---

# Code size

**Route:** `/health?view=code` (**Mushi health → Code size**). The old `/code-health` link
redirects there. Until October 2026 this was its own page, called Code health.

> **Scenario:** Your mobile CI posts bundle KB and god-file LOC on every push to
> `main`. You want one console view that shows whether the app is getting heavier
> or sprouting unmaintainable files — without opening GitHub Actions logs.

Mushi Mushi only **reads** here: the view never triggers a scan. Data arrives via
`POST /v1/ingest/metrics` from your repo's CI workflow.

---

## What you see

| Section | Source |
|---------|--------|
| **Status sentence** | How many files are over or close to the 2,000-line budget, the largest file, and the latest bundle KB |
| **Oversized files** | A bar per large file, longest first, against the budget line (`code_health.*` gate) |
| **Bundle size over time** | Sparkline per `bundle.*` metric from `metric_series` |
| **Largest file over time** | The longest file's line count per run, when CI sends it |
| **How to split each file** | Each oversized file with its split hint |

Known security holes in your dependencies are not repeated here: one line links to
[Full-stack audit](/admin/fullstack-audit), where they are listed and managed.

---

## Wiring CI ingest

1. Mint an SDK **ingest** key on [Manage apps](/admin/projects).
2. Add repo secrets: `MUSHI_API_URL`, `MUSHI_INGEST_KEY`.
3. In CI, build a JSON body of `metrics` (names starting `bundle.` or `code_health.`)
   and `findings`, then post it with the key in the `X-Mushi-Api-Key` header:

```yaml
- name: Push code-health metrics to Mushi Mushi
  env:
    MUSHI_API_URL: ${{ secrets.MUSHI_API_URL }}
    MUSHI_INGEST_KEY: ${{ secrets.MUSHI_INGEST_KEY }}
  run: |
    curl -sf -X POST "${MUSHI_API_URL}/v1/ingest/metrics" \n      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \n      -H "X-Mushi-Api-Key: ${MUSHI_INGEST_KEY}" \n      --data-binary @mushi-payload.json
```

Mushi Mushi does not ship the script that writes `mushi-payload.json`; your CI builds it.
Reference implementation: `kensaurus/yen-yen`, `.github/workflows/bundle-budget.yml`
with `scripts/scan-god-files.mjs`.

---

## API

```bash
GET /v1/admin/code-health?project_id=<uuid>
POST /v1/ingest/metrics   # CI push — apiKeyAuth, prefix allow-list bundle.* / code_health.*
```

From your editor, the MCP tool `get_code_health` returns the same data
(trends default to the last 30 days; pass `days` for more). Pass a god file's
`id` to `explain_finding` for its fix in one sentence. A project key reads its
own project; an account-level key needs `projectId` (`project_id` on the API).

## Compliance

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/compliance

---
title: Compliance
description: The Compliance view in the Mushi Mushi console has SOC 2 control evidence, retention policies, data subject requests and residency, and prints an evidence PDF.
---

# Compliance

**Route:** `/team?view=compliance` (**Team → Compliance**; the old `/compliance` address redirects there)

Compliance needs the `soc2` entitlement, which only the **Enterprise** plan includes.
Without it the Team tab is hidden, and opening the address shows which plan includes it.

> **Scenario 1:** A customer asks how you handle security before signing. You want
> to show the current control status and retention settings in one place, and
> export the audit log as a CSV (Team → Audit), without a meeting. Mushi Mushi is
> not SOC 2 certified; it collects evidence toward it.
>
> **Scenario 2:** A user emails saying they want all their data deleted (GDPR Article
> 17). You need to log the request, track its status, and respond within 30 days.

The Compliance view in Mushi Mushi handles both in the console. It has five tabs:
**Overview**, **Evidence**, **Retention**, **DSARs** and **Residency**.

---

## Navigating the page

On the Overview tab, filter chips focus the page:

| Chip | Shows |
|------|-------|
| **All** | Every section: controls, DSARs, retention, residency |
| **Open** | Failing or warning controls, plus pending and in-progress DSARs |
| **Failing** | Failing controls, plus open DSARs 21 days old or older |
| **At risk** | Controls with warnings |
| **Legal hold** | Projects on legal hold; retention sweeps are paused |

The snapshot strip shows **Controls** (passing out of total), **Open DSARs**, **Legal
holds** and the **Cluster** region.

---

## SOC 2 control evidence

The evidence table shows a snapshot of your control state across SOC 2 trust service
criteria. Each row is a control that the `soc2-evidence` edge function assesses
automatically.

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **PASS** ✓ | Control is satisfied — evidence is clean |
| **WARN** ⚠ | Control is partially satisfied — needs attention |
| **FAIL** ✗ | Control is violated — action required before audit |

The table shows Control, Label, Project, Status and Generated. The payload button on a
row opens the raw JSON evidence that was used to compute the status.

**To generate a fresh snapshot:** click **Refresh evidence**. This triggers the
`soc2-evidence` edge function which re-assesses all controls against the current state.

**To export for an auditor:** click **Export PDF**. It opens the browser's print dialog
for the page, so you can save it as a PDF.

---

## Data residency

Each project can be pinned to a region: `us`, `eu`, `jp` or `self`.

Pinning records the region; it does not move data today. Mushi Mushi cloud runs on a
single Supabase project, and the regional hostnames are reserved for future routing, so
every region currently resolves to the same API. Once pinned, a project cannot be
re-pinned from the console (the API answers 409); moving regions means contacting
support.

---

## Retention policies

Control how long Mushi Mushi keeps different data categories for each project. A project
with no custom policy shows **Set a custom policy**.

| Category | Default | When to change |
|----------|---------|---------------|
| **Reports** | 365 days | Shorten if you have GDPR delete obligations; lengthen for longer-term trend analysis |
| **Audit log** | 730 days | Keep at 730 (2 years) for SOC 2 CC7.2; shorten only if legally required |
| **LLM traces** | 90 days | Shorten for cost (storage); lengthen if you need longer A/B test history |
| **BYOK audit** | 365 days | Keep at 365 for key rotation audit trails |

**Place on legal hold** / **Lift legal hold**: suspends automated deletion for a project.
Use it when you receive a litigation hold notice.

Changing a value opens a confirmation that says what the nightly sweep will delete;
the change saves when you confirm.

---

## Data Subject Access Requests (DSAR)

Use this section to manage requests from users exercising their rights under GDPR, CCPA,
or similar regulations.

### Filing a DSAR

1. On the DSARs tab, choose the **Request type**: Access, Export, Deletion or Rectification.
2. Enter the **Subject email**, and the **Subject user ID (optional)** if you have it.
3. Add **Notes (optional)** with any context from the user's email.
4. Click **File DSAR**.

The request appears in the DSAR table with status `pending`.

### DSAR workflow

| Status | Action | When |
|--------|--------|------|
| `pending` | **Start triage** | Soon after receipt |
| `in_progress` | **Complete** | When data export/deletion is done |
| `in_progress` | **Reject…** | Only with a valid legal basis; you must give a **Rejection reason** |

**Age** turns amber at 21 days and shows **overdue** at 30 days for an open request.
Open requests 21 days old or older also appear under the **Failing** chip.

---

## Common tasks

### Preparing for a SOC 2 audit
1. Open the **Failing** filter and resolve every failing control first.
2. Switch to **At risk** and plan remediation for controls with warnings.
3. Click **Refresh evidence** to get a fresh snapshot.
4. Click **Export PDF** and share with your auditor.

### Responding to a deletion request (GDPR Article 17)
1. Choose **Deletion**, enter the subject email, then **File DSAR**.
2. Click **Start triage**.
3. Delete the user's data. Filing a DSAR does not delete anything by itself; your
   backend can call `POST /v1/sdk/erase-subject` for that end user.
4. Click **Complete** once deletion is done.
5. The DSAR row stays as your compliance record.

### Checking a project's recorded region
1. Open the **Residency** tab.
2. Find the project and its pinned region. Remember that pinning is a record today, not
   a separate data location (see [Data residency](#data-residency)).

---

```bash
GET   /v1/admin/compliance/evidence

PATCH /v1/admin/compliance/dsars/:id               { status, rejection_reason, evidence_url, notes }

```

## Connect

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/connect

---
title: Connect
description: The Connect page wires GitHub, the SDK, MCP, the CLI and your editor to a Mushi Mushi project, and shows when your installed SDK is out of date.
---

# Connect

**Route:** `/connect` (sidebar: **Connect**)

> **Scenario:** Your repo is on GitHub, the SDK is installed, but your editor still
> can't ask Mushi Mushi what broke, and you're a couple of versions behind on
> `@mushi-mushi/web`. This page wires GitHub, the SDK, MCP, the CLI and upgrade PRs
> in one place.

A row of status pills at the top (**App checked in**, **SDK version**, **Editor**)
says what is already connected. Below them, the page opens with a client picker:
pick your AI client, then a lane (MCP / CLI / Skills). Connecting GitHub enables the
**Create Upgrade PR** flow; the SDK and MCP sections work without it.

---

## Client picker (3 lanes)

| Lane | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| **MCP** | One-click install for Cursor, VS Code, Claude Code, Windsurf and other clients (`ClientConnectButton` mints a scoped key, then opens a deeplink or gives you config JSON) |
| **CLI** | Three commands to copy: `npm install -g @mushi-mushi/cli@latest`, `mushi login`, then `mushi setup --ide ` |
| **Skills** | Copy skill setup for the selected client |

If your only key is an SDK key, a note under the picker offers **Add an MCP key**
(`mcp:read`), which your editor needs to read this app's reports.

---

## Sections

| # | Section | What it does |
|---|---------|--------------|
| 1 | Client picker | MCP / CLI / Skills lanes (above) |
| 2 | **GitHub** | Link the repo so upgrade PRs, autofix and CI secret sync can use its token. **Manage** opens Integrations. |
| 3 | **SDK health** | Problems that stop bug reports from arriving, each with a fix (see [SDK health](/admin/sdk-health)) |
| 4 | **Bug capture SDK** | Framework tabs and a copy-ready install snippet; **Make a key and fill it in** fills in the key |
| 5 | **Native app CI secrets** | Diagnose, and one-click sync of `NEXT_PUBLIC_MUSHI_*` into GitHub Actions |
| 6 | **Update center** | Per-package freshness and **Create Upgrade PR** |

---

## Native app CI secrets

Capacitor, Expo, and React Native apps bake `NEXT_PUBLIC_MUSHI_*` at **compile
time**. A missing secret silently disables `initMushi()` and the lime banner
never appears in the store build.

The **Native app CI secrets** card calls `GET /v1/admin/projects/:id/sdk-diagnostics`
and shows a fused verdict:

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `ci-secret-missing` | Required var absent from GitHub Actions secrets/variables |
| `native-never-seen` | Web heartbeats exist but no `capacitor://` / native UA |
| `banner-disabled` | The SDK banner is turned off in the SDK config |
| `healthy` | All CI secrets present and the SDK has reported from the expected origins |
| `unknown` | Not enough to tell yet |

**One-click sync:** `POST /v1/admin/projects/:id/sync-ci-secrets` mints a
scoped ingest key and writes each required var via sealed-box encryption.

The Mushi GitHub App requests `Contents` + `Pull requests` only — not Actions
secrets. Auto-write works when a fine-grained PAT with **Actions secrets: Read
and write** is stored in project settings. Otherwise the card expands guided
`gh secret set` commands and a CI `env:` YAML block.

See also: [Self-hosting](/self-hosting) · [`AGENTS.md` native CI section](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/blob/master/AGENTS.md#native-ci-secrets-diagnostic--auto-write-jun-2026)

---

## SDK upgrade PR

When a package is outdated or deprecated:

1. Click **Create Upgrade PR** on the Update center row.
2. Backend enqueues `sdk_upgrade_jobs` → `sdk-upgrade-worker` bumps
   `@mushi-mushi/*` in `package.json` files only (never `workspace:` / `file:`).
3. Draft PR opens on GitHub, auto-readied, status streams via SSE.

The bump edits `package.json` only. Add the
[lockfile helper workflow](/admin/sdk-upgrade-lockfile) to your repo and the PR
opens after your own package manager has refreshed the lockfile, so
`npm ci` / `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` pass.

CLI equivalent: see [SDK reference → CLI](/sdks/cli) (`mushi upgrade` for local bumps).

---

## Quick path (5 minutes)

### Connect GitHub
Install the Mushi GitHub App on your primary repo (or paste a fine-grained PAT
with Contents + PR + Actions secrets if you need CI auto-write).

### Install SDK
Copy the framework snippet → paste into your app → deploy or run locally.

### Wire MCP
In the client picker's **MCP** lane, click **Add to Cursor** (or your client's
button), restart the IDE, then run `mushi doctor`.

### Wire CLI (SDK + env + MCP)
`mushi connect` saves credentials, writes the SDK env vars to `.env.local` and wires
Cursor MCP. The Set up page's CLI strip and the project success panel give you this
command with your project ID filled in:

```bash
MUSHI_API_KEY=mushi_xxx mushi connect \
  --project-id <uuid> \
  --endpoint https://dxptnwrhwsqckaftyymj.supabase.co/functions/v1/api \
  --write-env --wire-ide --wait
```

Run `mushi login` first if you need to paste an API key interactively. SDK-only: `mushi init --project-id `.

### Verify
Click **Send test report** on the app's row in [Manage apps](/admin/projects), or
submit a report from your app.

## Content checks

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/content

---
title: Content checks
description: The Content checks page in the Mushi Mushi console queues low-scoring or flagged AI-generated copy, release notes and knowledge snippets so you can fix them.
---

# Content checks

**Route:** `/content` (sidebar: **Content checks**, under Verify)

With nothing open and no filter from a link, the page is its empty state with
**Show past issues**; the filter row appears once there is something to filter.

> **Scenario:** AI-generated copy, release notes, or knowledge snippets scored
> poorly or got user flags, and you need a queue of fixable assets.

Your own app sends these items to Mushi Mushi (`POST /v1/content-quality` with your
project API key). Content checks lists the ones that need review:

| Reason | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `low_judge_score` | The score the source app sent (`judge_score`) is below its threshold. A source may send a vote score here rather than an AI judge grade, so the console calls it "Low score" |
| `user_flag` | End users flagged the content |
| `low_star_rating` | Aggregate star rating is low |
| `high_downvote_ratio` | Downvotes dominate |

Open a row (`/content/:id`) to inspect scores and click **Regenerate & push**. Your app
judges the new candidate and promotes it only if the score improves.

To clear noise in bulk, tick rows or filter the list (status, reason, content
type, source, score band), then choose **Dismiss selected** or **Dismiss all
matching**. The dialog states the exact number of rows and needs a reason,
which goes to the audit log. One run dismisses at most 10,000 rows. A
dismissed row stays dismissed when the source re-sends the same item; only new
flags, new downvotes or a clearly lower score reopen it.

## AI spend

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/cost

# AI spend

**Route:** `/team?view=spend` (**Team → AI spend**; the old `/cost` address redirects there)

The AI spend view shows the LLM calls Mushi Mushi made for the selected project and
what they cost, as estimated from token counts.

## What's tracked

Every AI call an edge function makes for the project (diagnosis, fixes, reviews,
judging and the rest) is written to the `llm_invocations` table with the function and
stage, the primary and used model, whether a fallback ran, status, latency, input and
output tokens, cache tokens, the prompt version, which key paid (`key_source`), and
`cost_usd`, an estimate from the model's price list.

---

## Tabs

- **Overview**: a **Daily spend** chart, a budget forecast, and **Compare to plan usage**
  (a link to Billing)
- **Breakdown**: cost **By operation** and **By model**
- **Raw log**: the **Invocation log**, one row per call

---

## Controlling costs

| Lever | Where to set it |
|-------|----------------|
| **Monthly AI budget** | Settings → General → Spend limits, or the budget card on the Overview tab (team owners and admins). Generation calls stop for the rest of the month once spend reaches it; embeddings count toward it but are not blocked |
| **Auto-fix limits** | Settings → General → Spend limits: spend per 30 days, automatic fixes per day, and an approval threshold |
| **Improvement run size** | Each run on [Improvement runs](/admin/iterate) sets its own iteration target |

## Spend credits

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/credits

---
title: Spend credits
description: Spend credits lists expiring Cursor and Firecrawl credits and every way Mushi Mushi can spend them fixing bugs, improving apps with skills and checking sites.
---

# Spend credits

**Route:** `/credits` (sidebar: More pages → Account → Spend credits)

Cursor and Firecrawl credits that lapse at the end of a period are worth more spent on your apps. This page shows when each key's credits expire and lists every place Mushi Mushi can spend them, with a switch for each. The full form behind each switch stays where it was (Settings → AI keys, Settings → Web tools, Inventory → Discovery); this page answers one question: is anything spending them, and on what?

## Cursor: fix bugs

Each Cursor key shows its hint, label and expiry ("expires Oct 28 (6 days)").

- **Fix open bugs before the credits expire** turns [spend-down](../concepts/agent-pr-review#spend-down-and-its-safety-stop) on or off for that key. While it is on, Mushi sends your best open reports to Cursor on its own, inside each app's auto-fix limits, and every fix opens a draft pull request. The switch is off until the key has an expiry date; set it in Settings → AI keys. A key your organization shares can be changed by an owner or admin, and someone else's universal key only by its owner.
- When every app has nothing left to send, the row says so. Watching more of your live sites (below) is the way to find more.
- **Review follow-ups** sends a pull request the Opus review marked "fix first" back to a new Cursor agent with the review's findings, at most twice per pull request and never on a "hold". The line names the model each round uses; when a **Last round model** is set in Settings → AI keys, the second round, which only happens after the first did not satisfy the reviewer, runs on it (for example Opus while the first stays on Grok).

## Cursor: improve your apps with skills

A **skill run** applies one skill from your synced skills catalog to one part of one app, for a few rounds, on that app's own Cursor key. Pick:

- **App** and **Skill**: only skills whose result an agent can measure and that need no product decision are offered, such as accessibility, layouts at every width, loading/empty/error states, page UX, readability, forms, native feel, one design system, translations, SEO, performance, bundle size, error handling, dead code, unit tests and the parked-work register (BACKLOG.md, measured by what it adds and closes). Under the picker, the page says what each round measures.
- **What to work on**: a part of the app, such as "the /settings pages", "the checkout flow" or "src/components/cards". A run never works outside it.
- **Rounds at most** (1 to 5) and **Merge each round when Opus approves and CI passes** (on by default).
- **Run on**, when you have a [local worker](pipeline#workers) lane for the app in fix or skill mode: Cursor in the cloud, or that lane on your machine. A round for a lane waits in its queue and never goes to the cloud.

Each round is a report that spend-down sends to Cursor with the skill's instructions. The agent measures first, makes the changes in that part only, and opens a pull request with the numbers before and after. Opus reviews it like any fix. With merging on, an approved round goes into the [merge queue](fixes#merge-when-ready), and the next round builds on what merged. A run ends when the agent finds nothing left to change or after its last round. It stops when the agent says the rest needs your decision, when you dismiss a round, or when you press **Stop**. Each app can have up to 5 runs going.

## Firecrawl: find bugs on your live sites

The first line is the Firecrawl balance and when it resets. Unused credits do not roll over. The next line is the pace: what the site watches use a day, what that comes to before the reset, and what would go unused at that pace.

Each app has a row:

- **Watch the live site daily** turns its [live-site watch](./inventory) on or off. Turning it on uses the address shown, the app's suggested address, or one you type, at 25 pages a check. Turning it off asks first, then deletes the Firecrawl monitor; reports it already filed stay.
- **Watch up to 100 pages** appears when a watch reads fewer pages than one check allows.
- An app with no Firecrawl key it can use says so. Add a key, or share yours with all your apps, in Settings → Web tools.

A broken page becomes a bug report only after a second check confirms it, and spend-down can then send it to Cursor.

### Site audit

Under each app's watch, **Audit links, accessibility and translations** turns its [site audit](https://github.com/kensaurus/mushi-mushi/blob/master/docs/adr/0040-site-audit-deterministic-live-site-checks.md) on or off. It starts weekly and reads up to 200 pages. While it is on, **Daily**, **Every 3 days** or **Weekly** sets how often it runs (a schedule outside those three stays shown), and the page menu sets how many pages a run reads: 50, 100, 200, 500, or the limit already saved. One Firecrawl credit a page; the row shows that cost. The first run starts within the hour. Mushi maps the live site, reads every page under its address up to that limit, and checks:

- links to the site's own pages, to other sites and to images that are 404, 410, 5xx or unreachable (a 401, 403 or 429 is often a bot wall and does not count; Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X and calendar links are skipped);
- pages with no title, meta description or ``;
- on `/th`, `/zh`, `/en` … pages: a title or description in another language, another locale's text in the page, and links that drop the visitor's language;
- images without alt text.

Each failing rule files one report listing the pages and evidence, with how to check it is fixed, and spend-down can send it to Cursor. While that report is open, later runs refresh it instead of filing again; a report you dismiss is not filed again; a fixed one that fails again files a new report. **Run now** starts a run (3 an hour per app). The row shows the last run: pages read, rules failing and reports filed.

### Search rank

Each app can also track where it ranks in web search for the words its users would type. **Add keywords** opens a box: one query per line, at most 10, with `@JP`, `@TH` … at the end for another country (US by default). Mushi looks for the app's watched or audited address in the top 20 results, once a week per keyword (about 4 Firecrawl credits each), and **Check now** reads them straight away (3 an hour). Each keyword shows its position, the change since the last check ("#2 (was #5)"), or "not in the top 20"; hover it to see the leading sites. It is a visibility number for you and files no reports.

## Where the fixes go

Fixes these levers open are on [Fixes](./fixes). The **Opus: merge** filter there lists the open pull requests the Opus review already said to merge.

## Home

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/dashboard

---
title: Home
description: Home in the Mushi Mushi console shows how one app is doing: is it up, what needs you, what is shipping, which pages have bugs and who can reach it.
---

# Home

**Route:** `/dashboard` (sidebar: **Home**, first tab **Today**)

> **Scenario:** You open Mushi Mushi in the morning and want to know in 30 seconds whether
> your app is up, whether anything broke overnight, and what needs you today.

Home is one page per app. It answers five questions without opening any other page:
is the app up, what needs me, what is shipping, which pages have bugs, and who can
reach it. Every number links to the list it counts. A part that is not connected yet
is grey and its button says how to connect it; a part whose read failed says
"Could not read" instead of showing a 0.

All of it comes from one call, `GET /v1/admin/projects/:id/home`.

Home has more tabs beside **Today**: **Overview** ([all apps](/admin/overview),
`?view=apps`), **User activity** ([sessions](/admin/activity), `?view=users`),
**Users & funnels** (`?view=funnels`) and **Weekly insights**
([intelligence reports](/admin/intelligence), `?view=insights`). The old paths
`/overview`, `/activity`, `/analytics` and `/intelligence` open these tabs. This page
describes **Today**.

---

## App card

A screenshot of your live site, the app's name and address, its platforms (Web, iOS,
Android) and the version Mushi last saw deployed.

- The screenshot is taken with **your own Firecrawl key** (Settings → Web tools);
  Mushi never uses its own key for it. It is stored privately and shown through a
  link that expires after an hour.
- While the [live-site watch](/admin/credits) is on, Home takes a new screenshot
  once a week when you open it. **Refresh picture** takes one now (once every
  10 minutes per app; viewers do not see the button).
- Without a screenshot the card shows the app's store icon, then its site icon, then
  its initials, and says what is missing ("Add a Firecrawl key…").

## Health lights

Four lights, each with a word beside its colour:

| Light | Green | Amber | Red | Not connected |
|-------|-------|-------|-----|---------------|
| **Site up** | No broken pages | Last check failed, not checked for 3 days, or pages answer slower than 3 s | Pages the watch confirmed broken | Turn on the live-site watch |
| **Errors today** | New reports today (UTC), none critical | At least 5 new and double yesterday | Any critical report | Install the SDK |
| **SDK sending** | Your app checked in today | Quiet for 1–7 days | Silent for over a week | Create a key and add the SDK |
| **CI on main** | The latest run on your default branch passed | The test machine stopped (not a code failure) | A check failed | Connect your repo |

Click a light to open where its number came from (broken pages, the report list,
[SDK health](/admin/sdk-health), [CI](/admin/ci)).

## Needs you

At most five things, most costly first, each one sentence and one button: a broken
live site, critical bugs waiting for a fix, fixes Opus put on hold, CI failing on main,
an app that stopped sending, stuck fixes in the [pipeline](/admin/pipeline) (agent
failed, approved but not queued, red release train), and an SDK update. Pipeline
items use the same groups and counts the Pipeline page shows, so the click lands on
the same number. When nothing needs you, it says so.

While a setup step is still open, the setup card above Home names the step and its fix.

## Release

- **Stations:** fix ready → CI → in train → merged → deployed, with the number of
  fixes at each and how many are stuck. Same stages as [Pipeline](/admin/pipeline).
- **Train and deploy:** the release train on the tracks (or the last one) and the
  version last seen live ([Releases](/admin/releases)).
- **Bugs waiting:** one bar split by severity (critical, high, medium, low, not
  rated yet). Each colour opens the open bugs of that severity.

## Pages

A small map of your busiest pages: visits in the last 7 days (from the SDK's session
tracker), bug reports in the last 14 days, and pages the live-site watch found broken.
Page ids (`/lessons/42`) are grouped as `/lessons/:id`. With no visits, reports or
site checks yet, it says what fills it.

## Access and details

Your repo and default branch, the people on the app, the SDK version you run against
the latest one, your keys (label and last use only, never the key itself), and links
to Fix history, User activity and, on plans that include it, the [Audit log](/admin/audit).

## This week vs last week

Bug reports, critical bugs, fixes merged and (with session tracking) user visits, this
week against last week. The change is green when it moved the right way for that row
(fewer bugs, more fixes).

## Recent activity

What happened, grouped into plain sentences: "3 fixes merged today", "12 bug reports
came in this week", "2 deploys seen this week, latest v1.4.0".

## How this works

What Mushi does with a bug in four steps. Open by default only on a new app with no
reports yet.

---

## Common tasks

### Morning check (1 minute)
1. All four lights green? Move on.
2. Clear **Needs you** from the top.
3. Glance at **Bugs waiting**: any red (critical)?

### After a deploy
1. Check the version on the app card and under **Release** matches what you shipped.
2. Watch **Errors today** and **CI on main** for the next hour.

---

A confetti burst and toast appear the first time a fix-worker PR is merged for your
project: the "first merged fix" milestone.

## Design system

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/design

---
title: Design system
description: The Design system page in Mushi Mushi shows tokens, contrast pairs, type scale and a deviance score for off-token code. Token and rule edits open a draft PR.
---

# Design system

**Route:** `/design`

The Design system page in Mushi Mushi reads the token files `mushi.recipe.json` points at and shows them for the active project. It is the design plane of the [app recipe](/concepts/app-recipe). With no project selected, the page asks you to switch to one.

**App blueprint** in the header opens `/recipe`. **Tokens** and **Directions** switch the view. Directions is `?view=directions`.

With no token files read yet, the page is one step: point Mushi at the files where your colours, spacing and fonts live (**Show me how** opens the recipe-file guide).

## Tokens

A status chip (OK, Needs attention, Not checked yet, Not set up, or Check failed) sits with the reason and where the snapshot came from: repo files, a CI push, derived data, or a connector, plus the short commit when one is recorded. When the scan is OK but the token files have issues, the chip reads Needs attention and the reason counts those issues. A failed refresh or scan is printed under the chip.

Under it, **Your colours** shows the colour tokens as swatches and **Drift from your design** draws the deviance score over time (lower is better; unscored checks are left out).

When the project has more than one token set, a switch lists them and marks the active set from `mushi.recipe.json`. The view then shows:

| Section | What you see |
| --- | --- |
| **Token issues** | Severity, message, and file or token path. Empty: "No token issues in this set." |
| **Drift from your design** | The deviance score, a per-rule breakdown, a trend, the top findings, and **Check for drift**. |
| **Contrast** | An "Aa" sample for each declared pair, the ratio, the minimum it needs, and Pass, Fail, or Not judged. |
| **When the score is too high** | A 0–100 threshold and two switches, off until an owner or admin turns them on. |
| **Token catalogue** | Closed until the edit queue has an edit. Swatches, Latin and Thai type samples, spacing bars, radius boxes, motion values, and other tokens. Filter by name. The first 12 tokens in a section, then **View all**. **Edit** queues a new value. |
| **CSS variables by scope** | One column per `:root`, `@theme`, or declared selector, when the API sends scopes. |
| **Components** | Name and file for each primitive matched from the recipe's component globs. |
| **Drift rules** | Enabled, severity (`info`, `warn`, `error`), allowed values, skipped-file globs, and whether the rule is from `mushi.recipe.json` or a Mushi default. |

If editing is off, the page says so and gives the reason. The two switches under **When the score is too high** are **Fail mushi recipe check --push above the threshold** and **Dispatch a fix for new drift above the threshold**. When dispatch is on and Autofix is off for the project, a warning says nothing will be dispatched until Autofix is on. Its spend and per-day caps apply.

## The deviance score

The score is a whole number from 0 to 100. **0** means the scanned code follows the design tokens. **100** means it does not. The card reads "/ 100 · lower is better." Beside it: Pass, Warn, Fail, Scan error, or Running; when the scan finished; the short commit; files and lines scanned; and findings stored. A partial scan says the file or size cap stopped it early, so the score covers only the files scanned.

**Not scored** means no scan has run, the scan is still running, the scan matched no files, or no enabled rule had anything to judge. The trend chart leaves unscored runs out. Density in the breakdown is findings per 1,000 scanned lines. For contrast, density is the failing share of pairs. Each finding names the rule, file, line, the value, and a suggested token when the scan has one.

**Check for drift** refreshes the tokens, then scans the repo in the background. The page polls until the scan finishes and reloads.

## How an edit becomes a draft PR

Token edits and rule edits share one path: preview the diff, then confirm. Owners and admins of the project's team open the pull request. The preview stays available so you can share it with one of them.

1. On a token, choose **Edit**, set the value (a colour token also has a picker), and **Add to queue**. **Queued token edits** lists each path and its new value. **Remove** and **Clear queue** drop edits. For a rule, change its row and choose **Propose rules change**. Only the fields you changed are sent. Rules live in `mushi.recipe.json`.
2. The preview shows each file, its additions and deletions, the unified diff, and any path left out, with the reason. The page says nothing is written yet.
3. **Open draft PR** sends that same diff. The page then links **Draft PR #N** on its branch. The pull request stays a draft, so CI does not run until you mark it ready. If the server returns no pull request, the page says none was opened. **Discard preview** throws the diff away. **Done** closes the result, and clears a token queue once a pull request is open.

**Directions** draws every art direction side by side from its own tokens: palette, computed contrast, type, a phone mock, assets, and deviance. Only the active direction is scanned. **Set active direction** and **Duplicate / edit direction** (a new folder name, an optional display name, and optional colour edits on the copy) use the same preview and draft PR. With no art directions, the view says none were found.

## Related

- [App recipe](/concepts/app-recipe) — token files, contrast pairs, and deviance rules (`/docs/concepts/app-recipe`)

## Docs bridge

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/docs-bridge

---
title: Docs bridge
description: The docs bridge is the Mushi Mushi console's sign-in relay that lets the docs site sync your migration checklist progress, after you click Allow.
---

# Docs bridge

**Route:** `/docs-bridge`

The docs bridge is a sign-in relay between the Mushi Mushi console and the documentation
site (`kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs`). The docs use it to sync your migration checklist
progress (the Migration Hub) with your account, without asking you to sign in again.

You will never navigate here directly. The docs site opens `/docs-bridge` in a popup,
you confirm, the bridge posts a short-lived token back, and the popup closes.

---

## How it works

1. The docs site opens `kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/admin/docs-bridge?nonce=<one-time-nonce>&returnOrigin=<docs-origin>` as a popup.
2. If you are not signed in to the console, you go through the login page first and
   come back here.
3. The bridge checks that `nonce` is present and that `returnOrigin` is on the allowlist.
4. It asks: **Sign in to the docs as** *your email*? Nothing is sent until you click
   **Allow**. **Cancel** sends nothing.
5. After **Allow**, it reads your current session and posts a message to the opener at the
   exact `returnOrigin` (never `*`). The message holds the short-lived access token (never
   the refresh token), its expiry, your email, the active project and organization, and the
   API URL.
6. The popup closes itself 500 ms later. The docs site checks the origin, nonce and
   message type, then keeps the token in `sessionStorage`, so the docs session ends with
   the tab.

---

## Status messages

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **Connecting your Mushi account to the docs…** | Reading the session |
| **Docs sign-in** | Waiting for you to click **Allow** or **Cancel** |
| **Cancelled** | You clicked Cancel; the docs did not get your sign-in |
| **Docs sync connected** | Token posted; your checklist progress will sync |
| Sign in first | No session in this browser; sign in to the console, then reopen from the docs |
| Missing nonce | The `?nonce=` parameter was absent; close the window and try again from the docs |
| Not on the allowlist | `returnOrigin` is not an allowed docs origin; this is a safety check |
| Can't talk back | The opener window is gone; reopen the bridge from the docs site |

---

## Security

- `returnOrigin` must be on the allowlist (`VITE_DOCS_ORIGIN_ALLOWLIST` on self-hosted
  consoles). Local docs origins are allowed only when the console itself runs locally.
- Nothing is posted without an explicit **Allow** click.
- The `nonce` is a one-time value from the docs site, sent back unchanged so the docs can
  match the reply to its request.
- Only the short-lived access token is forwarded, never the refresh token.

---

- [Manage apps](/admin/projects): if you need a persistent API key for scripts or CI, generate one there instead
- [Editor agents](/admin/mcp): for AI assistant integrations that need API access

## Schema changes

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/drift

---
title: Schema changes
description: The Schema changes view in Mushi Mushi compares API routes, app map and database tables with the last scan, showing what changed and what may break a caller.
---

# Schema changes

**Route:** `/health?view=schema` (**Mushi health → Schema changes**). The old `/drift` link
redirects there. Until October 2026 this was its own page, called Drift scanner.

**First on the page:** one sentence on what changed since the baseline, with
**Review changes** when any wait. Once scanned, **Changes found per day** draws the
changes over time with a dashed line per release and a dot on each day with a serious
change (red while one is open). Never scanned: one **Run first scan** step and nothing
else.

> **Scenario:** You shipped a refactor last Friday. It's Monday and a screen that calls
> your API shows nothing. You suspect a route was renamed or a handler was removed. You
> run a scan and see which routes no longer line up.

Each scan in Mushi Mushi builds a fresh **contract snapshot** from three sources, then
compares them with each other:

- your **OpenAPI spec**, if you set its URL for the project
- the **API calls in your app map** (inventory `api_dep` nodes)
- your **database schema**, from the latest backend schema snapshot

A source that is not set up is reported as not configured, not as "no changes". There
is no scheduled scan: scans run when you start one.

---

## When to run it

- **After every deploy**, especially refactors, route changes or renamed handlers.
- **Before an improvement run**, to confirm there is no regression before the loop starts.
- **When reports spike**: a broken screen often matches a finding you haven't seen yet.

---

## Tab: Run a scan

Enter **Max paths to walk** (a whole number from 10 to 1000; the field starts at 200)
and click **Run scan**.

When it completes, a **Scan complete** box shows:
- **discovered**: how many findings the scan produced
- **new stored**: how many were stored. A finding already stored with the same type,
  surface and path in the last 24 hours is not stored again.
- **snapshot**: the ID of the contract snapshot the scan used

### If the scan fails

The error names the step that failed (for example the snapshot builder could not read
your OpenAPI spec). Fix that source and run the scan again.

---

## Tab: Changes

Your list of findings. The summary counts at the top are **Changes to review**,
**Serious**, **Warnings** and **Scans**.

Each row shows **Severity**, **Surface** (`api` or `inventory`), **Path**, **Message**
and when it was **Found**. Today's scan writes four kinds of finding:

| Type | Severity | Meaning |
|------|----------|---------|
| `missing_inventory` | warn | The OpenAPI spec defines a route that your app map does not have |
| `dead_handler` | warn | A route in your app map has no handler function |
| `undocumented_route` | info | Your app map has a route that the OpenAPI spec does not list |
| `unmapped_route` | info | A route has no obvious database table behind it |

Click a row to open the detail drawer with:
- The **Expected** and **Actual** values
- **→ Lesson** (shown on findings marked critical only): turns the finding into a candidate
  lesson, reviewed under [Lessons](/admin/lessons)
- **Dismiss**: marks a known or intentional change. Mushi then checks that route less often.

### What to do with a finding

1. Open it and read Expected against Actual.
2. Intentional (you renamed the route on purpose)? **Dismiss** it.
3. A regression? Fix the route or the spec, or start a fix from [Fixes](/admin/fixes),
   then scan again.

---

## Tab: Scans

The last 20 contract snapshots, each with its ID, edge count and time. Use it to see
when the baseline last changed.

---

## Common tasks

### Post-deploy check (the fast path)
1. Open the **Run a scan** tab and click **Run scan**.
2. Open **Changes**. No new warnings? Carry on.
3. A warning? Open it, compare Expected and Actual, then dismiss or fix.

### Investigating a screen that stopped loading
1. Run a scan with a higher max paths, such as 500.
2. In **Changes**, look for `dead_handler` or `missing_inventory` findings on the route
   the screen calls.
3. If the route was removed by mistake, start a fix.

---

## API

```bash
POST /v1/admin/drift/scan             { "project_id": "<pid>", "max_paths": 50 }
GET  /v1/admin/drift?project_id=<pid>&limit=100
GET  /v1/admin/drift/snapshots?project_id=<pid>
PATCH /v1/admin/drift/<id>            { "status": "dismissed" }
POST  /v1/admin/drift/<id>/create-lesson
```

- [Lessons](/admin/lessons) — where a promoted finding goes

## Experiments

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/experiments

---
title: Experiments
description: The Experiments page in the Mushi Mushi console defines and runs A/B tests on your app and analyses them with CUPED variance reduction and sequential testing.
---

# Experiments

**Route:** `/experiments` (a Lab: under **More pages** in the sidebar unless you keep it there)

The Experiments page in Mushi Mushi lets you define A/B tests, launch them, collect results, and run
statistical analysis (CUPED variance reduction + mSPRT sequential testing) to determine
a winner without a fixed sample size.

---

## Tabs

The tabs are **Summary**, **Experiments** and **New**. The summary counts include
**Total**, **Running**, **Ready to launch** and **Winners**.

### Experiments

The experiments table shows:

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Name** | Experiment label |
| **Status** | `Draft`, `Running`, `Stopped` or `Completed` |
| **Variants** | Count of configured variants |
| **Split** | **Shifts to winner** when bandit mode is on, otherwise **Even split** |
| **Created** | Timestamp |

**Actions:** **Launch** (draft) and **Stop** (running). Click a row to open the drawer.

### New

Create a new experiment, then click **Create experiment**:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Name** | Short experiment label (required) |
| **Hypothesis** | What you expect to observe and why |
| **Send more users to the version that is winning** | Bandit mode: Thompson Sampling moves traffic toward better-performing variants |
| **Variants** | A name and a **Weight (0–1)** for each. Two to start; **+ Add variant** adds more. |

---

## Experiment detail drawer

Opens when you click a row. Shows:
- Status, **Shifts to winner** and **Winner found** badges
- **Hypothesis** text
- **Variants** list — each with traffic weight, Thompson Sampling α/β parameters, and a **winner** highlight if analysis identified it
- **Launch** / **Stop** / **Analyze** buttons, **Add variant**, and **Delete draft** for a draft

### Analysis results

Click **Analyze** to run the statistical analysis. Results show:
- **SRM check** — sample ratio mismatch detector (flags if traffic split is off)
- **p-value** — classical significance
- **mSPRT log-LR** — sequential test log-likelihood ratio (valid at any sample size)
- **Relative lift** — % improvement vs. control
- **Recommendation** — plain-English verdict
- **Per-variant stats table** — conversions, exposures, rate

mSPRT (mixture Sequential Probability Ratio Test) lets you analyze results at any
time — you don't need to pre-commit to a sample size. This prevents the "peeking problem"
common in fixed-horizon tests.

---

## Bandit mode (Thompson Sampling)

When bandit mode is enabled, traffic weights are updated continuously based on observed
performance. The `α` (successes + 1) and `β` (failures + 1) parameters for each variant
are shown in the experiment drawer. Better-performing variants receive more traffic
automatically.

---

## API

```bash
# List experiments
GET /v1/admin/experiments?project_id=<pid>

# Create
POST /v1/admin/experiments
{ "name": "...", "hypothesis": "...", "bandit_enabled": false, "project_id": "<pid>" }

# Add a variant
POST /v1/admin/experiments/<id>/variants
{ "name": "Variant B", "traffic_weight": 0.5 }

# Launch / Stop
POST /v1/admin/experiments/<id>/launch
POST /v1/admin/experiments/<id>/stop

# Analyze
POST /v1/admin/experiments/<id>/analyze
```

---

## Related pages

- [Unusual spikes](/admin/anomalies) — detect metric shifts caused by experiment variants
- [AI prompts](/admin/prompt-lab) — A/B test the prompts behind Mushi Mushi's own AI steps (a separate feature)

## Code map

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/explore

---
title: Code map
description: The Code map page in the Mushi Mushi console is a visual, searchable map of your indexed source files, with architectural layers, imports and search by meaning.
---

# Code map

**Route:** `/explore` (sidebar: More pages → Fix → Code map; also called Codebase Atlas. It is a Lab: switch it on under **Settings → Display & sidebar → Labs** to keep it in the sidebar)

The Code map page in Mushi Mushi turns the raw indexed source files into a visual, navigable map of how your project is architecturally structured. It is the fastest way to answer "where does X live?", "what imports what?", and "which layer handles this concern?" — without opening your editor.

  **Prerequisite:** Most of the page requires codebase indexing. **Copy digest** and **Map → Diagram** only need a connected GitHub repo. Turn indexing on in the **Codebase indexing** card on [Integrations](/admin/integrations) (`/integrations/config`), or upload a local folder with `mushi index `. The hourly sweep fills the index in batches up to your plan's file limit (see [below](#how-much-of-a-large-repo-is-indexed)).

---

## Tab groups

The page has five groups (URL `?tab=`):

| Group | Views | Purpose |
|------|------|---------|
| **Summary** | Summary | Index health, file counts, last index attempt and error |
| **Understand** | Ask · Tour · Domains · Knowledge | Chat with citations, guided walkthrough, business domains, wiki/docs knowledge merged into Ask |
| **Map** | Graph · Layers · Diagram | Visual architecture map and an AI architecture diagram (detailed below) |
| **Search** | Search | Semantic search (detailed below) |
| **Index** | Index | Indexer debug: repo, webhook, embedding coverage, last error |

MCP equivalents: `ask_codebase`, `get_file_summary`, `get_codebase_tour`, `search_codebase`, `get_codebase_domains`, `analyze_codebase_impact`, `analyze_wiki_knowledge`, `get_repo_digest` (on the default feature set; needs no index).

---

## Copy digest

**Copy digest** (top of the page) copies your repo as one paste for an AI chat or coding agent: the folder tree plus the most useful files, in this order — README, manifests (`package.json`, …), entry points, source, then tests. Pick a size first; the digest stops at that many tokens (an estimate: characters ÷ 4) and says what it left out.

- It reads GitHub at one commit and names the commit, so the paste matches a real version of your code.
- Real env files (`.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.production`), private keys and similar files are never included. Env templates such as `.env.example` are included, because they explain the setup. Any file that looks like it holds a secret, templates too, is replaced with a notice.
- On a bug report, **Copy code for this bug** puts the bug's files first: files from its stack trace, files earlier fixes changed, related code from the index, then the files that import them.

The same digest is the MCP tool `get_repo_digest`, on the default tool set.

---

## Map views

### Diagram

An AI drawing of the main parts of your app and how they connect. Mushi reads the repo on GitHub at the latest commit and asks the AI for the parts, their folders or files, and the links between them. Then Mushi checks every path against the real repo: a path that does not exist is removed and the part is marked, so a made-up file never becomes a link.

- **Draw diagram** costs one AI call. Diagrams are stored per commit and never redrawn on their own, not even on a push: that would spend an AI call on commits that change nothing, and a public page must only show what you previewed. **Update to latest commit** draws only when there is a new commit; **Redraw** asks the AI again.
- Click a part to read what it does and open its folder or file on GitHub at that commit.
- Badges on each part count its open bug reports and its code findings from the last 30 days. Click the part to list them: reports open their detail page, findings open the file and line on GitHub. A report lands on a part through its stack trace or the files its fixes changed; reports and findings in files no part covers are counted under the diagram.
- **Public page** (optional, owner or admin): share the diagram at `kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/r//`. The preview shows exactly what becomes public: part names, descriptions and paths, never file contents. A private repo needs you to tick a consent box first. The page shows the commit it was drawn from, keeps showing that drawing until you publish again, and **Unpublish** removes it. Visitors can report a wrong or unwanted diagram privately: the report goes to Mushi's own inbox, never to a public issue. Once live, the card gives you a README badge to copy and a Markdown copy of the page for AI agents. Search engines index the page.
- **From your editor:** the MCP tool `get_repo_diagram` returns the latest diagram; pass `overlay: true` to also get the open reports and findings on each part. It reads the stored drawing and never draws a new one.
- **With an API key:** the preview, publish and unpublish routes take a key with `mcp:read` (preview) or `mcp:write` (publish, unpublish) as well as the console session. A key can publish a public repo's diagram. A private repo's diagram can only be published from the console, because the consent box is a person reading the preview.

### Graph

A ReactFlow canvas laid out in deterministic swimlane columns (one column per architectural layer), with every file as a node coloured by layer. Nodes are freely draggable within the canvas:

| Layer | Colour | What lands here |
|-------|--------|-----------------|
| UI | Blue | `app/`, `pages/`, `components/`, `.tsx` / `.jsx` files |
| Library | Green | `lib/`, `utils/`, `hooks/`, `shared/`, `common/` |
| Backend | Red/Amber | `server/`, `api/`, `supabase/functions/`, `routes/` |
| Tests | Purple | `tests/`, `__tests__/`, `.test.ts`, `.spec.ts` files |
| Config | Muted blue | `config/`, `.github/`, `.json`, `.yaml`, `.toml` files |
| Other | Grey | Everything else |

Each node chip shows:
- **Left accent bar** in the layer colour
- **Filename** truncated to fit
- **File extension badge** (`.tsx`, `.ts`, `.py`, …)
- **Directory context** (last two path segments) below the filename

Import edges are drawn as directed arrows. Hover a node for its full path tooltip. Click a node to open the **detail panel** on the right.

**Controls:**
- Drag — pan the canvas
- Scroll — zoom in/out
- Layer legend (bottom-left) — expands to show counts and a proportional fill bar per layer
- File/edge counter badge (top-left)
- Zoom in / Zoom out / Fit view (bottom-right)

### Layers

A horizontal Sankey flow that groups files left-to-right: **UI → Library → Backend → Tests → Config → Other**.

Each column shows:
- Layer name and file count in the layer's colour
- A proportional fill bar (wider = more files relative to the largest column)
- **Hub node** — the file with the highest import degree in that column (most-imported or most-importing)
- File cards with filename, `.ext` badge, and line count

Import edges are drawn as bezier curves with directional arrows between columns. This makes cross-layer dependencies immediately obvious.

Click any file card to open the detail panel below the lane.

### Search

Semantic search over vector embeddings. Type a natural-language description of what you're looking for — the search finds the most relevant files and symbols ranked by cosine similarity.

**Layer filter tabs** appear after a search to narrow results to a single architectural layer (e.g. "Tests only" or "Backend only"). Click the layer chip, or click **All** to clear the filter.

Each result shows:
- Symbol or filename in monospace
- Layer badge
- File path
- A **colour-coded similarity bar** (green ≥ 70%, amber ≥ 50%, red below 50%)
- Content preview (first 240 characters of the indexed content)

Click a result to open the detail panel. Click the panel's **View in graph** button to switch to Graph view with that file selected.

---

## The detail panel

Clicking any node (in any view) opens a detail panel with:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| Layer badge | Architectural layer with colour highlight |
| Extension badge | File type (`.tsx`, `.ts`, `.py`, …) |
| Line count | Total lines in the file or symbol |
| Filename / Symbol name | Large heading |
| File path | Full path with **Copy** button |
| Language | Detected language from the indexer |
| Lines | Start–end line range |
| Node type | `code_file` or `code_symbol` |
| Preview | Content with line numbers, starting from `line_start` |
| View in graph | Switches to the Graph tab with this file selected |
| Bug reports | Opens `/reports?component=` to see Mushi reports filed against this file |

---

## Layer filter chips

The **Filter:** row above Map views lets you narrow Graph, Layers, and Search simultaneously. Click `64 Tests` and the graph shows only test nodes and their inter-test edges, the Layers lane collapses to just the Tests column, and Search results are pre-scoped to Tests.

Click the chip again (or **Clear**) to restore the full view.

---

## Node and edge counter

Above the graph, a counter such as `64/115 nodes · 80/210 edges` shows how many nodes and edges the current filters leave visible, out of the total.

---

## Density toggle

Switch between **Files** (one node per file) and **Symbols** (one node per exported function, class, or constant). Symbol mode gives a much denser graph suited for large codebases where you want to trace a specific function's callers.

---

## Indexing

### Turn on indexing for the connected repo

On [Integrations](/admin/integrations) (`/integrations/config`), the **Codebase indexing** card turns indexing on for the app's GitHub repo and starts a sweep at once. With the Mushi GitHub App installed, each `push` re-indexes the changed files.

### Or upload a local folder

For a private repo the GitHub App cannot read, install the CLI and upload a folder:

```bash
npm install -g @mushi-mushi/cli
mushi index ./src            # add --dry-run to list files first
```

`mushi index ` uses the project and key saved by `mushi login` / `mushi init`, walks the folder (skipping `node_modules`, `.git`, `dist`, `build`, `.next`, `.turbo` and `coverage`), and uploads `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.js`, `.jsx`, `.py`, `.go` and `.rs` files under 500 KB. `--language ts` limits it to one language.

Connected with a Personal Access Token instead of the App? Add a repo webhook in GitHub (**Settings → Webhooks**). Point it at the URL the Codebase indexing card shows (your API endpoint plus `/v1/webhooks/github`). Use content type `application/json` and the webhook secret the card revealed, and tick **Pushes** and **Check runs**. Each push to the default branch then re-indexes the changed files.

### How much of a large repo is indexed

Your plan sets how many files the index may hold: 300 on the free plan, and more on paid plans. The hourly sweep fetches files in batches, starting with the files named in open error stack traces and your application source. It keeps going until the whole repo or the plan limit is covered.

The Codebase indexing card shows coverage in files, for example `1,500 of 4,700 files`, in one of four states:

- **all**: every indexable file is in the index.
- **still filling**: later sweeps will add more files.
- **plan limit**: the limit is reached. Diagnoses and fixes only see the indexed files. A path filter limits the sweep, and the count, to the directories that matter.
- **stuck**: the last sweep could not add a file, for example because GitHub kept refusing a file or the embedding API kept rejecting it. The card shows the error. The sweep retries daily instead of hourly.

The path filter is the repo's `path_globs`, the same globs the fix worker uses to pick its target files. They limit indexing too: a sweep indexes only matching files, and removes files a narrowed filter no longer matches from the index (unless the project indexes more than one repo, since they share one index). `**/` also matches the repo root, so `**/*.ts` includes `index.ts` and `src/**/*.ts` includes `src/a.ts`. If you set globs on a repo only to route fixes, check that they cover the code you want diagnoses to see.

"Last sweep" counts partial sweeps too. A partial sweep is never shown as a complete index. Pushes count against the plan limit as well: a push re-indexes files already in the index, and adds new files only while the index is under the limit.

  The sweep reads files from GitHub, so only committed files are indexed. To keep generated or vendored folders out, set the repo's path filter (**Path filter (advanced, optional)** on the Codebase indexing card).

---

## What the search understands

The semantic search uses the same embeddings that power RAG-augmented bug review and fix suggestions. It understands:

- **Concepts**: "authentication and session handling", "rate limiting", "error boundary"
- **Patterns**: "component that wraps children with a loading state", "hook that fetches paginated data"
- **Behaviour**: "where payment processing happens", "what sends the push notification"
- **Cross-language**: works across TypeScript, Python, Go, Swift, Kotlin, and any other language with indexed content

It does **not** understand:

- Exact symbol names (use your editor's Go-to-symbol for that)
- Regex or glob patterns
- File system structure queries ("all files in `src/screens/`") — use the Graph or Layers view instead

---

## API reference

The Explore page is backed by two project-scoped REST endpoints:

### `GET /v1/admin/projects/:id/codebase/explore`

Returns the full graph payload.

**Query parameters:**

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `symbols` | `0` \| `1` | When `1`, returns symbol-level nodes instead of file-level |

**Response:**

```jsonc
{
  "nodes": [
    {
      "id": "uuid",
      "node_type": "code_file",
      "label": "auth-guard.tsx",
      "metadata": {
        "file_path": "components/auth-guard.tsx",
        "symbol_name": null,
        "signature": null,
        "line_start": 1,
        "line_end": 142,
        "language": "tsx",
        "layer": "ui",
        "content_preview": "export function AuthGuard({ children, ..."
      }
    }
  ],
  "edges": [
    {
      "id": "uuid",
      "source_node_id": "uuid",
      "target_node_id": "uuid",
      "edge_type": "imports",
      "weight": 1
    }
  ],
  "layers": { "ui": 12, "lib": 3, "test": 64, "other": 36 },
  "total_files": 115
}
```

### `POST /v1/admin/projects/:id/codebase/search`

Semantic search over vector embeddings.

**Body:**

```jsonc
{
  "query": "authentication logic",
  "k": 20
}
```

**Response:**

```jsonc
{
  "results": [
    {
      "id": "uuid",
      "file_path": "components/auth-guard.tsx",
      "symbol_name": "AuthGuard",
      "signature": null,
      "line_start": 1,
      "line_end": 142,
      "content_preview": "export function AuthGuard...",
      "layer": "ui",
      "similarity": 0.87
    }
  ],
  "query": "authentication logic"
}
```

Similarity scores range from 0 to 1. Scores above 0.7 are usually highly relevant. Below 0.3 is coincidental overlap.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---------|-------------|-----|
| "Codebase not indexed yet" | No files in `project_codebase_files` | Turn on the Codebase indexing card, or run `mushi index ` |
| Most files show as "Other" | Files are in non-standard directories | Narrow the repo's path filter to your source folders; re-index |
| 0 import edges | Project uses only path aliases (`@/`, `~/`) | Import edges only resolve relative imports; switch to Symbols view for finer granularity |
| Search returns no results | Missing OpenAI key for embeddings | **Settings → AI keys** → add an OpenAI key |
| Slow graph render | Very large project (1,000+ files) | Use layer filter chips to scope down, or switch to Layers view |

## Fine-tuning

Source: https://kensaur.us/mushi-mushi/docs/admin/fine-tuning

---
title: Fine-tuning
description: Fine-tuning jobs in Mushi Mushi export classified reports, train a small OpenAI or Bedrock model, validate it, and swap it in for the fast filter or diagnosis.
---

# Fine-tuning

**Where:** **AI prompts** (`/prompt-lab`) → **Advanced: fine-tuning & synthetic** →
**Fine-tuning jobs**. The old `/fine-tuning` link redirects to `/prompt-lab`; there is no
separate Fine-tuning page any more.

A fine-tuning job in Mushi Mushi exports your project's classified reports, trains a
fine-tuned model with a vendor, checks it against recent reports, and, if you promote it,
makes it the model for one classification step.

---

## Start a job

Click **New job** and choose:

| Field | Options |
| ----- | ------- |
| **Vendor / base model** | **OpenAI — gpt-4o-mini (self-service)**, the default, or **Bedrock — Claude 3 Haiku (requires AWS setup)** |
| **Promote to stage** | `stage1` (fast filter) or `stage2` (diagnosis). Type it exactly. |

Bedrock training is off unless the server sets `MUSHI_BEDROCK_FINETUNE_ENABLED=1` and
`BEDROCK_OUTPUT_S3_URI`, and the project has AWS credentials as a BYOK key.

---

## Job steps

Each job row has a button for its next step:

1. **Export training samples.** Mushi gathers classified reports from the job's time
   window with a confidence of at least 0.85 (the default), skipping dismissed reports.
   When the job asks for judge-confirmed labels only, it keeps reports the grader agreed
   with.
2. **Upload and start training.** The samples go to the vendor and a training job starts.
3. **Check status.** Asks the vendor whether training has finished. OpenAI can also
   report back through a webhook.
4. **Validate.** Runs the model on up to 500 recent classified reports. It passes when
   accuracy is at least 85%, the drift score is at most 0.25, and no training data leaked
   into the check.
5. **Promote.** Only a validated job can be promoted. It sets the project's fine-tuned
   model for the chosen stage (`stage1` or `stage2`) and writes an audit event.

**Reject** asks for a short reason (at least 4 characters) and records it. **Delete**
removes the job.

The table shows **Status**, **Model**, **Promote to**, **Samples**, **Accuracy**,
**Created** and the actions.

---

- [AI prompts](/admin/prompt-lab) — where this card lives, and where you A/B test prompts
- [Triage grading](/admin/judge) — the grader whose verdicts can filter training samples
- [Concepts → Judge & self-improvement](/concepts/judge-loop) — how grading and prompts fit together
